question: What does it mean for a sequence of messages to be suitable in concurrent composition?
answer: A sequence of messages is suitable if each message is either identical creation queries or query-index pairs with valid indices, and if certain conditions regarding creation queries and query spaces are met.

evidence.text:
# 4. Concurrent Composition of Continual Mechanisms 

Composition of NIMs. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{N}_{i}$ be an NIM with input domain $\mathcal{X}_{i}$, and let $\sim_{i}$ be a neighboring relation on $\mathcal{X}_{i}$. The composition of the NIMs $\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}$ is represented by a non-interactive mechanism $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ with the domain $\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_{k}$. This mechanism takes a tuple of datasets $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ as input and returns

$$
\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right](x)=\left(\mathcal{N}_{1}\left(x_{1}\right), \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\left(x_{k}\right)\right)
$$

Define $\sim$ as a neighboring relation on $\mathcal{X}$, where two tuples $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ and $x^{\prime}=\left(x_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, x_{k}^{\prime}\right)$ satisfy $x \sim x^{\prime}$ if and only if $x_{i} \sim_{i} x_{i}^{\prime}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq k$. The composition of NIMs $\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}$ is said to be $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP if the non-interactive mechanism $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim$ (see Definition 2.2).

In the proofs of this section, we consider $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ not as a non-interactive, but instead as an interactive mechanism with initial state space $\mathcal{X}$ that receives $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ not as input, but instead as its first message. Immediately after receiving this message it executes $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ on its initial state and returns its output. Upon receiving a second message, this interactive mechanism halts the communication.
Concurrent Composition of IMs. Vadhan and Wang [20] extended the definition of the composition of NIMs to the concurrent composition of IMs, where an adversary interacts with $k$ interactive mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ at the same time. In concurrent composition, the adversary generates a message and determines the receiver of this message (one of the $\mathcal{M}_{i} \mathrm{~s}$ ) adaptively based on all the previous messages exchanged between the adversary and the mechanisms $M_{1}, \ldots, M_{k}$. To

formalize this, Vadhan and Wang [20] introduced an interactive mechanism ConComp[ $\left.\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$, which internally runs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and, upon receiving a message $(q, j)$, forwards the query $q$ to $\mathcal{M}_{j}$ and returns its response.

The initial state space of $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ is $S_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\text {init }} \times \cdots \times S_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}^{\text {init }}$, where $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}$ is the initial state space of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$. Let $\sim_{i}$ be a neighboring relation on each $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}$, and define the neighboring relation $\sim$ on $S_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\text {init }} \times \cdots \times S_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}^{\text {init }}$ as follows: for any two initial states $s=\left(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{k}\right)$ and $s^{\prime}=\left(s_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, s_{k}^{\prime}\right)$, we have $s \sim s^{\prime}$ if and only if $s_{i} \sim_{i} s_{i}^{\prime}$ for every $i \in[k]$.

Vadhan and Wang [20] show that if each IM $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\epsilon_{i}$-DP w.r.t $\sim_{i}$, and if the composition of NIMs $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, 0}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, 0}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against an adaptive adversary. Lyu [18] extends this result for $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP IMs.

In the concurrent composition of IMs, queries asked to each mechanism are chosen adaptively, not only based on that mechanism's previous responses but also using the responses of the other mechanisms up to that point. The results of [20] and [18] show that this concurrency and additional adaptivity do not compromise privacy guarantees. As a result, all $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP composition theorems for NIMs, such as the basic [6], advanced [9], and optimal [15] composition theorems, can also be applied to the concurrent composition of IMs.
Concurrent Composition of CMs. We extend the definition of the concurrent composition for IMs to the concurrent composition of CMs, where an adversary can create new CMs or ask pairs of queries from the existing ones. Depending on the type of composition, the created mechanisms are constrained, and the sequence of query pairs asked from each CM satisfies certain properties. Based on a secret bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, each CM either receives the first element of every query pair asked from it or the second element. In Section 4.1, we generalize ConComp to ExtConComp and give a formal definition for the concurrent composition of CMs.

To extend Lyu's result on the privacy guarantee of the concurrent composition of IMs to the concurrent composition of CMs, we want to use the following intermediate lemma from their paper: For every $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP interactive mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ and any pair of neighboring initial states $s$ and $s^{\prime}$ for $\mathcal{M}$, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{P}$ such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the IMs $\mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}(b)$ are equivalent. However, as we discuss in Section 4.2, there are hidden assumptions in the proof of this lemma. Additionally, we show there that the construction of $\mathcal{P}$ in [20], for $\epsilon_{i}$-DP IMs, satisfies a property, required for a later proof.

In Section 4.3, we analyze the privacy of the concurrent composition of $k$ fixed $\mathrm{CMs} \mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. In this composition, the adversary first creates the mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and then asks pairs of queries from each mechanism, ensuring that the sequence of query pairs for each mechanism is valid. In Section 4.4, we extend this composition by fixing $k$ privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$ and allowing the adversary to adaptively choose the $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ over time.
4.1. Formalization. We extend the definition of ConComp in [20] and introduce ExtConComp that allows the creation of new mechanisms in addition to queries to existing ones. A creation query $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$ is a message that requests the creation of a continual mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ with the initial state $s$ and asserts that $\mathcal{M}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. the verification function $f$. The mechanism ExtConComp accepts creation queries and messages of the form $(q, i)$, where $q$ is a query for the $i$-th created mechanism. The formal definition of ExtConComp is as follows:
Definition 4.1. Extended concurrent composition, ExtConComp, is a continual mechanism that receives two types of messages:

- A creation query $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, where $\mathcal{M}$ is a CM with a single initial state $s$ that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$, and
- a query-index pair $(q, i)$, where $i$ is a positive integer, and $q$ is any message.

Upon receiving $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, ExtConComp creates an instance of $\mathcal{M}$ with the initial state $s$, and when receiving $(q, i)$, it forwards $q$ to the $i$-th created mechanism and returns its response. If less than

$i$ mechanisms have been created, ExtConComp halts the communication. The state of ExtConComp is a sequence of pairs $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}^{\prime}\right)$, where the $i$-th pair represents the $i$-th created mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ and its current state $s_{i}^{\prime}$. The single initial state space of ExtConComp is the empty sequence () . Both query set and answer set of ExtConComp are the universal message set $\mathcal{U}$ in Remark 3.4.

To define DP for the extended concurrent composition, we must impose constraints on the created mechanisms and their query pairs to limit the adversary's power. We force a set of constraints using a verifier $\mathcal{V}[f]$, where $f$ is a verification function returning $\perp$ whenever the adversary misbehaves. We define variants of the concurrent composition of CMs by choosing different verification functions $f$ :

Definition 4.2. For any verification function $f$, the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs is the interactive mechanism $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp.

Differential privacy for the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs follows the standard definition for IMs:

Definition 4.3 (DP for $f$-Concurrent Composition of CMs). For a verification function $f$ and privacy parameter $\epsilon \geq 0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries if the interactive mechanism $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim_{01}$. Equivalently, this holds if the continual mechanism ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$ against adaptive adversaries.

Although verification functions $f$ for ExtConComp vary for different compositions, they must all ensure that the format of the adversary's messages is compatible with $\mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp. An adversary is expected to either create a new CM or send a pair of queries to an existing one. The creation of a new mechanism is independent of the initial state of $\mathcal{I}$. Thus, when requesting the creation of a new mechanism, the adversary must send a pair of identical creation queries to $\mathcal{V}[f]$. Moreover, due to the definition of $\mathcal{I}$ and ExtConComp, to request asking one of the queries $q_{0}$ and $q_{1}$ from the $i$-th created mechanism according to $\mathcal{I}$ 's initial state, the adversary must send the message $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right)$ to $\mathcal{V}[f]$.

Next, we formalize these shared constraints by defining suitable message sequences. Later, when defining specific verification functions $f$ for different concurrent compositions, we set $f\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}\right)=$ $\perp$ whenever the sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is not suitable.
Definition 4.4 (Suitable Sequence of Messages). A sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is suitable if for every $1 \leq j \leq k$, (i) $m_{j}$ is of the form $\left(m_{j}^{0}, m_{j}^{1}\right)$, where $m_{j}^{0}$ and $m_{j}^{1}$ are either identical creation queries or messages of the forms $\left(q_{0}, \ell\right)$ and $\left(q_{1}, \ell\right)$ with the same index $\ell$; (ii) for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, if $m_{j}^{b}=(q, \ell)$, then there are at least $\ell$ creation queries in the sequence $m_{1}^{b}, \ldots, m_{j-1}^{b}$; (iii) for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, if $m_{j}^{b}=(q, \ell)$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\ell}$ is the $\ell$-th mechanism requested to be created in $m_{1}^{b}, \ldots, m_{j-1}^{b}$, then $q$ is in the query space of $\mathcal{M}_{\ell}$, i.e., $q \in Q_{\mathcal{M}_{\ell}}$; and (iv) if $m_{j}^{0}=m_{j}^{1}=(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, then $\mathcal{M}$ is a CM with a single initial state $s$, and it is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$.
4.2. $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP IMs and $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$. Lyu [18] shows that for every $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP IM $\mathcal{M}$ and every pair of neighboring initial states $s_{0}$ and $s_{1}$, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ (with a single initial state) such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{b}\right)$ are identical. Vadhan and Wang [20] show the same result in the special case where $\delta=0$.

Although not explicitly stated, the constructions of $\mathcal{T}$ proposed in both [18] and [20] require the answer distributions of $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{0}\right)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{1}\right)$ to be discrete. This assumption is formally defined as:
Definition 4.5. An IM $\mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions if $A_{\mathcal{M}}$ is countable, and for every initial state $s$, integer $t \in \mathbb{N}$, history $\left(q_{1}, a_{1}, \ldots, q_{t-1}, a_{t-1}\right) \in\left(Q_{\mathcal{M}} \times A_{\mathcal{M}}\right)^{t-1}$, and new query $q_{t} \in Q_{\mathcal{M}}$, the distribution of $\mathcal{M}(s)$ 's answer in respond to $q_{t}$ conditioned on having the history $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, a_{t-1}\right)$ has a probability mass function (PMF).

This is generally not a restrictive assumption in differential privacy. In practice, the binary nature of computers and the fact that the total number of memory bits in the world is finite ensure that every distribution sampled computationally is inherently discrete. Theoretically, when dealing with real-valued outputs, one can enforce discrete answer distributions by rounding each output to the nearest multiple of a sufficiently small constant $\alpha$. This discretization post-processing preserves the privacy of the mechanism and has a negligible effect on the accuracy. An example of this approach will be provided in Section 7.

Lyu [18] additionally assumes that there exists a pre-fixed upper bound $c$ on the number of queries $\mathcal{M}$ answers. In Appendix A, we will modify their proof to remove this additional assumption. Let $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ be a continual mechanism that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. By Corollary 3.8, $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ is an IM that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim_{01}$. Replacing $\mathcal{M}$ in Lemma A. 1 with $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, we get:

Lemma 4.6 ([18]). For $\epsilon>0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be a CM that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. Suppose $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions and responds to at most $c$ queries. Then, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ with a single initial state () such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the IMs $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ are equivalent.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an IM that is $\epsilon$-DP w.r.t. a neighbor relation $\sim$. For every pair of neighboring initial states $s_{0}$ and $s_{1}$, Vadhan and Wang [20] construct an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ (with a single initial state) such that for each bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{b}\right)$ are identical. Appendix B, we will review their construction and show that for any query sequence $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$, if the distributions of the $t$ answers of $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{0}\right)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{1}\right)$ to the queries $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$ are identical, then $\mathcal{T}$ does not need to know the output of $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ in the first $t$ steps. This observation allows us to delay the interaction of $\mathcal{T}$ and $\operatorname{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ as much as possible.

Let $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, where $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ is an $\epsilon$-DP CM w.r.t. $f$. By definition, upon receiving a query sequence $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$ where each $q_{j}=\left(q_{j}^{\prime}, q_{j}^{\prime}\right)$ is a pair of identical queries, $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(0) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(1) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ have the same answer distribution, implying the following lemma:

Lemma 4.7 ([20]). For $\epsilon \geq 0$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be a CM that is $\epsilon$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. Suppose $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions. Then, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ with a single initial state () such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$,

- the IMs $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ are equivalent, and
- as long as $\mathcal{T}$ receives pairs of identical queries, it does not interact with $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$.

Remark 4.8. Since $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$ is a NIM, in both Lemma 4.6 and Lemma 4.7, the IPM $\mathcal{T}$ interacts with $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$ at most once.
4.3. Concurrent Composition of CMs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ be a CM with the initial state space $S_{i}=\left\{s_{i}\right\}$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$, and $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ has discrete answer distributions. In the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$, an adversary is restricted to the following steps: (1) It first creates the fixed mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and (2) then adaptively issues pairs of queries for them such that the sequences of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $f_{i}$-valid. Note that creating the $\mathrm{CM} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ means creating an instance of $\mathcal{M}_{i}\left(s_{i}\right)$, where $s_{i}$ is the unique initial state of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$. Based on a secret bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, each CM either receives the first element of every query pair addressed to it or the second element, and the adversary tries to guess $b$ using the answers of all $k$ mechanisms.

To formalize this type of concurrent composition of CMs, we introduce the verification function $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$. Intuitively, this verification function enforces that the adversary creates the mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ in their first $k$ messages and then only sends messages containing pairs of queries for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ s. Additionally, it ensures that the sequence of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $f_{i}$-valid. The formal definition of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ is as follows:

Definition 4.9 $\left(f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}\right)$. For $i \in[k]$, let $\alpha_{i}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$ denote a creation query. For any input sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$, the outcome of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ returns $\top$ if and only if all of the following conditions hold:
(i) The sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is suitable. For $j \in[t]$, let $m_{j}=\left(m_{j}^{0}, m_{j}^{1}\right)$.
(ii) For $j \leq \min \{t, k\}$, the messages $m_{j}^{0}=m_{j}^{1}=\alpha_{j}$.
(iii) For $i \in[k]$, the sequence of $\left(q^{0}, q^{1}\right)$ s in the messages of the form $\left(\left(q^{0}, i\right),\left(q^{1}, i\right)\right)$ is $f_{i}$-valid.

With the above definition of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$, we refer to the $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$-concurrent composition of CMs as the concurrent composition of the continual mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. Therefore, the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries if ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ against adaptive adversaries.

Recall that in Section 3, we generalized the notion of neighboring relations for interactive mechanisms to verification functions for continual mechanisms. The neighboring initial states for an interactive mechanism are chosen non-adaptively at initialization. However, the choice of messages forming a valid sequence w.r.t. a verification function is adaptive and happens over time. That is, an adversary generates two different query sequences for a CM, and the choice of differing sequences is made adaptively throughout the interaction.

In the concurrent composition of IMs, queries to each mechanism are chosen adaptively, not only based on that mechanism's previous responses but also using the responses of the other mechanisms up to that point. By definition, the choice of neighboring initial states for the interactive mechanisms is non-adaptive. However, in the concurrent composition of CMs, the choice of differences between query sequences, i.e., the neighboring query sequences is adaptive, based on not only the responses of the corresponding mechanism but also the responses of other mechanisms. (Note that, unlike IMs, CMs inherently have a single fixed initial state; hence, no choice of initial state is involved.) Despite this additional adaptivity, in the following theorem, we show that the privacy results of [18] for $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ also hold for $\mathcal{V}\left[f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp.

Theorem 4.10. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ be a continual mechanism with initial state space $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}=\left\{s_{i}\right\}$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$ against adaptive adversaries, and $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ has discrete answer distributions. For $\epsilon>0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, if the composition of non-interactive mechanisms $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries.

Proof. Let $\alpha_{i}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$ for each $i \in[k]$, and let $f$ denote $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ for simplicity. Our goal is to show that ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$. To prove so, we construct an IPM $\mathcal{P}$ with a single initial state and show that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent.

Since $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P}$ is an IPM with a single initial state, Lemma 2.15 implies that if $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$ DP. Hence, for any adversary $\mathcal{A}$, the views of $\mathcal{A}$ when interacting with the mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((0)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((1)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are $(\epsilon, \delta)$-indistinguishable. As we will show below, by construction, these views are identical to those obtained by interacting with the original mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp, implying that the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP.

In $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp, when $\mathcal{I}(b)$ receives pairs of identical creation queries from $\mathcal{V}[f]$, it forwards one of them to ExtConComp, which then creates an instance of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns $\top$. Subsequently, when $\mathcal{I}(b)$ receives two queries for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$, it forwards them to $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ through ExtConComp and returns its response. This procedure can be equivalently represented by an IM $\operatorname{IECC}(b)$ as follows: when receiving pairs of identical creation queries from $\mathcal{V}[f], \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ creates an instance of $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns $\top$. Subsequently, when receiving $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right)$, it forwards $\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)$ to $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns its response. By definition of $f$ and $\mathcal{I}$, the mechanisms

$\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ are equivalent. Next, we define $\mathcal{P}$ explicitly and show $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*}$ Comp $\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ be the IPM for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ given by Lemma 4.6, and let $t_{i}$ be its single initial state. The initial state of $\mathcal{P}$ is a pair of empty sequences. Let $\left(\sigma_{1}, \sigma_{2}\right)$ denote the state of $\mathcal{P}$. When receiving the first left message, $\mathcal{P}$ interacts with its right mechanism, Comp $\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$, and sets $\sigma_{1}$ to its output sequence $\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{k}\right) . \mathcal{P}$ never interacts with its right mechanism again.

Upon receiving a left message $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)^{2}, \mathcal{P}$ adds $\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}, t_{i}\right)$ to $\sigma_{2}$ and returns $\top$. Moreover, upon receiving a left message $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right), \mathcal{P}$ sends $\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)$ as a left message to $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ and returns its response. If $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ requests a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}, \mathcal{P}$ provides it with the previously stored sample $r_{i}$. Formally, $\mathcal{P}$ executes $\left(t_{i}, v, m\right) \leftarrow \mathcal{T}_{i}\left(t_{i}, \mathrm{~L},\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)\right)$ and as long as $v=\mathrm{R}$, it runs $\left(t_{i}, v, m\right) \leftarrow \mathcal{T}_{i}\left(t_{i}, v, r_{i}\right)$. Once $v=\mathrm{L}, \mathcal{P}$ returns the message $m$ to $\mathcal{V}[f]$. (By Remark 4.8, $v=\mathrm{R}$ at most once.) By Lemma 4.6, each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$, provided with the sample $r_{i}$ from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$, simulates $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ identically. Hence, by definition of IECC and $\mathcal{P}$, the mechanisms $\operatorname{IECC}(b)$ and $\mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent, finishing the proof.
4.4. Concurrent Composition of CMs with Fixed Parameters. The concurrent composition of CMs with fixed parameters generalizes the concurrent composition of fixed CMs by allowing the adversary to select the CMs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ adaptively over time, instead of forcing them to create a fixed set of mechanisms in their first $k$ messages. Each selected mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ must be $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$, where the multiset of privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$ is fixed in advance, but the verification functions $f_{i}$ are chosen by the adversary. Note that this implies that at most $k$ continual mechanism are created by the adversary. Moreover, due to the aforementioned technical reasons, each $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ must have discrete answer distributions.

For instance, an adversary may first create a continual mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ that is $\left(\epsilon_{3}, \delta_{3}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{3}$. Then, after interacting with $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ for some time and analyzing its responses, the adversary may then select a mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ from the class of $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right)$-DP CMs. Similar to the concurrent composition of fixed CMs, the adversary's sequence of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ must be $f_{i}$-valid.

To formally define this composition, we introduce a verification function, $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ as follows:
Definition 4.11 $\left(f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right)$. For any input sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$, the function $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ returns $\top$ if and only if all of the following conditions hold:
(i) The sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$ is suitable.
(ii) There are at most $k$ pairs of identical creation queries in the sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$. Let $\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\prime}$ denote the $i$-th created mechanism and $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ and $f_{i}^{\prime}$ be its privacy parameters and verification function, respectively. $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}^{\prime}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}^{\prime}$ has discrete answer distributions. Moreover, the multiset of the privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ of the created mechanisms is a sub-multiset of the fixed privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$. Note that $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ is adaptively chosen by the adversary, while $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$ is a predetermined publicly-known parameter.
(iii) For each $i \in[k]$, the sequence of $\left(q^{0}, q^{1}\right)$ s in the messages of the form $\left(\left(q^{0}, i\right),\left(q^{1}, i\right)\right)$ is $f_{i}^{\prime}$-valid.

We refer to the $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$-concurrent composition of CMs as the concurrent composition of CMs with privacy parameters $\left(\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)\right)_{i=1}^{k}$. A slight adaptation of the proof of Theorem 4.10 implies the following theorem.

Theorem 4.12. For $\epsilon, \epsilon_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}>0$ and $0 \leq \delta, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \delta_{k} \leq 1$, if the composition of non-interactive mechanisms $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then the concurrent composition of $k$ CMs with the privacy parameters $\left(\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)\right)_{i=1}^{k}$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries.

Proof. The proof is identical to the proof of Theorem 4.10 with the following modification in the construction of $\mathcal{P}$ : Recall that $\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{k}\right)$ denotes the output of $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$. In the proof of Theorem 4.10, the $i$-th creation query was known to be $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$. Consequently, $\mathcal{T}_{i}$

expected $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$ as its right mechanism, and when $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ needed a response from its right mechanism, $\mathcal{P}$ sent $r_{i}$ to it. However, in the concurrent composition with fixed parameters, the IPM requesting the sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$ need not necessarily be $\mathcal{T}_{i}$. To handle this, we modify $\mathcal{P}$ so that it maps each output sample $r_{i}$ to the appropriate IPM $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ needing a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$.

Let $\left(\mathcal{M}_{j}^{\prime}, s_{j}^{\prime}, \epsilon_{j}^{\prime}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}, f_{j}^{\prime}\right)^{2}$ denote the $j$-th pair of identical creation queries received by $\mathcal{P}$ from the verifier, and let $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ be the corresponding IPM given by Lemma 4.6. When $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ requests a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{j}^{\prime}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}}, \mathcal{P}$ iterates over $\sigma_{1}$ to find the smallest $i^{*} \in[k]$ such that the $i^{*}$-th element of $\sigma_{1}$ is not null and $\epsilon_{j}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{i^{*}}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}=\delta_{i^{*}}$. After sending $r_{i^{*}}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{j}, \mathcal{P}$ updates $\sigma_{1}$ and sets $r_{i}$ to null. This adjustment ensures that even when there are duplicate privacy parameters among $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$, each sample $r_{i}$ is sent to at most one $\mathcal{T}_{j}$. Note that by the definition of $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}, i^{*}$ always exists.

question: How do diagrammatic categories contribute to understanding exotic subfactors?
answer: Diagrammatic categories provide visual tools that simplify complex mathematical concepts, making it easier to explore conjectures about semisimplifications at roots of unity. This contributes significantly to understanding exotic subfactors in mathematical physics by offering new perspectives on their interactions.

6.5.4. Symmetric trivalent ribbon categories. We can combine previous results to get the following, essentially due to Cvitanović [Cvi08].

Proposition 6.91. Suppose that $(C, X, \tau)$ is a symmetric trivalent ribbon category with $\operatorname{dim} C(4) \leq$ 5 and $\operatorname{dim} X=d$. Then after rescaling the self-duality appropriately one of the following holds for the symmetrically self-dual object $X$ with multiplication defined by $\tau$ :

- $X$ is an Sym-algebra object, and hence $1 \oplus X$ is a normalized commutative Frobenius algebra object in the additive completion of $C$.
- $X$ is a G2-algebra object, and hence $1 \oplus X$ is a Hurwitz algebra object in the additive completion of $C$.
- $X$ is an F4-algebra object, and hence $1 \oplus X$ is a cubic Cayley-Hamilton fordan algebra object in the additive completion of $C$.
- $X$ is a Lie algebra object satisfying the classical Exceptional relations.

Proof. By Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 3.5, we satisfy (QEJac- $\alpha$ ) for some $v, \alpha$. Since $C$ is symmetric, looking at the trivalent twist we see $v^{6}= \pm 1$, and hence $v$ is a 12 th root of unity. If $v= \pm 1$ then $X$ is a Lie algebra object satisfying the classical Exceptional relations by Corollary 6.83. If $v$ is a third or sixth root of unity then $X$ is a G2-algebra object by Proposition 6.85. If $v$ is a primitive 4th root of unity and $b+[3] \alpha \neq 0$ then $X$ is an $F 4$-algebra object by Proposition 6.87. If $v$ is a primitive 4 th root of unity and $b+[3] \alpha=0$ then by Lemma $6.89, X$ is again an $F 4$-algebra object (using for the first time that $C$ is symmetric in addition to $v^{12}=1$ ).

The only remaining case is where $v$ is a primitive 12th root of unity. Then (QECross- $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) implies

$$
1+\frac{b}{d-1}(-\frac{b}{d-1}=0
$$

This relation together with symmetry implies that $X$ is an Sym-algebra object.
Note that the symmetric assumption was essential in the case where $v$ is a primitive 12th root of unity, see Remark 6.75 for more details.

Remark 6.92. The above cases are not mutually exclusive. Indeed both $\operatorname{Rep}\left(S_{3}\right)$ and $(\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)$, $V_{1}^{-}$) appear in both the $F 4$ and $\operatorname{Sym}(t)$ families, and $S O(3)$ appears in both the G2 and Exceptional families. In these overlapping cases some care must be taken in applying the above result, because the appropriate rescaling of $\tau$ might be different in the two families! This occurs in the case $\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)$ where the Frobenius algebra structure from Remark 6.26 and the cubic CayleyHamilton Jordan algebra structure from Example 6.61 are not isomorphic.

Remark 6.93. Proposition 6.91 can be proved more directly. In a symmetric ribbon category the symmetric group $S_{n}$ acts on $C(n)$. Since symmetric group representations are easier to study than braid group representations this can be analyzed directly. First, $C(3)$ is 1-dimensional so $S_{3}$ either acts by the trivial or sign representation. Since $\operatorname{dim} C(4) \leq 5$, the six diagrams
![img-74.jpeg](img-74.jpeg)
span a representation of $S_{4}$ of dimension at most 5 . It is easy to see what 6 -dimensional representation of $S_{4}$ these six diagrams span: the first three span the induced representation of the trivial representation of the group $G=(\mathbb{Z} / 2)^{2} \rtimes \mathbb{Z} / 2$ while the latter three span the induced representation from a certain 1-dimensional representation of $G$ which depends on the twist. Then we can directly analyze all possible quotients of these two specific 6 -dimensional representations of $S_{4}$.

Corollary 6.94. Suppose that $G$ is a compact Lie group of non-zero dimension, and $X$ is a non-trivial symmetrically self-dual irrep $G$ of dimension $d$ with $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Hom}\left(X^{\otimes 3}, 1\right)=1$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Hom}\left(X^{\otimes 4}, 1\right) \leq$ 5. Then one of the following holds:

- The map $X \otimes X \rightarrow X$ is anti-symmetric, and $X \cong \mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra with a compatible G-action.
- The map $X \otimes X \rightarrow X$ is anti-symmetric, and $X$ is not the adjoint representation, in which case there's a Hurwitz algebra $A \cong 1 \oplus X$ with a compatible $G$-action.
- The map $X \otimes X \rightarrow X$ is symmetric, in which case there's a cubic Cayley-Hamilton Jordan algebra $A \cong 1 \oplus X$ with a compatible $G$-action.

Proof. This follows from Proposition 6.91, except that in the case where the multiplication is commutative, we need to rule out the possibility that $1 \oplus X$ is a commutative Frobenius algebra object. In this case we would have a functor $\operatorname{Sym}(t) \rightarrow \operatorname{Rep}(G)$, and since the latter is unitary, this functor factors through the quotient by negligible morphisms. Hence we get a functor $\operatorname{Rep}\left(S_{n}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Rep}(G)$ for some $n$, from which it follows that $G$ is a subgroup of $S_{n}$ which contradicts the assumption on $\operatorname{dim} G$.

An interesting corollary here is that there must be some cubic Cayley-Hamilton algebra attached to each Lie group in the $F 4$ family. We already explicitly identified these algebras, so this doesn't provide any new results, but it explains why we got lucky and were able to find such Jordan algebras.
6.6. Specializations to exceptional Lie algebras. Suppose that $V$ is a self-dual representation of a quantum group ribbon category such that there's a unique map $V \otimes V \rightarrow V$ and such that $V \otimes V$ has no more than 5 distinct summands all of which are multiplicity free. Then Theorems 1 and 2 apply, and some instance of the quantum exceptional relations must hold. In this section we explicitly identify a number of quantum group categories as quotients of the quantum exceptional series following this outline.

We begin by proving classical specialization, following [EN19, Thm. 2.1], [Kup96, Thm. 5.1], and [GSZ23, Thm. 5.3].
Definition 6.95. We say that a simple Lie (super)algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is an Exceptional Lie algebra if it appears in Table 7, an expanded version of Table 1 (excluding the trivial group). We let $\lambda=-6 / h^{\vee}$ where $h^{\vee}$ is the dual Coxeter number. For the Lie algebras in the table (excluding $\mathfrak{o s p}(1 \mid 2)$ ), let $\mathfrak{f}$ denote the compact form of $\mathfrak{g}$ and consider the group $G_{\mathfrak{f}}=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{f})$ of Lie algebra automorphisms. Explicitly, this is the semidirect product of the adjoint form of the compact Lie group $K$ attached to $\mathfrak{f}$ by the group of Dynkin diagram automorphisms. Since the group of Dynkin diagrams automorphisms is discrete, the Lie algebra of $G_{\mathfrak{f}}$ is $\mathfrak{f}$. See Table 7 for more details about the values of $\lambda$, the groups, and the representations. As in $\S 2.2, \Delta$ is the ratio of the squared length of the long roots to the squared length of the short roots.

Recall that the Killing form (and hence any of the other normalizations we use for the inner product) restricted to $\mathfrak{f}$ is negative definite, and that any automorphism of $\mathfrak{f}$ automatically preserves the Killing form since it is defined by a matrix trace of compositions of brackets. Hence the construction of $G_{\mathfrak{f}}$ from $\mathfrak{f}$ follows exactly the procedure from $\S 6.1$.

Here $\mathfrak{o s p}(1 \mid 2)$ uses notation from $\S 2.5 .2$, and for other groups fundamental weights are ordered as they are in KM's quantum groups Mathematica package [Mor06]. In each case the representation is the adjoint representation. Also recall from $\S 2.4$ that we choose $q=q_{S}$ in our quantum group conventions.

Proposition 6.96. Suppose that $\mathfrak{f}$ is the compact form of an Exceptional Lie algebra that is not $\mathfrak{G S p}(1 \mid 2)$. Then there is a full and dominant functor $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda} \rightarrow \operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{\mathfrak{f}}\right)$.

Proof. This is easy to check directly using the skein theoretic description of $S O(3)_{q}$ in the case $\mathfrak{g}=A_{1}$. In all other cases $\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathfrak{g}$ is a sum of 5 distinct simple objects as a representation of $G_{\mathfrak{f}}$ (but not necessarily as a representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ ).

Using the Convenient form, we have that $\mathfrak{g}=V_{\theta}$ is a metric Lie algebra object in $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{\mathfrak{f}}\right)$, and thus takes a functor from the category of Jacobi diagrams $\mathrm{Jac}_{\mathbb{C}, \operatorname{dim}(\mathfrak{g}), 12}$. Thus, by Proposition 6.82, the classical exceptional relation with parameter $\lambda$ holds for some $\lambda$. By Lemma 3.14 we see that $2 \lambda$ and $2(1-\lambda)$ are the unique non-zero eigenvalues of the ladder operator on $\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathfrak{g}$ not coming from the summands $\mathfrak{g}$ or 1 . But, by Corollary 2.9 , the eigenvalue on the summand $V_{2 \theta}$ is $-12 / h^{\vee}$. Thus (by the symmetry exchanging $\lambda$ and $1-\lambda$ ) we may take $\lambda=-6 / h^{\vee}$. Hence the functor descends to one out of $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}$.

This functor is full and dominant by Proposition 6.5 and Remark 6.6.
We expect that Proposition 6.96 also holds for $\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)$ at $\lambda=-4$, but we do not prove that result here since we would need the appropriate version of Tannaka-Krein duality and the right analogue of compactness in the proof of Proposition 6.5.

In particular, the category of representations of the corresponding group on the right of Table 1 is the Cauchy completion of a quotient of $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}$. This result is in the style of the first fundamental theorem of invariant theory; one would also like an explicit characterization of the kernel of this quotient, which we do not have. If $\operatorname{End}(1)=\mathbb{C}$ in $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}$, in particular if Conjecture 1.3 holds, then the kernel of this quotient can be characterized abstractly as the tensor ideal of negligible morphisms.

Now we turn to the quantum version, a more precise version of Proposition 1.16.
Proposition 6.97. With $\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{f}, G_{\mathfrak{f}}, \lambda$, and $\Delta$ from the exceptional family in Table 7, and for $q$ in some dense subset of $\mathbb{C}$ (in the complex topology), there is a full and dominant functor from $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, q^{-\Delta / \lambda}, q^{-\Delta}}$ to the category of representations of $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{\mathfrak{f}}\right)_{q}$.

On the $\mathfrak{a}_{1}$ line, a fractional power of $q$ appears; any root will work, as discussed in $\S 6.3$. There is also a fractional power on the $\mathfrak{a}_{2}$ line, but recall that parameters $(v, w)$ and $(-v, w)$ give the same category.

Proof. First suppose that $G_{\mathrm{t}}$ is not $\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)$. In addition, we have already analyzed the case $G_{\mathrm{t}}$ is $\operatorname{PSU}(2)$ in Lemma 6.66. Otherwise, let $V$ be the adjoint representation of $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{\mathrm{t}}\right)_{q}$, let the trivalent vertex be the deformation of the Lie bracket map $V \otimes V \rightarrow V$, and choose the Convenient normalization. Our main theorem applies, so (QEJac- $\alpha$ ) holds for an appropriate $v$ and $\alpha$. We can compute $v$ directly, as follows. The highest weight vector in the adjoint representation is a long root $\theta$, and thus by $\S 2.4$ and Table 2 the negative trivalent twist is $-v^{6}=-q^{(\theta, \theta+2 \rho)_{S} / 2}=-q^{h^{\vee} \Lambda}=$ $-q^{-6 \Delta / \lambda}$. (We can also double-check this using that the negative crossing acts on the cup by the positive twist, which is $v^{12}=q^{(\theta+2 \rho, \theta)_{S}}=q^{2 h^{\vee} \Lambda}$.) $$
q^{-(\theta, \theta)_{S}}=q^{-2 \Delta}
$$

We would like to apply Lemma 3.12. First we need to verify that $(v, \alpha)$ as $v$ varies does not lie entirely on an excluded line from Lemma 3.12. This can be seen by, for instance, taking the limit of $d$ as $v \rightarrow 1$ : for the excluded lines we get 3 or -2 , which is not $\operatorname{dim} \mathfrak{g}$. Therefore, at all but finitely many values of $q$ we can apply Lemma 3.12, to see that, up to symmetry, we may take $w=q^{-\Delta}$. To see that we can take the correct root of $v^{6}$ and get $v=q^{-\Delta / \lambda}$, look near $q=1$ and use Lemma 3.14 and continuity; see also $\S 4$. This can be easily checked directly using the skein theoretic description of $\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)_{q}$. Alternatively, $\operatorname{SOSp}(1 \mid 2)_{q}$ with its adjoint representation $V_{g}^{*}$ as a tensor generator is isomorphic to $S O(3)_{q}$ with $V_{(4)}$ as a tensor generator, and then the result can be deduced from Proposition 6.100 below.

Note that $\Delta$ appears because we used $q=q_{S}$; the formulas would be slightly nicer if we used $q=q_{L}=w^{-1}$. In addition, note that $v=q_{C}$, the $q$-variable corresponding to the Convenient form.

One can instead argue that a version of the previous result holds over $\mathbb{C}(q)$, but one needs to be a little careful in applying our main theorem since that field is not algebraically closed.

For $q$ in the dense set from Proposition 6.97, as before the category of representations of the corresponding group on the right of Table 1 is the Cauchy completion of a quotient of $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C},-q^{-\Delta / \lambda}, q^{-\Delta}}$. If $\operatorname{End}(1)=\mathbb{C}$ in QExc, in particular if Conjecture 1.14 holds, then the kernel of this quotient can be characterized abstractly as the tensor ideal of negligible morphisms.

In particular, we see that if $\mathfrak{g}$ is Exceptional and not $\mathfrak{a}_{1}$, the braiding on the 4box space of $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{\mathrm{t}}\right)_{q}$ has an eigenvector for the braiding of eigenvalue -1 . question: Are optically selected galaxy catalogs used for tracing galaxy cluster centers over a wide range of redshifts?
answer: Yes, optically selected galaxy catalogs are used for tracing galaxy cluster centers over a wide range of redshifts.

evidence.text:
### 4.3.2. The impact on masking galaxy contribution

As demonstrated in Section 4.2.1, galaxy contributions predominantly influence filament reconstruction, highlighting the crucial role of masking slice selection. We now compare the impact of varying frequency slice numbers on filament reconstruction for two masking scenarios: "Mask MGS" and "Mask All".

As illustrated in Figure 15, the "Mask MGS" case exhibits a moderate decline in signal amplitude and standard deviation with increasing frequency width. Notably, even in the 21-slice case, these values remain significantly higher than the previously estimated average filament signal. In contrast, the "Mask All" scenario reveals a steep downward trend, with signal amplitude and standard deviation dropping from $9.70 \mu \mathrm{~K}$ (1-slice) to $2.76 \mu \mathrm{~K}$ (3-slice), ultimately becoming negligible. This reinforces the notion that faint galaxies, rather than bright MGS-like galaxies, predominantly influence filament signal estimates. It also emphasizes the importance of selecting an appropriate masking frequency width to reduce the contribution of these galaxies. However, achieving this requires a deep galaxy survey that covers the Hi IM region of interest, providing more detailed information about the faint galaxies, including their positions and frequency widths. This goal may be attainable with powerful instruments like the SKA in the future.

Our current pairwise stacking analysis relies on an optically selected galaxy catalog, which is well-suited for tracing galaxy cluster centers over a wide range of redshifts. However, galaxies selected in the radio band are expected to form a distinct sample compared to the optically selected ones. With upcoming large-area deep Hi surveys, an Hi emission line-selected galaxy sample could offer an alternative set of tracers for such analyses. We will explore these possibilities in future work.

question: What is the significance of studying semileptonic decays in heavy baryons?
answer: Studying semileptonic decays in heavy baryons is significant because it provides valuable information about the standard model parameters, such as CKM matrix elements. These studies can also reveal potential new physics effects beyond the standard model if deviations from predictions are observed.

evidence.text:
## I. INTRODUCTION

Probing hadronic structures, as a primary purpose of various experiments and research, can be accomplished by systematic studies of heavy hadrons. Particularly, singly heavy baryons have provoked a great deal of interest. Due to prominent experimental progress, a wide range of these singly heavy baryons have been established in the ground and excited states. The BABAR Collaboration [1] observed the $\Omega_{c}$ [2] and discovered the $\Omega_{c}^{*}$ state [3] in the radiative decay $\Omega_{c}^{0} \gamma$, where the $\Omega_{c}^{0}$ baryon is reconstructed in the decays to the final states $\Omega^{-} \pi^{+}, \Omega^{-} \pi^{+} \pi^{0}, \Omega^{-} \pi^{+} \pi^{-} \pi^{+}$, and $\Xi^{-} K^{-} \pi^{+} \pi^{+}$. $\Xi_{c}(3055)$ and $\Xi_{c}(3123)$ were observed by BABAR Collaboration [4] and extremely narrow states, $\Omega_{c}(3000), \Omega_{c}(3050), \Omega_{c}(3066), \Omega_{c}(3090)$, and $\Omega_{c}(3119)$ observed by LHCb [5]. The Belle Collaboration found evidence for two excited charm-strange baryon states, $\Xi_{c}(2980)$ and $\Xi_{c}(3077)$, decaying strongly to $\Lambda_{c}^{+} K^{0} \pi^{-}$and $\Lambda_{c}^{+} K^{-} \pi^{+}$ [6]. In the bottom sector, $\Xi_{b}^{-}[7,8]$ was observed by D0 [9] and CDF [10] Collaborations. LHCb established $\Lambda_{b}(5912)$ and $\Lambda_{b}(5920)$ in the $\Lambda_{b}^{0} \pi^{+} \pi^{-}$spectrum [11]. It also reported the discovery of the $\Xi_{b}(6327)$ and $\Xi_{b}(6333)$ [12]. The CDF Collaboration presented an observation of four $\Lambda_{b}^{0} \pi^{ \pm}$resonances interpreted as $\Sigma_{b}^{ \pm}$and $\Sigma_{b}^{* \pm}$baryons in the reconstructed decay mode $\Lambda_{b}^{0} \rightarrow \Lambda_{c}^{+} \pi^{-}$, where $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+}$[13].

The study of singly heavy baryons from different aspects, especially decay properties, is of crucial importance. A variety of theoretical investigations into the strong, weak, and radiative decays of the singly heavy baryons can be found in the literature[14-24]. Weak decays of singly heavy baryons receive great concentration since a detailed experimental survey on various weak decay channels can be employed to obtain the standard model (SM) parameters, such as the CKM matrix elements. Any obvious deviation from SM predictions, clarify the feasible existence of new physics effects beyond the standard model (BSM). In particular, the semileptonic weak decays provide us with a lot of useful information, and they have been discussed within several approaches such as the relativistic quark model [25], covariant confined quark model [26], light cone QCD sum rules [27-30], nonrelativistic quark model [31], light front

[^0]
[^0]:    *Electronic address: leila.khajooee@ut.ac.ir
    ${ }^{\dagger}$ Electronic address: kazem.azizi@ut.ac.ir; Corresponding author

quark model [32], and lattice QCD [33]. Most of these studies concentrate on spin $\frac{1}{2} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2} \rightarrow \frac{3}{2}$ transitions, which the total angular momentum of the initial singly heavy baryon is $\frac{1}{2}$.

In this work, we study the semileptonic weak decay of a singly heavy baryon with total angular momentum $J=\frac{3}{2}$, $\Sigma_{b}^{* 0}$, into a singly heavy baryon with $J=\frac{1}{2}, \Sigma_{c}^{+}$, within the three point QCD sum rule method. This approach is a powerful and predictive nonperturbative method in which a hadron-to-hadron transition matrix element is expressed in terms of a correlation function in both hadronic and quark-gluon level. Considering the previous consistent predictions of this method with the experiments, it is found to be a reliable approach and can be employed to determine different hadronic parameters [27, 34-39]. In particular, we consider the $b \rightarrow c$ transition at quark level in semileptonic weak decay $\Sigma_{b}^{* 0} \rightarrow \Sigma_{c}^{+} \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell}$ and compute the responsible form factors and decay widths in three lepton channels.

The structure of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, the construction of the QCD sum rules for corresponding form factors of the $\Sigma_{b}^{* 0} \rightarrow \Sigma_{c}^{+} \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell}$ transition is explained. Numerical results after analyzing the obtained sum rules for transition form factors and fixing the working regions of auxiliary parameters, are exhibited in Sec. III. Utilizing the fit functions of form factors in terms of transferred momentum squared, the decay widths of these processes in all lepton channels are calculated in Sec. IV. Finally, Sec. V is dedicated to the Summary and Conclusion; and some features of the computations are presented in the Appendixes.

question: What conditions lead to synergism in Domar aggregation of productivity shocks?
answer: Synergism in Domar aggregation occurs under specific conditions where sectoral productivity shocks interact positively due to network transformations influenced by substitution elasticities. These conditions allow for enhanced propagation effects that amplify overall economic output beyond simple additive effects.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

The economy-wide production network, i.e., the monetary input-output coefficients, will no longer be stable against the general equilibrium propagation of sectoral productivity shocks, when the substitution elasticities of sectoral production are nonneutral. The associated network transformation hence renders nonlinearity in aggregating sectoral productivity shocks into the economy's output, i.e., Domar aggregation. In this study, we demonstrate the possibility of production networks being transformed into a singular one. We also explore the conditions under which the productivity shocks experience synergism in Domar aggregation.


Keywords Productivity propagation $\cdot$ Elasticity of substitution $\cdot$ Input-output linkages $\cdot$ Singularities $\cdot$ Fallacy of composition

question: In what way does the habit reference point affect financial decision-making under uncertainty?
answer: The habit reference point affects financial decision-making by expanding the perceived loss region as it increases, making agents more loss-averse and altering their austerity thresholds compared to other parameters.

question: Is it necessary to explicitly teach correspondence between genes and proteins to the OmniBioTE model?
answer: No, it is not necessary to explicitly teach correspondence between genes and proteins to the OmniBioTE model.

evidence.text:
### 2.1 Joint Sequence Representations Arise Emergently

We found that it is trivial to learn a low-rank projection that extracts joint features from the OmniBioTE embeddings and readily generalizes in contrast to the single-omic models (Figure 2.a-b). Despite OmniBioTE never being explicitly (or even implicitly) taught a correspondence between genes and their corresponding translated protein sequences, the model naturally learns these associations from the underlying distributions consistent with the central dogma of molecular biology. We hypothesize that this is due to the efficient coding hypothesis [57], where, if $N$ protein sequences and their corresponding genes occur in the same dataset, it is considerably more efficient to memorize one of the modalities and learn the mapping between them, rather than memorize both sequences separately. This property holds at all scales, indicating that multi-omic training robustly learns joint representations for genes and protein sequences, even at low parameter counts.

question: How do sectoral and spatial spillovers affect inter-firm learning about imports?
answer: While sectoral and spatial spillovers exist, the study finds robust evidence of network effects even after accounting for these factors, indicating that direct connections within production networks are crucial for learning about new import opportunities.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

Using administrative data on the universe of inter-firm transactions in Spain, we show that firms learn to import from their domestic suppliers and customers. Our identification strategy exploits the panel structure of the data, the firm-time variation across import origins, and the network structure. We find evidence of both upstream and downstream network effects, even after accounting for sectoral and spatial spillovers. We estimate that an increase of 10 percentage points in the share of suppliers (customers) that are importing from a given region increases the probability of starting importing from that region by $10.7 \%$ (19.2\%). Connections with geographically distant domestic firms provide more useful information to start importing. Larger firms are more responsive to this information but less likely to disseminate it.

question: Does the multi-grid approach depend on specific line shapes?
answer: No, the multi-grid approach does not depend on specific line shapes.

evidence.text:
# 2.4. Interpolation technique for the line-by-line modeling 

Apart from improved algorithmic approaches for the Voigt function, interpolation techniques are essential for speeding-up line-by-line modeling. Notable works in this domain are: Clough, Kneizys, and Davies [30], Edwards [33], West, Crisp, and Chen [34], Gordley, Marshall, and Chu [35], Sparks [36], Fomin [6], Titov and Haus [37], Kuntz and Höpfner [8], Kruglanski and De Maziere [38], and Schreier [39]. The technique proposed by Clough and Kneizys [40] is based on decomposition of line shape into several sub-functions, each estimated on the individual grid. It was used in FASCODE [41] and LBLRTM [3] (based on FASCODE) and later gave an impulse for developing this method further for other line shapes. Unfortunately, this approach lacks flexibility with changing input line shapes because it requires recalculating the sub-functions for each new line shape. To ensure universality, schemes independent on the specific line shape are necessary. The so called multi-grid approach addresses this, by making estimations on a sequence of grids with increasing step sizes regardless of the shape function. The concept behind these algorithm is straightforward: moving away from the center of a spectral line results in the profile becoming progressively smoother, as in the case of a Lorentzian wing, where the profile follows $\sim 1 /\left(\nu-\nu_{0}\right)^{2}$. The line profile is divided into sections corresponding to the number of grids. On the finest grid, the central, sharpest parts of the lines are summed. On the next, coarser grid, the smoother parts adjacent to the center are summed, and so on. Once all parts of the lines have been summed on their respective grids, the discrete functions obtained on these grids are interpolated onto the finest grid, resulting in the desired spectrum. In most studies two or three grids are considered and with different interpolation methods. Adjusting the grid step according to the atmospheric level might be introduced to resolve narrowest lines [42].

We use the multi-grid interpolation technique described by Fomin [6], which was employed in calculation of absorption coefficients by Kuntz and Höpfner [8] and highlighted in several

intercomparison studies [21, 20]. We have confirmed that in presence of large line cut-offs, 2 or 3 grids may not be enough to achieve the desired balance between speed and accuracy. To address this, our scheme employs 11 grids with increasing resolution. Interpolation technique is performed on $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$-length intervals. Number of points in the finest grid is set to $N=20481$ leading to a resolution of $10 /(N-1) \approx 4.88 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$. This is usually sufficient to resolve typical Doppler lines in upper atmosphere in IR-region. The number of points in other grids follow a rule: $N_{i}=10 \cdot 2^{i-1}+1, i=1,10$ which by our experience is sufficient to describe distant line wings with line cut offs up to $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$ and beyond. Resolution of $\sim 5 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$ might be excessive for calculations in the near-IR region. To address this, dynamic or user-controlled resolutions are planned in future releases of MARFA.

Important fact is that the interpolation requires significantly less computational time compared to calculation of line profiles on each grid. Interpolations between coarse and fine grids are performed only once (per subinterval $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$ step) and are independent of the number of lines, making the computation time for spectra logarithmically dependent on the line's half-width. We maintain the ratio of distances between points in adjacent grids during the interpolation process from coarse to fine grids, using a simple polynomial interpolation method. For a more detailed description of the method or interpolation errors, please refer to the original study [6].

question: How does the concept of absolute sensitivity differ from traditional sensitivity analysis in CRNs?
answer: Absolute sensitivity is a basis-independent measure that quantifies how changes in one chemical's concentration affect another within a CRN. Unlike traditional sensitivity analysis, which depends on the choice of basis for the stoichiometric matrix, absolute sensitivities provide intrinsic values that remain consistent regardless of basis selection.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

The theory of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) is an indispensable tool for the understanding of biochemical phenomena. Models based on CRN have successfully been employed to gain insights into various biological functions such as cell signaling pathways [20, 46], circadian clocks [18, 21], proofreading kinetics $[25,6]$, and many more $[41,2]$.

The thorough mathematical basis of chemical reaction theory has enabled much of its continuous success in applications. Originating in the fundamental work of Horn, Jackson, and Feinberg [27, 13, 26, 15], modern CRN theory uses the theory of differential equations [14, 42], algebraic geometry [8, 28, 10], graph theory $[9,12]$, homological algebra [24], and, in the recent years, information geometry. By realizing that the vector of chemical concentration is a distribution on a finite set, it was possible to adapt techniques from information theory and statistics to CRN theory [56, 54, 35]. In particular, the equilibrium and quasi-thermostatic steady state manifolds have the same mathematical shape as exponential families from information geometry [4, 36]. This approach has improved the geometrical understanding of growing systems [53], thermodynamic uncertainty relations and speed limits [39], and finite time driving [38].

To be more precise, the stoichiometric polytopes of a CRN should be thought of as analogues of a probability simplex: A concentration vector has linear quantities which are conserved by the internal CRN dynamics, analogous to the conservation of probability. However, the linear conserved quantities of a CRN can be controlled and externally changed. From the mathematical point of view, this gives the concentration space two distinguished directions: The direction of internal dynamics within stiochiometric polytopes and the complementary direction which shifts the polytopes. The main technical contribution of this article is to construct a Cramer-Rao bound for quasi-thermostatic CRNs which is adapted to detect changes in the latter direction.

In CRN theory, the influence of an infinitesimal change of the linear conserved quantities on the steady state concentrations is known as sensitivity analysis [49]. The understanding of sensitivity is a prerequisite for the understanding of concentration robustness $[7,3,5]$, absolute concentration robustness [50], perfect adaptation [22, 34], and for chemical switches [1, 55, 48]. Sensitivity has been extensively analyzed in the literature $[51,49,52,50,43,17,44,24$, $29,40,30,10,23,31,47]$, yet, the problem remains that the sensitivity matrix is not an object that is intrinsic to the CRN but depends on the choice of a basis of $\operatorname{Ker}\left[S^{T}\right]$ (where $S$ is the stoichiometric matrix of the CRN). This means that the respective numerical values of the sensitivity matrix elements have no immediate physical meaning as, for example, arbitrary scaling of the basis vectors of $\operatorname{Ker}\left[S^{T}\right]$ will lead to arbitrary scaling of the respective elements. In this article, basis independent quantities, termed absolute sensitivities, are defined and analyzed. The definition is given for any steady state manifold whenever locally there is a continuously differentiable parametrization of the manifold by the vector of conserved quantities.

The idea behind the definition of absolute sensitivity is as follows: If, at a steady state, the concentration of a chemical $X_{i}$ is perturbed by an amount of $\delta x_{i}$, a new steady state is adopted by the CRN. Thereby, the perturbation $\delta x_{i}$ distributes to concentration changes of all chemicals, prescribed by the coupling through the linear conserved quantities. The absolute sensitivity $\alpha_{i \rightarrow j}$ of the

chemical $X_{j}$ with respect to the chemical $X_{i}$ quantifies the fraction of infinitesimal concentration change of $X_{j}$ after this redistribution, i.e., the concentration change of the chemical $X_{j}$ is given by $\alpha_{i \rightarrow j} \delta x_{i}$, to first order in $\delta x_{i}$. In particular, the diagonal terms $\alpha_{i}:=\alpha_{i \rightarrow i}$ quantify the fraction of concentration that remains with the chemicals $X_{i}$ in the shifted steady sate. The independence of the choice of basis of $\operatorname{Ker}\left[S^{T}\right]$ for the absolute sensitivities is not only aesthetically pleasing but has immediate consequences for the analysis of concentration robustness, negative feedback, and (hyper)sensitivity: In this article, it is proven that $\alpha_{i} \in[0,1]$ holds for quasi-thermostatic CRN. However, for systems with non-ideal thermodynamics, $\alpha_{i}<0$ and $\alpha_{i}>1$ can occur, corresponding to selfregulation and hypersensitivity, respectively. Moreover, absolute concentration robustness poses very strict conditions on the CRN model, for example it is not compatible with the complex balancing condition [50] By employing the concept of absolute sensitivity, it is possible to find weaker and therefore more practically feasible notions of concentration robustness. It might often be of biological interest that the concentration of a certain chemical $X_{i}$ is insensitive to concentration changes of a particular chemical $X_{j}$, which is captured by the vanishing of $\alpha_{j \rightarrow i}$. In contrast, absolute concentration robustness in $X_{i}$ requires the $\alpha_{j \rightarrow i}$ to vanish for all $i$.

A second remarkable feature of absolute sensitivities, in addition to the independence of the $\operatorname{Ker}\left[S^{T}\right]$ basis, is that they do not explicitly depend on kinetic parameters ${ }^{1}$. This leads to efficient procedures for sampling the space of physiologically feasible concentration vectors and to obtain resulting distributions of absolute sensitivities which allow to infer general robustness properties of each of the chemicals. The linear algebraic formalism developed in this article allows for computationally efficient implementations as is illustrated by using the core module of the IDHKP-IDH glyoxylate bypass regulation system as an example. Moreover, the approach reveals a surprising symmetry at the level of distributions which is not presents at the level of individual concentration vectors.

It is worth mentioning that quantities related to absolute sensitivities have been defined in the past: In [16], Feliu has introduced sign-sensitivities for CRNs to analyze whether the steady state concentrations of $X_{i}$ increases or decreases when the concentration of $X_{j}$ is perturbed. In other words, Feliu has analyzed the signs of the $\alpha_{j \rightarrow i}$. However, the work was done from the point of view of computational algebraic geometry and therefore the information geometrical interpretation of the $\alpha_{j \rightarrow i}$ as well as the exact formulae in the case of complex balanced systems, as derived in this paper, were not accessible in the previous work.

The article is structured as follows: This introductory section contains a paragraph introducing the mathematical notation and then provides a summary of the main results. The terminology for CRN is introduced in Section 2. The absolute sensitivity is defined in Section 3 and its basic properties, including the basis independence, are proven. In general, a CRN does not allow for an explicit parametrization of the steady state manifold by the conserved quantities and thus no explicit expressions for the absolute sensitivities exist. However, quasi-thermostatic steady state manifolds can be analyzed with the information

geometric techniques which lead to the formulation of a Cramer-Rao bound and to a linear algebraic characterization of the absolute sensitivities as scalar products between the projections of the canonical vectors to a certain linear space. This is presented in Section 4. In Section 5, an example is given to illustrate the concepts developed in this article.

question: Does the M-type allow for infinite paths?
answer: Yes, the M-type allows for infinite paths.

# 2.2 The W-type and the M-type 

The type W, due to Martin-Löf [20,21], is the type of well-founded, labelled trees. A tree of type W can be infinitely branching, but every path in the tree is finite. W takes two parameters $S$ : Type and $P: S \rightarrow$ Type. We think of $S$ as the type of shapes of the tree, and for a given shape $s: S$, the tree has $(P s)$-many positions. The key property of W is that it is the universal type for strictly positive inductive types, i.e. any strictly positive inductive type can be expressed using W.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { data W }(S \text { : Type) }(P: S \rightarrow \text { Type }) \text { : Type where } \\
& \text { sup-W }:(s: S) \rightarrow(P s \rightarrow \mathrm{~W} S P) \rightarrow \mathrm{W} S P
\end{aligned}
$$

- Example 1. We encode the type of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ by defining $S$ and $P$ as below (where $A \uplus B$ is the sum type of $A$ and $B$ with constructors inl and inr).

$$
\begin{aligned}
S & =\top \uplus \top \\
\mathrm{P}(\text { inl } \ldots) & =\perp \\
\mathrm{P}(\text { inr } \ldots) & =\top
\end{aligned}
$$

S encodes the possible constructors we can choose (inl is for zero, inr is for succ), and P encodes the number of subtrees (or recursive arguments) each choice of $S$ has. Thus W S P encodes $\mathbb{N}$. For example, zero is represented by the tree on the left below, succ zero by the tree on the right, and so on.
![img-0.jpeg](img-0.jpeg)

The type M, first studied by Abbott et al. [3] and van den Berg and De Marchi [25], is the type of non-well-founded, labelled trees. A tree of type M can have both finite and infinite paths. M takes two parameters $S:$ Type and $P: S \rightarrow$ Type, and we think of them similarly as for W. Dually to W, M is the universal type for strictly positive coinductive types.

```
record M ( }S\mathrm{ : Type) ( }P\mathrm{ : }S\mathrm{ \rightarrow Type): Type where
    coinductive
    field
        shape : }S
        pos : P shape }->\mathrm{M}S
```

- Example 2. If we define $S$ and $P$ as in Example 1, then $M S P$ is an encoding of the conatural numbers $\mathrm{N} \infty$.
