question: How do the concepts of Deligne's conjecture extend to quantum analogs within mathematical categories?
answer: Deligne's conjecture is extended to quantum analogs by defining ribbon categories with skein relations that deform classical relations. This involves introducing parameters like $v$ and $\alpha$ and exploring their effects on category structures, ensuring properties like semisimplicity under specific conditions.

evidence.text:
# Conjecture 1.8 (Deligne's conjecture). There exists 

- a ring $R$ which is a localization of $\mathbb{Q}[\lambda]$ at finitely many polynomials;
- a rigid symmetric monoidal category $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}^{D e l}$ where the objects are non-negative integers and morphism spaces are finitely-generated $R$-modules; and
- a symmetric monoidal functor eval from $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}$ to $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}^{D e l}$, that is the identity on objects and surjective on morphisms.
For any map $\varphi: R \rightarrow S$ we can define a base extension $\operatorname{Exc}_{S, \varphi(\lambda)}^{D e l}=\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}^{D e l} \otimes_{\varphi} S$. Furthermore $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}^{D e l}$ has the following properties for an open dense subset $U \subset \mathbb{C}$.
- The Cauchy completion of $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}^{D e l}$ is semisimple for $\lambda \in U$.
- $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}^{D e l}(n)$ has dimension $1,0,1,1,5,16,80$ for $\lambda \in U$ and $n=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$, respectively.
- If $\lambda$ is one of the special values in Table 1, then the Cauchy completion of the quotient of $\operatorname{Exc}_{\mathbb{C}, \lambda}^{D e l}$ by negligible elements is equivalent to the category of representations of the corresponding supergroup.
Conjecture 1.8 follows from Conjectures 1.3, 1.4, and 1.7 (using Proposition 1.16). Conjecture 1.8 should be viewed as closer to Conjecture 1.4, since it doesn't say anything about the kernel of eval; Conjecture 1.3 says that the classical exceptional relation is the only skein relation needed to define $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}^{D e l}$.

Remark 1.9. We have learned that Vogel has computational evidence against Deligne's conjecture (private communication). Note that it is possible for the quantum Conjectures 1.14 and 1.15 to hold even if the classical conjectures do not. See Remark 1.23.
1.2. Laurent polynomial conventions. The bulk of this paper deals with quantum versions of the sufficiency and consistency conjectures, now involving two variables $v$ and $w .{ }^{2}$ Before stating these conjectures we fix some notation for certain Laurent polynomials appearing in our formulas. On the one hand, we would like to use formulas that are irreducible as Laurent polynomials in $v$ and $w$, so that we can easily read off which primes need to be inverted. On the other hand the Laurent polynomials that occur in our formulas are often even or odd under $v \leftrightarrow v^{-1}$ and/or $w \leftrightarrow w^{-1}$, so we would also like our formulas to have this symmetry. So we often combine two irreducible factors into a single expression. For example, $v-v^{-1}=v^{-1}(v-1)(v+1)=$ $\left(v^{\frac{1}{2}}-v^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(v^{\frac{1}{2}}+v^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ but there is no way to factor it into odd or even Laurent polynomials so we

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{2}$ We avoid the letter $q$, because the relation of our parameters to the quantum group parameters is not obvious; see $\S 6.6$.

will leave $v-v^{-1}$ alone in our formulas. This will never cause any confusion since any time the irreducible factor $(v-1)$ appears it will have a corresponding $(v+1)$ factor.

Definition 1.10. We define

$$
\begin{aligned}
{[k \lambda+n] } & =w^{k} v^{n}-w^{-k} v^{-n} \\
\{k \lambda+n\} & =\frac{[2 k \lambda+2 n]}{[k \lambda+n]}=w^{k} v^{n}+w^{-k} v^{-n}
\end{aligned}
$$

Warning 1.11. Unlike with the usual quantum numbers, there is no denominator. To get suitable limiting behavior, we need equal number of terms in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\lim _{\substack{v, w \rightarrow 1 \\ w=v^{2}}} \frac{[a \lambda+b]}{[c \lambda+d]}=\frac{a \lambda+b}{c \lambda+d}
$$

(In this equality, $\lambda$ is a formal variable in expressions of the form $[k \lambda+n]$ and a rational number otherwise.)

Note that $\{k \lambda+n\}$ is always irreducible, while $[k \lambda+n]$ is reducible if $k$ and $n$ have a common factor. (In particular, for $n, k>1$, [1] divides [ $n$ ] and $[k \lambda]$.) When $k=0$ we will generally avoid $[n]$ and instead factor into the following symmetrized cyclotomic polynomials. (Strictly speaking we should use a similar convention for factoring $[k \lambda]$, but this is not needed in practice.) Let

$$
\Psi_{n}(v)=\prod_{\xi: \xi^{n}= \pm 1 \text { and } \xi^{m} \neq \pm 1 \text { for } m<n}\left(v^{\frac{1}{2}}-\xi v^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)
$$

or, in terms of the usual cyclotomic polynomials $\Phi_{n}$ and Euler's totient function $\varphi$,

$$
\Psi_{n}(v)=v^{-\varphi(n)} \Phi_{n}\left(v^{2}\right)
$$

In particular, when $n$ is odd $\Psi_{n}$ vanishes exactly at primitive $n$th and primitive $2 n$th roots of unity, while when $n$ is even, $\Psi_{n}$ vanishes exactly at primitive $2 n$th roots of unity. The notation $\{k \lambda+n\}$ can be viewed as another case of this: $\{k \lambda+n\}=\Psi_{2}\left(w^{k} v^{n}\right)$, and for $n$ a power of $2,\{n\}=\Psi_{2 n}(v)$. For convenience, here are the values of $\Psi_{n}$ that appear in this paper.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Psi_{1}(v)=[1]=v-v^{-1} & \Psi_{2}(v)=\{1\}=v+v^{-1} \\
\Psi_{3}(v)=\frac{[3]}{[1]}=v^{2}+1+v^{-2} & \Psi_{4}(v)=\{2\}=v^{2}+v^{-2} \\
\Psi_{5}(v)=\frac{[5]}{[1]}=v^{4}+v^{2}+1+v^{-2}+v^{-4} & \Psi_{6}(v)=\frac{[6][1]}{[3][2]}=v^{2}-1+v^{-2} \\
\Psi_{7}(v)=\frac{[7]}{[1]}=v^{6}+v^{4}+v^{2}+1+v^{-2}+v^{-4}+v^{-6} & \Psi_{8}(v)=\{4\}=v^{4}+v^{-4} \\
\Psi_{10}(v)=\frac{[10][1]}{[5][2]}=v^{4}-v^{2}+1-v^{-2}+v^{-4} & \Psi_{12}(v)=\frac{[12][2]}{[6][4]}=v^{4}-1+v^{-4}
\end{array}
$$

1.3. Quantum exceptional conjectures. We now turn to our main conjectures. Our first goal is to give a definition of a ribbon category QExc which looks like a quantum deformation of Exc. In particular we need skein relations which deform the Jacobi relation, the classical exceptional relation, and the symmetric relation between the overcrossing and undercrossing. Our specific choices of relations will be motivated below by our main theorems.

Definition 1.12. Let $R$ be an algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $v$ and $w$ invertible elements of $R$ such that $[\lambda]$, $[\lambda-1], \Psi_{1}$, and $\Psi_{6}$ are invertible. Let $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$ be the ribbon category whose objects are collections of $n$ points on a line, and whose morphisms spaces from $n$ to $m$ consist of $R$-linear combinations of planar graphs in a rectangle with $n$ boundary points on the bottom, $m$ boundary points at the top, and consisting of trivalent vertices and 4 -valent braided crossings modulo planar isotopy, the usual Reidemeister 2 and 3 relations for a crossing, the "Reidemeister 2.5" relation saying you can pull a trivalent vertex through a crossing, and the following circle, lollipop, bigon, triangle, quantum anti-symmetry, and quantum Killing symmetry relations.
![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)
where

$$
\begin{aligned}
d & =-\frac{\Psi_{4}[\lambda+5][\lambda-6]}{[\lambda][\lambda-1]} \\
b & =\{\lambda+2\}\{\lambda-3\} \Psi_{3} \\
t & =\Psi_{2}\left(\Psi_{2}\{2 \lambda-1\}+\left(v^{4}-v^{2}-1-v^{-2}+v^{-4}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

To these skein relations, we add three more relations:

- the quantum exceptional Jacobi relation
$(\mathrm{QEJac}-\mathrm{w}) v^{-3} \bigodot+v \bigodot-v^{-1} \bigodot-\frac{[\lambda][\lambda-1]}{\Psi_{1}} \bigcap+v^{4} \bigodot+v^{-4} \bigcap=0$.
- the quantum exceptional square relation
$(\mathrm{QESq}-\mathrm{w}) \bigodot+\frac{-\Psi_{2} \Psi_{6}^{2}[\lambda][\lambda-1]}{\Psi_{1}^{2}} \bigvee+\frac{x_{1}}{\Psi_{1}} \bigvee+\frac{x_{2}}{\Psi_{1}} \bigvee+\frac{x_{3}}{\Psi_{1}^{2}}+\frac{x_{4}}{\Psi_{1}^{2}} \bigcap=0$
where the $x_{i}$ are Laurent polynomials in $v$ and $w$ from Appendix A.
- the quantum exceptional crossing relation
$(\mathrm{QECross}-\mathrm{w}) \bigvee-\bigvee+\frac{\Psi_{1}}{\Psi_{6}} \bigcap-\bigvee \bigcap+\frac{\Psi_{1}[\lambda][\lambda-1]}{\Psi_{6}} \bigcap(-\bigwedge]=0$.
Note that if you set $w=v^{\lambda}$ and take the limit $v \rightarrow 1$ these relations recover the classical Jacobi relation, classical exceptional relation, and the relation in a symmetric tensor category saying that the overcrossing equals the undercrossing. In order to make this specialization process purely algebraic, we would need to introduce a larger ring with formal symbols for expressions like $\frac{w-w^{-1}}{v-v^{-1}}$.

Warning 1.13. Although (QEJac-w) looks like an analogue of the ordinary Jacobi relation with lower order terms, it is important to emphasize that it is only the correct analogue of the Jacobi relation in the exceptional setting. In particular, we do not expect any similar relation for quantizations of non-exceptional Lie algebras.

We now state our main conjectures. Let $\mathbf{P}$ be the set of Laurent polynomials in $v, w$

$$
\mathbf{P}=\left\{v, w, \Psi_{1}, \Psi_{2}, \Psi_{3}, \Psi_{6},[\lambda],[1-\lambda]\right\}
$$

(This list includes the polynomials that we assume to be invertible to define $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$.)
Conjecture 1.14 (Quantum sufficiency). If the polynomials in $\mathbf{P}$ are invertible in $R$, the space of $n$ boundary point diagrams in $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module for every $n$. Furthermore, $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(0)$ is generated by the empty diagram, $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(1)$ is the zero module, $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(2)$ is generated by the strand, $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(3)$ is generated by the trivalent vertex, and $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(4)$ is generated by
![img-4.jpeg](img-4.jpeg)

As before we have conjectured spanning sets for $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(n)$ for $n=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$; see Conjecture 5.1.

Conjecture 1.15 (Quantum consistency). So long as the polynomials in $\mathbf{P}$ are invertible, $R$ injects into $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$ as multiples of the empty diagram. In particular, any two ways of applying the above relations to a closed diagram to return a rational function in $v$ and $w$ will yield the same rational function.

As in the classical case, from this conjecture we get that if $d$ (resp. $d$ and $b$ ) are invertible, then $R$ also injects into $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(2)$ (resp. $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(3)$ ) as multiples of the strand (resp. trivalent vertex), and under some other invertibility assumptions $R^{S}$ injects into $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}(4)$ as linear combinations of the five diagrams in (10) (see Lemma 3.10).

Proposition 1.16 (Quantum specialization). If $\lambda$ is one of the values on the left of Table 1, then there is a full and dominant functor from $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, v^{\lambda}}$ to the category of representations of the quantum version of the corresponding group, for $v$ in some dense subset of $\mathbb{C}$.

As before, the category of representations of the corresponding group on the right of Table 1 is the Cauchy completion of a quotient of $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, v^{\lambda}}$. If Conjecture 1.3 holds, then the kernel of this quotient can be characterized abstractly as the tensor ideal of negligible morphisms.

We expect that quantum specialization holds for all $v$ that are not roots of unity. This conjecture could also be stated more algebraically by working over the generic point $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}(v), v, v^{\lambda}}$. Moreover, if you replace the quantum group category with the appropriate tilting modules at roots of unity, then it should hold except at some small roots of unity.

Quantum specialization is stated precisely and proved as Proposition 6.97 in $\S 6.6$, again following an idea appearing in [EN19]. (The precise statement has the correspondence between the parameters $q$ and $v$, which is somewhat subtle.)
Conjecture 1.17 (Quantum semisimplicity). There is an open dense subset $U \subset \mathbb{C}^{2}$ for which the Cauchy completion of $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, w}$, for $(v, w) \in U$, is semisimple.

We expect that it's enough to assume that $[k \lambda+\ell]$ is nonzero for all integers $k$ and $\ell$ (in particular, $v$ is not a root of unity).

To justify the definition of the QExc we have the following theorems, which we can summarize as saying that under some mild assumptions, any trivalent ribbon category where the $n$-box space has dimension at most $1,0,1,1,5$ for $n=0,1,2,3,4$ satisfies a version of (QEJac-w). Furthermore, again under some mild assumptions, (QEJac-w) implies (QESq-w) and (QECross-w). To allow for more general statements, we use another set of variables, $(v, \alpha)$ in place of $(v, w)$ above, at the cost of messier formulas.

Definition 1.18. A trivalent ribbon category $(\mathcal{C}, X, \tau)$ is a ribbon category $\mathcal{C}$ over $R$ with an object $X$ where

- the 1-box space is zero, and
- the $0-, 2-$, and 3 -box spaces are rank 1 free $R$-modules generated by the empty diagram, the strand, and a 'trivalent vertex' $\tau \in \mathcal{C}(3)$ respectively,
such that
- the category is generated as a ribbon category by $\tau$,
- the value of the circle is a non-zero multiple $d$ of the empty diagram, and
- the value of the bigon is a non-zero multiple $b$ of the strand.

Being generated as a ribbon category by $\tau$ is the same as saying that $\mathcal{C}$ is generated as a pivotal category by $\tau$ and the crossing. In particular, a trivalent ribbon category need not be trivalent in the sense of [MPS17] where the trivalent vertex alone is assumed to generate $\mathcal{C}$ as a pivotal category. Also we have weakened the non-degeneracy condition from [MPS17], replacing it with the assumption that the circle and bigon are non-zero.

Theorem 1. Suppose $(\mathcal{C}, X, \tau)$ is a trivalent ribbon category over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4) \leq 5$. Then there exists $v, \alpha, b, d, t \in \mathbb{C}$ such that the relations in (9) hold with

$$
\begin{aligned}
& {[5] b=-\alpha(d+\{8\})} \\
& \text { \{2\} } t=b-[5] \alpha
\end{aligned}
$$

as well as
$(\mathrm{QEJac}-\alpha)$

$$
v^{-3}+v+v^{2}-v^{-1} \quad+\alpha \quad+v^{4}+v^{-4} \quad \text { 1 }=0 .
$$

If $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4)=5$ then relation (QEJac- $\alpha$ ) is the only relation of this form up to simultaneously sending $v \mapsto-v$ and $\alpha \mapsto-\alpha$, but if $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4)<5$ then there will be at least two linearly independent such relations.

Theorem 2. Suppose $(\mathcal{C}, X, \tau)$ is a trivalent ribbon category over $\mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4) \leq 5$ and there exist $v$ and $\alpha$ satisfying (QEJac- $\alpha$ ), with $v^{10} \neq 1$ and $v^{12} \neq 1$. Then $\alpha$ and $b+[3] \alpha$ are also non-zero, $v^{8} \neq 1$, and we have the following relations:

- $d=-\frac{[5] b}{[2]}-[8]$.
- $t=\frac{b-[5] \alpha}{[2]}$.
- The quantum exceptional square relation:
$(\mathrm{QESq}-\alpha)$
![img-5.jpeg](img-5.jpeg)
where the $y_{i}$ are Laurent polynomials in $b, \alpha$, and $v$ given in Appendix A.

- The quantum exceptional crossing relation:
(QECross- $\alpha$ )

$$
\left.\left.1-\frac{\Psi_{1} \Psi_{2} \Psi_{3} \Psi_{4}}{b+[3] \alpha}\right| \cdots\right\rangle\left.\left.1-\frac{\Psi_{1}^{2} \Psi_{2} \Psi_{3} \Psi_{4} \alpha}{b+[3] \alpha}\right| \cdots\right\rangle=0 .
$$

To get back to the $(v, w)$ variables and nicer formulas in Definition 1.12, we make a change of variables motivated by the Kontsevich integral approach and Deligne's change of variable from $d$ to $\lambda$. (See Lemma 3.12 for an alternate motivation.) We first remind the reader of some very elementary mathematics which we nonetheless found quite confusing.

Remark 1.19. Consider the rational change of variables from $(x, y)$ to $(x, w)$ with $w=\frac{y}{x+y}$, which makes sense when $y \neq-x$. The inverse change of variables is given by the rational function $y=\frac{w x}{1-w}$, which makes sense when $w \neq 1$. However, in order for these transformations to be inverse we need to check that

$$
y \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{x \frac{y}{x+y}}{1-\frac{y}{x+y}}=\frac{x y}{x}
$$

which requires in addition that $x \neq 0$. In this case, $y$ as a function of $w$ and vice versa are fractional linear transformations, which are invertible as long as the determinant of the corresponding $2 \times 2$ matrix $\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 1 & x\end{array}\right)$ is nonzero. More generally, by the inverse function theorem the transformation $(x, y) \mapsto(x, w)$ fails to have an inverse exactly when $\partial_{y} w=\frac{(x+y)-y}{(x+y)^{2}}=0$.

When $b+[3] \alpha$ is non-zero and the relevant square roots exist in $R$ we can make the change of variables from $\alpha$ to $w$ given by

$$
\frac{w^{2}}{v}+\frac{v}{w^{2}}=\frac{\{1\} b-[3\}\{5\} \alpha}{b+[3] \alpha}
$$

Note that there are generically four values of $w$ for each value of $\alpha$. We see that $\partial_{\alpha}\left(w^{2} / v+v / w^{2}\right)=$ 0 exactly if $0=\{1\} \cdot[3]+1 \cdot[3]\{5\}=\Psi_{1} \Psi_{2} \Psi_{3} \Psi_{4} \Psi_{6}$, so when $v$ is not an 8 th or 12 th root of unity the (multi-valued) change of variables is invertible, with (single-valued) inverse given by

$$
\alpha=-\frac{b[\lambda][\lambda-1]}{\{\lambda+2\}\{\lambda-3\} \Psi_{1} \Psi_{3}}
$$

Finally, we observe that if we rescale the choice of self-duality so that $b=\{\lambda+2\}\{\lambda-3\} \Psi_{3}$, formulas (QEJac- $\alpha$ ), (QESq- $\alpha$ ), and (QECross- $\alpha$ ) are generically identical to the formulas in terms of $v, w$ given earlier as (QEJac-w), (QESq-w) and (QECross-w).

Corollary 1.20. Suppose $(\mathcal{C}, X, \tau)$ is a trivalent ribbon category over $\mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4) \leq 5$ so that (QEJac- $\alpha$ ) holds with $v^{10} \neq 1$ and $v^{12} \neq 1$. Then, there is a $w \in \mathbb{C}$ and an evaluation functor $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, w} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ sending the trivalent vertex to $\tau$.

This corollary justifies our definition of QExc, since if the quantum exceptional family exists in any form it would have to satisfy our quantum exceptional relations.

Remark 1.21. Throughout the paper, when we say that "(QEJac- $\alpha$ ) holds" in a trivalent ribbon category, we implicitly include the choice of $v$ and the elementary relations (9) in the statement.

1.4. From classical to quantum. The classical conjectures from $\S 1.1$ and the quantum conjectures from $\S 1.3$ are related, but there are no formal implications between them. From the point of view of the quantum conjectures, the classical specialization $v=1$ is excluded by the assumption that $\Psi_{1}$ is invertible. There is a partial implication the other direction: Conjecture 1.8 implies a corresponding quantum conjecture.

Conjecture 1.22 (Quantum version of Deligne's conjecture). There exists

- a ring $R$ satisfying the hypotheses of Definition 1.12;
- a trivalent ribbon category $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}^{\text {Del }}$ where the objects are non-negative integers and morphism spaces are finitely-generated $R$-modules; and
- a ribbon functor Qeval from $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$ to $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}^{\text {Del }}$, that is the identity on objects, surjective on morphisms, and sends the trivalent vertex to the trivalent vertex.

Theorem 3. If Conjecture 1.8 is true for $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}^{\text {Del }}$, then Conjecture 1.22 is true for $\operatorname{Exc}_{R((h)), v, w}^{\text {Del }}$ for $v=e^{h / 2}$ and $w=e^{\lambda h / 2}$ as formal Laurent series.

In interpreting Theorem 3, recall that we normalized $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}$ so $B=12$. In the language introduced in $\S 2.2$, this normalization of $B$ corresponds to what we call the "Convenient" choice of invariant inner product.

Theorem 3 is proved in $\S 4$.
1.5. Calculations. In $\S 5$ we calculate some properties of $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, w}$ and the corresponding 2variable knot polynomial, under the assumptions of our main conjectures.

First we give conjectural bases for the box spaces up to $n=6$, and check that these diagrams are linearly independent (assuming Conjecture 1.4). We unconditionally give a 16-dimensional representation of the 5 -strand affine braid group, and an 80 -dimensional representation of the 6 -strand affine braid group, obtained from the braid group actions on these 5- and 6-boundary point diagrams.

Using this, we give a divide-and-conquer algorithm for computing the conjectural quantum exceptional invariant of all knotted trivalent graphs of Conway width at most 6 . This includes all prime knots of at most 12 crossings, and nearly all prime links of at most 12 crossings, including many non-algebraic examples.

Note that without assuming any of our conjectures, by Proposition 1.16 these 2-variable knot polynomials must specialize at particular values of $w$ to give the quantum invariants of the adjoint representations of the actual Lie algebras. To our knowledge these are the first calculations of the quantum knot polynomials of non-torus knots for the adjoint representations of any of the exceptional Lie algebras, and they are much more efficient than doing the calculations directly in $U_{\mathrm{g}}(\mathfrak{g})$. (For torus knots these calculations can be done using the Rosso-Jones formula [RJ93], see [MMM16].)

Using our skein relations, we also compute the quantum versions of Cohen-de-Man's [CdM96] formulas for the dimensions of the objects appearing in the third tensor power of adjoint representation in the exceptional series. (For the summands of $\mathfrak{g}^{\otimes 2}$ such quantum dimension formulas were already given by Tuba-Wenzl [TW05].)

The programs internally work with formulas $\mathrm{QExc}_{\mathbb{C}, v, \alpha}$, since the degrees are smaller.
1.6. Symmetries and the parameter plane. For reference, we list some global symmetries of the category $\mathrm{QExc}_{R, v, w}$. Consider the following involutions on our parameters:

![table_1](table_1)

Of these, symmetries (12) and (13) do not change any of the skein relations. The first is an artifact of the parameterization, and specifically our insistence on formulas that are balanced under $w \leftrightarrow w^{-1}$. The second interchanges the roles of $\lambda$ and $1-\lambda$ in the quantum number formulas, and is thus a quantization of the symmetry of $\operatorname{Exc}_{R, \lambda}$ interchanging $\lambda$ and $1-\lambda$. For instance it switches two eigenvalues of the twist acting on the 4 -box space (Lemma 3.12).

Symmetry (14) rescales $b$ by -1 , as explained in $\S 1.1$. Specifically it acts on diagrams in $D$ with $n$ incoming vertices, $m$ outgoing vertices, and $k$ trivalent vertices by

$$
D \mapsto(-1)^{(m-n+k) / 2} \cdot D
$$

Symmetry (15) acts on diagrams by reflecting in the plane of the knot diagram, switching the sign of all crossings. (The powers of $v$ appearing in (QEJac- $\alpha$ ) were chosen so that $\alpha$ does not change under this reflection.)

These symmetries generate a group of order 16. (Symmetries (13) and (14) do not commute). If we restrict the action to the torus $v=e^{i \theta}$ and $w=e^{i \varphi}$ for real $\theta, \varphi$, one fundamental domain for the group is

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & \leq \theta \leq \pi / 2 \\
(\theta-\pi) / 2 & \leq \varphi \leq \theta / 2
\end{aligned}
$$

as shown in Figure 1, along with the lines $w=v^{\lambda}$ corresponding to the exceptional series and certain other lines explained in $\S 6.7$.
1.7. Special values. In $\S 6$, we look at what happens in certain special cases. For many of these special cases the change of variables is not well-defined, so we will often need to return to the $\alpha$-version of the main relations.

We begin by outlining how to prove specialization theorems in the style of Proposition 1.6, using ideas from Kuperberg's paper [Kup96, Thm. 5.1], as expanded on by [EN19, Thms. 2.1 and 2.3] and [GSZ23, Thm. 5.3].

Second in $\S 6.2$, we collect and expand upon some results about Deligne's symmetric group category, the classical $G 2$ and $F 4$ families, and the relationship between these three categories and Frobenius algebras, Hurwitz algebras, and cubic Cayley-Hamilton Jordan algebras.

Third, we write down explicitly which instances of the quantum exceptional relation hold in various special cases where $\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{C}(4)<5$ and so multiple relations hold.

Fourth, when $v$ is a 10th or 12th root of unity, Corollary 1.20 does not apply. We show that when $v= \pm 1$ then the classical exceptional relations must hold (see [Mou22] for some related results). We show that when $v= \pm i$ and an additional non-degeneracy assumption holds, the relations of the classical $F 4$ series must hold (see [GSZ23] for some related results). Finally we show that when $v$ is a primitive 3 rd or 6 th root of unity, then the relations of the classical $G 2$ series must hold (see [Boo98, Wes10, Str19, Bae01] for related results). We delay a full treatment of all root of unity cases to later work.

![img-6.jpeg](img-6.jpeg)

question: Is it possible for a principal to achieve more than the "maxmax" objective with certain learning algorithms?
answer: Yes, if the agent uses some learning algorithms that are no-regret but not no-swap-regret, then sometimes the principal can do better than the "maxmax" objective $\overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}^{\mathcal{R}}(\operatorname{CSReg}(T) / T)$.

evidence.text:
# 3 Reduction from Learning to Approximate Best Response 

In this section, we reduce the generalized principal-agent problem with a learning agent to the problem with an approximately-best-responding agent. We show that, if the agent uses contextual no-regret learning algorithms, then the principal can obtain an average utility that is at least the "maxmin" approximate-best-response objective $\overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}^{\mathcal{R}}(\operatorname{CReg}(T) / T)$ (to be defined below). On the other hand, if the agent does contextual no-swap-regret learning, then the principal cannot do better than the "maxmax" approximate-best-response objective $\overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}^{\mathcal{R}}(\operatorname{CSReg}(T) / T)$. In addition, if the agent uses some learning algorithms that are no-regret but not no-swap-regret, the principal can sometimes do better than the "maxmax" objective $\overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}^{\mathcal{R}}(\operatorname{CSReg}(T) / T)$.

question: Can market segments differ in any strongly monotone and saturated segmentation if the uniform price exceeds θ₁?
answer: No, they cannot differ; all such segmentations must have the same market segment as θ₁.

evidence.text:
# E Proof of Lemma 4 

Proof. First, if the uniform price of $\mu$ is $\theta_{1}$, there exists a unique segmentation that is saturated, the one that does not segment the market. Suppose now that the uniform price of $\mu$ is strictly greater than $\theta_{1}$. Let $\sigma \in \Sigma_{\Omega}(\mu)$ be strongly monotone and saturated. Denote as $\theta_{k}$ the maximal type that is in the segment $\theta_{1}$. By Definition 1, there exists $\theta_{i}$, with $\theta_{1}<\theta_{i} \leq \theta_{k}$ such that $\theta_{i} \in \mathcal{I}_{\sigma}\left(\theta_{1}\right)$. Consequently, any segmentation that is strongly monotone and saturated must have the same market segment $\theta_{1}$. Conclude by iterating the same argument for the other segments.

question: What is spatial confounding and why is it a problem in statistical models?
answer: Spatial confounding occurs when unobserved variables that influence both the exposure and outcome are not included in a model, leading to biased inferential results. This can distort the understanding of the true effect of an exposure on an outcome, making it a significant issue in spatial designs.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

This paper proposes a new approach to address the problem of unmeasured confounding in spatial designs. Spatial confounding occurs when some confounding variables are unobserved and not included in the model, leading to distorted inferential results about the effect of an exposure on an outcome. We show the relationship existing between the confounding bias of a non-spatial model and that of a semi-parametric model that includes a basis matrix to represent the unmeasured confounder conditional on the exposure. This relationship holds for any basis expansion, however it is shown that using the semi-parametric approach guarantees a reduction in the confounding bias only under certain circumstances, which are related to the spatial structures of the exposure and the unmeasured confounder, the type of basis expansion utilized, and the regularization mechanism. To adjust for spatial confounding, and therefore try to recover the effect of interest, we propose a Bayesian semi-parametric regression model, where an expansion matrix of

principal spline basis functions is used to approximate the unobserved factor, and spike-and-slab priors are imposed on the respective expansion coefficients in order to select the most important bases. From the results of an extensive simulation study, we conclude that our proposal is able to reduce the confounding bias more than competing approaches, and it also seems more robust to bias amplification.

Keywords: Air pollution; Bayesian; Principal splines; Spatial confounding; Spatial regression; Spike-and-slab.

question: How do Generalized Additive Models (GAM) contribute to mid-term electricity load forecasting?
answer: GAMs contribute by modeling non-linear relationships between inputs like temperature, seasonality, and holidays with the electricity load, allowing for more accurate predictions over a mid-term horizon.

evidence.text:
## 4. Methodology
### 4.1. Modelling Concept

As detailed in Subsection 2.1, accurately forecasting load is a challenging task due to its multifaceted characteristics. Load depends on deterministic information, i.e. the seasonalities of different periods and holidays, and is sensitive to temperature fluctuations. Moreover, it is influenced by past observations. Thus, autoregressive components and non-stationary components need to be incorporated into a forecasting model. To address these diverse characteristics, we propose a two-stage GAM model integrating

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ In all ETS models considered in this work, the trend component is assumed to be zero.

ETS and AR models. The general process of the model is illustrated by the flowchart in Figure 6 and described in the subsequent.

Let $Y_{t} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $X_{t}^{\text {Tonep }} \in \mathbb{R}$ be the electricity load and temperature at time $t$ for $t \in\{1, \ldots, T\}$, respectively. Additionally, we have access to deterministic information about seasonalities and holidays for the extended horizon $t \in\{1, \ldots, T+H\}$. It is the objective to forecast load over a mid-term prediction horizon $H$ of several weeks to one year, resulting in forecasts $\widehat{Y}_{T+1}, \ldots, \widehat{Y}_{T+H}$.
(i) Temperature forecast: In a first step, see Figure 6 on the left-hand side, the proposed model constructs temperature forecasts $\widehat{X}_{t}^{\text {Tonep }}, t \in\{T+1, \ldots, T+H\}$ for the mid-term horizon $H$. Since accurate weather and satellite imagery-based temperature forecasts are not feasible for mid-term horizons, we rely on deterministic seasonalities, i.e. the time of the day and the time of the year, as modeling inputs. Observed temperatures $X_{t}^{\text {Tonep }}, t \in\{1, \ldots, T\}$ are, first, preprocessed to a smoothed time series using an ETS model (see Tab. 1, col. 2) with fixed smoothing parameters. This removes fluctuations not capturable by deterministic seasonalities and creates more suitable inputs for the subsequent models to forecast temperature and load. A GAM model is, secondly, applied to the smoothed temperature. Recognizing the limitations of lagged components in GAMs for mid-term horizons, we employ an AR model on the residuals of this GAM. The forecasted temperature is obtained by summing the individual forecasts from both models. By this, we incorporate crucial short-term temporal dependencies while avoiding computationally expensive solutions, like multiple GAM estimations with differently recent lags.
(ii) States fit and forecast: In a second step, see Figure 6 middle part, the proposed model constructs level and seasonal states fit and forecast. For this purpose, firstly, load is modeled by a GAM from the smoothed temperatures obtained in (i) and deterministic seasonal and holiday information. Secondly, an ETS model (see Tab. 1, col. 3) with an annual seasonality is applied to this GAM's residuals and fitted states are retrieved. The forecasted states follow directly from these fits. To estimate the ETS model, we employ the TMAE calculated as the sum of in-sample MAEs over a multiple of the weekly period. By this, fluctuations occurring in a smaller period are smoothed and not mirrored by the fitted and forecasted states component, which is well-suited, particularly, in the context of mid-term forecasting.
(iii) Load forecast: Lastly, see Figure 6 right-hand side, load is forecasted. For this purpose, load is modeled again by a GAM with the smoothed temperatures, seasonal and holiday information and, additionally, with the ETS unit root states as inputs. This approach captures the unit root behavior in the load time series and mitigates the risk of the GAM inputs in (ii) adapting unduly to this non-stationary pattern. For the same rationale as in (i), autoregressive dependencies of the load time series are captured by a secondary AR model on the residuals. Finally, load is forecasted as the sum of the forecasts of these two models with the temperature, level and seasonal forecasts obtained in (i) and (ii) and the deterministic seasonal and holiday information over the horizon.

question: How many transactions can the blockchain process at a time?
answer: The blockchain can collect and process up to five transactions at a time.

evidence.text:
# 2 The Problem of Execution in Standard TFMs: An Example 

In this section, I illustrate the challenges associated with executing transactions in standard Transaction Fee Mechanisms (TFMs) through a simple example. Consider a blockchain system with two separate queues, Queue A and Queue B, each holding three transactions awaiting inclusion and execution in the blockchain. The expected values of the transactions in Queues A and B are $\mathbb{E}\left[v_{a}\right]=10$ and $\mathbb{E}\left[v_{b}\right]=6$, respectively.
Figure 1 depicts the state of the two queues. In each period, two new transactions arrive in each queue. However, due to the necessity for global consensus, the blockchain can collect and process up to five transactions at a time.
In Queue A, there are three transactions denoted as $a_{1}, a_{2}$, and $a_{3}$, with individual values of 15,10 , and 5 , respectively. Similarly, Queue B contains transactions $b_{1}, b_{2}$, and $b_{3}$, with values of 8,6 , and 4 . The higher expected value in Queue A indicates that, on average, transactions in this queue are more valuable to the network or its users compared to those in Queue B.

question: Does the response function in a Hawkes process need to satisfy any specific condition?
answer: Yes, the response function \(\mu(t)\) must satisfy \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \mu(s) d s<1\).

evidence.text:
# 2.2 Jumps as a function of a Hawkes Process 

To first give a little background, the Hawkes process was first introduced by its creator Alan Hawkes in Hawkes (1971) as a self-exciting process and he expanded on this theory in Hawkes and Oakes (1974) by discussing how this can be applied to problems in which the data exhibits a clustering effect. A one dimensional Hawkes process is a point process $N(t)$ which is characterized by its intensity $\lambda(t)$ with respect to its natural filtration,

$$
\lambda(t)=\lambda+\int_{0}^{t} \mu(t-s) d N(s)
$$

where $\lambda>0$ is the background intensity and the response function $\mu(t)$ is a positive function, often referred to as the excitation function, which satisfies $\int_{0}^{\infty} \mu(s) d s<1$. In more recent times, Hawkes processes have been applied to problems in finance, as explained in Bacry et al. (2015), where certain processes incur these self-exciting and clustering effects. These properties are also more consistent when modelling price processes with jumps in LOBs, which the empirical results show in Fodra and Pham (2015b). We, of course, in this paper specifically focus on their applications to modeling LOBs. Some examples of previous work related to modeling LOBs include Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), where they introduced the General Compound Hawkes Process (GCHP) in LOBs with an application in a SOC setting given in Roldan Contreras and Swishchuk (2022), or in Cartea et al. (2018b), where they use HPs to try and predict adverse selection within the LOB, also with applications under the SOC framework.

Here, like in Section 2.1., we model the price process with a diffusion and jump part as follows:

$$
S_{t}=S_{0} \pm g\left(\nu_{t}\right) t+\sigma W_{t}+\sum_{k=1}^{N(t)} a\left(X_{k}\right)
$$

where $g$ and the diffusion term are as defined before in Section 2.1. In Equation (8), $a$ maps the current state to a price movement, $X_{k}$ is again an ergodic Markov chain with ergodic probabilities $\left(\pi_{1}^{*}, \pi_{2}^{*}, \ldots, \pi_{n}^{*}\right)$, where the current state is computed using information from the previous state. Here, $N(t)$ is again a counting process independent of $X_{k}$ and $W_{t}$. Then using the diffusion approximation for the jump part in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), this becomes,

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{t} & =S_{0} \pm\left(g\left(\nu_{t}\right) \eta_{H P}\right) t+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\bar{\sigma}_{H P}^{2}+\left(\sigma^{*} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\tilde{\mu}}}\right)^{2}} W_{t}, S_{0}=S \\
& =S_{0} \pm\left(g\left(\nu_{t}\right) \eta_{H P}\right) t+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\bar{\sigma}_{H P}^{2}+\varsigma_{H P}^{2}} W_{t}, S_{0}=S
\end{aligned}
$$

The scaling limit for the diffusion approximation part of the midprice process in Equation (9) is formulated via the functional central limit theorem (FCLT) for the General Compound Hawkes process in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), where as before in Section 2.1, we use the scaling limit, $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}$, for $S_{t n}$, which holds in a weak sense in the Skorokhod topology. A proof of this claim can be found in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020). Similarly to the argument given in Section 2.1, the usefulness in Equation (9) is in terms of being able to prepare solutions to algorithmic and HFT trading problems, where the FCLT enables the use of a diffusion approximation, for the case when $n$ goes to infinity and $t$ is fixed. Here, the drift coefficient can be defined, as in Roldan Contreras (2023),

as,

$$
\eta_{H P}=a^{*} \frac{\lambda}{1-\hat{\mu}}
$$

where $a^{*}$ is a constant depending on the transition probabilities of the Markov chain. This can be defined, as in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), as $a^{*}:=$ $\sum_{i \in X} \pi_{i}^{*} a(i)$, where $\pi^{*}$ are the ergodic probabilities of the Markov chain $X$. $\lambda$ is again the background intensity and $\mu$ refers to the output of the response/excitation function. Here, $\varsigma_{H P}=\sigma^{*} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\hat{\mu}}}, \quad \sigma^{*}$ is again a constant depending on the ergodic probabilities of the Markov chain $X_{k}$. Since this kind of Markov chain has two states, where $X_{k} \in\{-\delta, \delta\}, \sigma^{*}$ can be defined, as shown by corollary 3 in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), as

$$
\sigma^{*}:=\sqrt{4 \delta^{2}\left(\frac{1-p^{\prime}+\pi^{*}\left(p^{\prime}-p\right)}{\left(p+p^{\prime}-2\right)^{2}}-\pi^{*}\left(1-\pi^{*}\right)\right)}
$$

Also, note that $\bar{\sigma}_{H P}$ can be defined as in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020) as,

$$
\bar{\sigma}_{H P}=\sqrt{\left(\sigma^{*}\right)^{2}+\left(a^{*} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\hat{\mu}}}\right)}
$$

where,

$$
\sigma^{*}=\hat{\sigma} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\hat{\mu}}} \text { and } \hat{\sigma}^{2}:=\sum_{i \in X} \pi_{i}^{*} v(i)
$$

where $v(i)$ represent the transitions in and out of states. Lastly, in Equation (9), $\lambda$ and $\hat{\mu}$ represent the background intensity and the excitation/response function, respectively. Recall, more formally, $\hat{\mu}$ can be defined, as also stated in Swishchuk and Huffman (2020), as,

$$
0<\hat{\mu}:=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mu(s) d s<1 \text { and } \int_{0}^{\infty} s \mu(s) d s<\infty
$$

question: How is the normalized log-unit price process of ETHUSDT expressed?
answer: The normalized log-unit price process of ETHUSDT is given by $\bar{W}(t)=x+\mu^{\prime} t+B_{t}$, where $x$ is the start point.

evidence.text:
## C. European LP Pricing

We are interested in evaluating:

$$
V(0)=\mathbb{E}(V(t))=\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{LP}}(t)\right)+\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{fee}}(t)\right)
$$

For the Uniswap V3 opsition, the stopping time $\tau$ is defined as:

$$
\tau=\inf _{t<\infty}\left\{S(t) \leq S_{L} \text { or } S(t) \geq S_{H}\right\}
$$

If the contract cannot be terminated before the stopping time, the current valuation of Uniswap V3 can be formulated as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{E}(0) & =\mathbb{E}(V(t)) \\
& =\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{LP}}(t)\right)+\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{fee}}(t)\right) \\
& =\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau} V_{\mathrm{LP}}(H)\right] S(\tau)=S_{H}]+\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau} V_{\mathrm{LP}}(L)\right] S(\tau)=S_{L}] \\
& +\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{fee}}(t)\right) \\
& =V_{\mathrm{LP}}(H) \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau}\right] S(\tau)=S_{H}]+V_{\mathrm{LP}}(L) \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau} \mid S(\tau)=S_{L}\right] \\
& +\mathbb{E}\left(V_{\mathrm{fee}}(t)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The normalized log-unit price process of ETHUSDT is given by:

$$
\bar{W}(t)=\frac{\ln P(t)}{\sigma}=\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma}-\frac{\sigma}{2}\right) t+B_{t}
$$

Let us denote:

$$
\mu^{\prime}=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}-\frac{\sigma}{2}
$$

Thus, we have:

$$
\bar{W}(t)=x+\mu^{\prime} t+B_{t}
$$

where $x$ is the start point, $a, b$ are designated as the unit bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b=\frac{\ln H}{\sigma}, b^{\prime}=b-x \\
& a=\frac{\ln L}{\sigma}, a^{\prime}=x-a
\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover, it also holds that:

$$
\tau=\inf _{t<\infty}\{\bar{W}(t) \leq a \text { or } \bar{W}(t) \geq b\}
$$

Utilizing the Laplace Transform, we can express the following expectations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau} \mid S(\tau)=S_{H}\right]=\exp \left(\mu^{\prime} b^{\prime}\right) \frac{\sinh \left[a^{\prime} \sqrt{\mu^{\prime 2}+2 r}\right]}{\sinh [(b-a) \sqrt{\mu^{\prime 2}+2 r}]} \\
& \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-r \tau} \mid S(\tau)=S_{L}\right]=\exp \left(-\mu^{\prime} a^{\prime}\right) \frac{\sinh \left[\left(b^{\prime} \sqrt{\mu^{\prime 2}+2 r}\right]\right.}{\sinh [(b-a) \sqrt{\mu^{\prime 2}+2 r}]}
\end{aligned}
$$

instrumental variable model, this example is a reduced form rather than a first stage, so we introduce additional terminology. The potential outcomes represent "alive" (which maps to treated) and "dead" (which maps to untreated). The four principal strata represent those for whom the intervention is "wasteful" (always takers, who are alive in intervention and alive in control), those for whom the intervention is "efficacious" (compliers, who are alive in intervention and dead in control), those for whom the intervention is "unsafe" (defiers, who are dead in intervention and alive in control), and those for whom the intervention is "futile" (never takers, who are dead in intervention and dead in control).

Figure 4 illustrates the experiment graphically. In intervention, 12 of 14 people are alive within 28 days, as compared with only 5 of 14 people in control. The Fisher exact test rejects the null hypothesis that the intervention is neither efficacious nor unsafe for anyone at the $2.6 \%$ level. The point estimate of the average effect indicates that the intervention increases survival by a whopping 50 percentage points, which given the sample size of 28 , implies 14 more compliers than defiers. While we can depict all possible distributions of potential outcomes in an experiment with 2 people in the ten rows of Figure 2, doing so in an experiment with 28 people would require 4,495 rows, so we only depict three.

As depicted in the highlighted row, our maximum likelihood decision rule shows that the joint distribution of potential outcomes that maximizes the likelihood in-

Figure 4: Illustration of the Zabet et al. (2016) Vitamin C Experiment
![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)
cludes 21 people for whom the intervention is efficacious (compliers), 7 people for whom the intervention is unsafe (defiers), and zero people for whom the intervention is wasteful or futile. The number of compliers net of defiers is $21-7=14$, which matches the point estimate of the average effect multiplied by the sample size.

As shown in the second column, in our maximum likelihood configuration, we can deduce how many people of each type were assigned intervention and control. Since the maximizer rules out that any of the 12 people who lived in intervention would have lived regardless, it must be efficacious for all 12 of them. By similar logic, our decision rule indicates that, by a chance imbalance, more of the people for whom the intervention is efficacious were assigned intervention ( 12 vs. 9 ), and fewer of the people for whom the intervention is unsafe were assigned control (2 vs. 5). Using terminology from Pearl (1999), the intervention was "necessary" for the deaths of the 2 people who died in intervention because it is unsafe for them, and they would have lived without it. Similarly, the intervention would have been "sufficient" for the deaths of the 5 people who lived in intervention because it is unsafe for them, so they would have died with it.

The second row of Figure 4 shows the result of the monotonicity decision rule: 10 people for whom the intervention is wasteful, 14 people for whom the intervention is efficacious, and 4 people for whom the intervention is futile. Like the maximum likelihood decision rule, this decision rule preserves the point estimate of the average effect. But, were this the true distribution of potential outcomes in the sample, the

realized data would have occurred with only a $12.9 \%$ probability, which is strictly lower than the $15.3 \%$ probability of the realized data under the maximum likelihood decision. The evidence in favor of the maximum likelihood decision, which indicates the presence of both compliers and defiers, is 1.19 stronger than the evidence for the monotonicity decision, as indicated by the likelihood ratio (15.3/12.9).

The final row shows the Fisher hypothesis distribution in which the intervention has no effect for anyone in the sample. This distribution has a much lower likelihood of $0.8 \%$, and the visualization in the second column provides intuition for this lower value. This configuration implies large imbalances between intervention and control among those for whom the intervention is wasteful ( 12 vs. 5 ) and those for whom the intervention is futile ( 2 vs. 9 ).

While the maximum likelihood and monotonicity decision rules imply different marginal distributions of potential outcomes, our design-based likelihood can also distinguish between distributions with the same marginal distributions. Consider an alternative distribution, not depicted, with 6 people for whom the intervention is wasteful, 18 people for whom the intervention is efficacious, and 4 people for whom the intervention is unsafe. That distribution has the same marginal distributions as the result of the monotonicity decision rule depicted in the second row $\left(\theta_{11}+\theta_{10}=24\right.$ and $\left.\theta_{11}+\theta_{01}=10\right)$, but it has a higher likelihood of $14.5 \%$. Incidentally, this example also demonstrates that there is more than one distribution with a higher likelihood than the result of the monotonicity decision rule.

The expressions in the final column help explain why the first row maximizes the likelihood and others do not. In an experiment with 28 people, there are $40,116,600$ ways to randomize 14 into intervention and 14 into control ( 28 choose 14). If the true distribution is the one depicted in the first row, there are 293,930 ways to randomize 12 of the 21 people for whom the intervention is efficacious (compliers) into intervention ( 21 choose 12) and 21 ways to randomize 2 of the 7 people for whom the intervention is unsafe (defiers) into intervention ( 7 choose 2 ). There are then exactly $6,172,530$ ways ( 21 choose 7 times 7 choose 2 ) for the true distribution to yield the observed data, representing approximately $15.3 \%$ of all possible ways. In other rows, there are fewer ways to yield the observed data, so the entropy-the numerator of the likelihood-is lower.

It need not be the case that the maximizer of the likelihood includes only two types. As Fisher (1935) recognized, it is always possible for all people in the experiment to be of two types - either compliers and defiers (as shown in the highlighted row) or always takers and never takers (as shown in the last row). However, maximization of the likelihood requires trading off between the higher likelihood of fewer types and the higher likelihood of balance between intervention and control within each type. In this example, the maximizer of the likelihood has only two types but some imbalance within each type. In the case of the third row, the imbalance within each type is much larger, and the likelihood is much lower. The second row, chosen by the monotonicity rule, is balanced within each type, but it has three types, which

decreases its likelihood. ${ }^{7}$
The maximum likelihood decision rule implies that the intervention is unsafe for some patients, and decision makers will need to decide what to do with that information. Those that ascribe to the "do not harm" principle might withhold the intervention (Cui and Han, 2023; Ben-Michael et al., 2024; Guggenberger et al., 2024), and those that only care about the average effect might want to continue using it. However, even those that care only about the average could improve the average if they could better target the intervention away from those for whom it is unsafe and towards those for whom it is efficacious. If machine learning methods cannot find heterogeneity in the intervention effect using covariates available by convenience, our maximum likelihood decision can justify collecting a richer set of covariates. It can also motivate the collection of data on a richer set of secondary outcomes that capture side effects. For example, in the Bernard et al. (2001) clinical trial testing the effect of recombinant human activated protein C on patients with sepsis, researchers identified a potential mechanism for how the intervention was unsafe: it led to severe bleeding.

question: What is the Heinz mean for two non-negative real numbers $\rho$ and $\sigma$?
answer: The Heinz mean for two non-negative real numbers $\rho$ and $\sigma$, with parameter $0 \leq \mu \leq 1$, is defined as $H_{\mu}=\frac{\rho^{\mu} \sigma^{1-\mu}+\rho^{1-\mu} \sigma^{\mu}}{2}$.

evidence.text:
# 3 Sharpening of the Heinz inequalities and its reverses with the Kantorovich Constant 

In this section, we make a refinement of Heinz inequality with the Kantorovich constant.

Lemma 3.1. Let $\rho, \sigma>0$ and $0 \leq \nu<\kappa \leq 1$. Then

$$
r\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma}-\sqrt{\sigma}\right)^{2}+K(\sqrt{h}, 2)^{r^{\prime}} \rho_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \sigma \leq \nu \rho+(1-\nu) \sigma-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left(\rho \nabla_{\kappa} \sigma-\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right)
$$

where $r=\min \left\{\frac{\nu}{\kappa}, 1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right\}, h=\frac{\rho}{\sigma}$ and $r^{\prime}=\min \{2 r, 1-2 r\}$.
Proof. An simple argument shows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \nu \rho+(1-\nu) \sigma-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\left(\rho \nabla_{\kappa} \sigma-\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right)=\nu \rho+(1-\nu) \sigma-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\left(\kappa \rho+(1-\kappa) \sigma-\rho^{\kappa} \sigma^{1-\kappa}\right) \\
& =\frac{\nu}{\kappa} \rho^{\kappa} \sigma^{1-\kappa}+\left(1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right) \sigma=\left(\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right) \nabla_{\frac{\kappa}{\kappa}} \sigma
\end{aligned}
$$

By applying the inequality (6) for the relation (17), it follows that

$$
r\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma}-\sqrt{\sigma}\right)^{2}+K(\sqrt{h}, 2)^{r^{\prime}} \rho_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \sigma \leq\left(\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right) \nabla_{\frac{\kappa}{\kappa}} \sigma
$$

Hence, the inequality (16) follows.
Lemma 3.2. Let $\rho, \sigma>0$ and $0 \leq \nu<\kappa \leq 1$. Then

$$
\nu \rho+(1-\nu) \sigma-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left(\rho \nabla_{\kappa} \sigma-\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right) \leq K(\sqrt{h}, 2)^{-r^{\prime}} \rho_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \sigma+R\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma}-\sqrt{\sigma}\right)^{2}
$$

where $R=\max \left\{\frac{\nu}{\kappa}, 1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right\}, h=\frac{\rho}{\sigma}$ and $r^{\prime}=\min \{2 r, 1-2 r\}$.
Proof. By applying the inequality (7) for the relation (17), it follows that

$$
\nu \rho+(1-\nu) \sigma-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left(\rho \nabla_{\kappa} \sigma-\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma\right) \leq K(\sqrt{h}, 2)^{-r^{\prime}} \rho_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \sigma+R\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma}-\sqrt{\sigma}\right)^{2}
$$

So, we get the inequality (18).
For two non-negative real numbers $\rho$ and $\sigma$, we define the Heinz mean in the parameter $\mu, 0 \leq \mu \leq 1$, as

$$
H_{\mu}=\frac{\rho^{\mu} \sigma^{1-\mu}+\rho^{1-\mu} \sigma^{\mu}}{2}
$$

Note that $H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)=H_{1}(\rho, \sigma)=\frac{\rho+\sigma}{2}$ and $H_{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho, \sigma)=\sqrt{\rho \sigma}$. It is easy to see that as a function of $\mu, H_{\mu}(\rho, \sigma)$ is convex, attains its minimum at $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$, and attains its maximum at $\mu=0$ and $\mu=1$. Moreover, $H_{\mu}(\rho, \sigma)=H_{1-\mu}(\rho, \sigma)$ for $0 \leq \mu \leq 1$. Thus, the Heinz mean interpolates between the geometric mean and the arithmetic mean:

$$
\sqrt{\rho \sigma} \leq H_{\mu}(\rho, \sigma) \leq \frac{\rho+\sigma}{2} \text { for } 0 \leq \mu \leq 1
$$

Theorem 3.3. Let $\rho, \sigma>0$ and $0 \leq \kappa<\kappa \leq 1$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& r\left[H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)+H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\frac{\kappa}{2}}(\rho, \sigma)\right]+K[\sqrt{h}, 2]^{r^{\prime}} H_{\nu}(\rho, \sigma) \\
& \leq H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left[H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $r=\min \left\{\frac{\nu}{\kappa}, 1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right\}, h=\frac{\rho}{\sigma}$ and $r^{\prime}=\min \{2 r, 1-2 r\}$.
Proof. Interchanging $\rho$ with $\sigma$ and $\sigma$ with $\rho$ in inequality (16), we get

$$
r\left(\sqrt{\sigma_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \rho}-\sqrt{\rho}\right)^{2}+K(\sqrt{h}, 2)^{r^{\prime}} \sigma_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \rho \leq \nu \sigma+(1-\nu) \rho-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left(\sigma \nabla_{\kappa} \rho-\sigma_{\kappa \nu}^{\kappa} \rho\right)
$$

Adding (16) and (22), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& r\left[\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \sigma}-\sqrt{\sigma}\right)^{2}+\left(\sqrt{\sigma_{\kappa}^{\kappa} \rho}-\sqrt{\rho}\right)^{2}\right]+K[\sqrt{h}, 2]^{r^{\prime}}\left(2 H_{\nu}(\rho, \sigma)\right) \\
& \leq 2 H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left[2 H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-2 H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

and so

$$
\begin{aligned}
& r\left[H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)+H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\frac{\nu}{2}}(\rho, \sigma)\right]+K[\sqrt{h}, 2]^{r^{\prime}} H_{\nu}(\rho, \sigma) \\
& \leq H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left[H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

In similar of proof of Theorem 3.3, we can prove the following result.
Theorem 3.4. Let $\rho, \sigma>0$ and $0 \leq \kappa<\kappa \leq 1$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)\left[H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)\right] \leq K[\sqrt{h}, 2]^{-r^{\prime}} H_{\nu}(\rho, \sigma) \\
& +R\left[H_{\kappa}(\rho, \sigma)+H_{0}(\rho, \sigma)-H_{\frac{\nu}{2}}(\rho, \sigma)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $R=\min \left\{\frac{\nu}{\kappa}, 1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right\}, h=\frac{\rho}{\sigma}$ and $r^{\prime}=\min \{2 r, 1-2 r\}$.

question: Why does standard inference fail when using quantiles from a normal distribution for $\widehat{L}(d)$?
answer: Standard inference fails because $\widehat{L}(d)$ is not normally distributed and data-dependent selection of $d$ complicates its distribution.

evidence.text:
# 2.1 Why Does Standard Inference Fail? 

To fix ideas, let us focus for now on inference for the lower bound $L(d)$ of a selected option rather than the entire identified set $[L(d), U(d)]$. More specifically, since $L(d)$ is a lower bound for the average potential outcome $W(d)$, we would like to obtain a probabilistic lower bound for $L(d)$. Under standard conditions, a central limit theorem implies $\hat{p}=\left(\hat{p}^{100}, \hat{p}^{010}, \hat{p}^{110}, \hat{p}^{101}, \hat{p}^{011}, \hat{p}^{111}\right)^{\prime}$ is normally distributed in large samples. So why not form a CI using $\widehat{L}(d)$ and quantiles from a normal distribution as the basis for inference? There are two reasons such an approach is (asymptotically) invalid:

1. Even in the absence of selection, $\widehat{L}(d)=\max \left\{\hat{p}^{1 d 0}, \hat{p}^{1 d 1}\right\}$ is not normally distributed in large samples.
2. Data-dependent selection of $d$ further complicates the distribution of $\widehat{L}(d)$.

Reason 1. is easy to see since $\widehat{L}(d)$ is the maximum of two normally distributed random variables in large samples when $d$ is chosen a priori. To better understand reason 2., note that the distribution of $\widehat{L}(d)$ given $d \in \widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the conditional distribution of the maximum of two normally distributed random variables given that the minimum of two other normally distributed random variables, $\widehat{U}(d) \equiv \min \left\{1-\hat{p}^{0 d 0}, 1-\hat{p}^{0 d 1}\right\}$, exceeds the maximum of yet another set of two normally distributed random variables, $\widehat{L}\left(d^{\prime}\right)=\max \left\{\hat{p}^{1 d^{\prime} 0}, \hat{p}^{1 d^{\prime} 1}\right\}$ for $d^{\prime} \neq d$. Unconditionally, $\widehat{L}(\hat{d})$ for any data-dependent choice of $\hat{d}$ is distributed as a mixture of the distributions of $\widehat{L}(0)$ and $\widehat{L}(1)$, neither of which are themselves normally distributed.

question: How can advanced methodologies enhance fairness and validity in assessing diverse populations' health outcomes?
answer: Advanced methodologies like multilevel modeling enhance fairness and validity by providing more accurate estimations of measurement equivalence across diverse populations. This ensures that assessments reflect true differences rather than biases introduced by inadequate analytical techniques.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

To examine the disproportionate impact of health interventions or other determinants on health outcomes for certain populations, including disadvantaged minorities, it is crucial to establish measurement equivalence when evaluating outcomes across groups differing in gender, ethnicity, and other demographic factors. While validating psychometric instruments has been a routine practice in research, critical evaluations of measurement equivalence, particularly through differential item functioning (DIF) analysis, have historically been limited [1]. In recent years, however, there has been significant progress in this area, with a growing body of research employing DIF analysis to investigate measurement equivalence [e.g., 2-7].

This growing research underscores the need for continued evaluation of health constructs and measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations. It is worth noting that some health studies did not clearly describe the method used for DIF analysis [e.g., 3], and conventional DIF methods based on single-level models were frequently used to analyze health survey data with a nesting structure [e.g., 2], for which recent DIF methods based on multilevel models are better alternatives in terms of accuracy of DIF estimation. By employing advanced methodologies for DIF, researchers can better evaluate health measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations.

question: Why might a smartphone report lower SINR values compared to a dedicated scanner?
answer: Smartphones may report lower SINR values because they can connect to weaker cells during handovers and have less sophisticated signal processing capabilities than dedicated scanners, which consistently connect to the strongest available signals.

evidence.text:
## F. Impact of UE's Receiver

The quality of the receiver has an impact on UEs performance too. To analyze this effect, we present measurements obtained by the Samsung SM-S911B phone, equipped with R\&S QualiPoc software, in terms of SINR. For comparison, Fig. 6 shows the SINR CDFs from the SM-S911B phone and the TSMA6B scanner, with both devices measuring the same operator, frequency band, and technology.

Our results indicate that the phone consistently reports lower SINRs than the scanner, with values deviating further as the flight altitude increases. This discrepancy likely arises due to receiver's quality. Moreover, it should be noted that, unlike the scanner, the phone is not always connected to the strongest cell due to the nature of handover process. As the UAV

![img-6.jpeg](img-6.jpeg)

Fig. 6. Samsung SM-S911B R\&S QualiPoc SINR CDFs at multiple altitudes for LTE B3 and NR n78 frequency bands.
moves, the phone may temporarily connect to weaker cells, resulting in lower SINR readings compared to the scanner, which consistently monitors the strongest signals.

Overall, this result highlights a crucial point: While highend scanners, like the TSMA6B, can be considered as highperformance UE (representing an idealized UAV receiver), the actual performance of UAVs in U-space will depend on the quality of the receiver used. As the quality of the receiver improves, so does the signal quality, but this comes at a higher cost. Therefore, UAVs equipped with better receivers can expect improved signal reception, but this needs to be weighed against the increased price and practical deployment considerations.

question: How does outer Lipschitz geometry determine triples associated with singularities?
answer: Outer Lipschitz geometry helps identify certain triples related to minimal good resolutions of singularities by analyzing how these geometrical structures interact and influence each other within the context of complex surfaces.

evidence.text:
# 5. APPLICATION TO POLAR EXPLORATION AND OUTER LIPSCHITZ GEOMETRY 

Now we will apply Theorem 4.1 to polar exploration of complex surface germs in the sense of the paper by Belotto, Fantini, Némethi, and Pichon in [BdSFNP22].

Let $(X, 0)$ be a complex surface germ embedded in $\left(\mathbb{C}^{k}, 0\right)$ and consider $\pi:\left(X_{\pi}, E\right) \longrightarrow(X, 0)$ a good resolution of $(X, 0)$, and denote by $E_{v_{1}}, \ldots, E_{v_{n}}$ the irreducible components of $E$. Let $\ell=\left(\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}\right):(X, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{k}, 0\right) \longrightarrow\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0\right)$ be a generic projection with respect to $\pi$ in the sense of Definition 2.18. Denote by $\Pi$ the generic polar curve of $\ell$. As in [BdSFNP22], we associate to $\pi$ a triplet $\left(\Gamma_{\pi}, L_{\pi}, P_{\pi}\right)$, where $\Gamma_{\pi}$ is the dual graph of $\pi$, and vectors $L_{\pi}:=\left(\ell_{1}^{*} \cdot E_{v_{i}}\right)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ and $P_{\pi}:=\left(\Pi^{*} \cdot E_{v_{i}}\right)_{1 \leq i \leq n}$ with $\ell_{1}^{*}$ and $\Pi^{*}$ being, respectively, the strict transforms of $\ell_{1}^{-1}(0)$ and the polar curve $\Pi$ by $\pi$. Belotto, Fantini, Némethi, and Pichon proved in [BdSFNP22] the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1 ([BdSFNP22, Theorem A]). Let $M$ be a real 3-manifold. There exists finitely many triples $(\Gamma, L, P)$, where $\Gamma$ is a weighted graph and $L$ and $P$ are vectors in $\left(\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\right)^{V(\Gamma)}$, such that there exists a normal complex surface germ $(X, 0)$ satisfying the following conditions:
(i) The link of $(X, 0)$ is homeomorphic to $M$.
(ii) $(\Gamma, L, P)=\left(\Gamma_{\pi}, L_{\pi}, P_{\pi}\right)$, where $\pi:\left(X_{\pi}, E\right) \longrightarrow(X, 0)$ is the minimal good resolution which factors through the blow-up of the maximal ideal and the Nash transform of $(X, 0)$.
A natural question to ask is if the statement of Theorem [BdSFNP22, Theorem A] still holds if we do not restrict ourselves to normal surface singularities? Here, we give a negative answer to this question with the following result stated as Theorem A in the introduction.

We will need the notion of integral closure of ideals to state our result.
Definition 5.2. Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $R$. The integral closure of $I$ is the ideal, denoted $\bar{I}$, of all elements $r$ in $R$ such that there exists $a_{i} \in I^{i}$ satisfying the equality

$$
r^{n}+a_{1} r^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1} r+a_{1}=0
$$

Theorem 5.3 (Theorem A). Let $(X, 0)$ be a normal complex surface germ. Let $\Lambda_{X}$ be the infinite set of integrally closed $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideals of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. There exists a family of complex surface germs with an isolated singularity $\left\{\left(X_{I}, 0\right)\right\}_{I \in \Lambda_{X}}$ such that
(i) $(X, 0)$ is homeomorphic to $\left(X_{I}, 0\right)$ for all $I \in \Lambda_{X}$ and is the common normalization of the germs $\left\{\left(X_{I}, 0\right)\right\}_{I \in \Lambda_{X}}$.
(ii) For all $I, J$ in $\Lambda_{X}$ we have that $\left(\Gamma_{\pi_{I}}, L_{\pi_{I}}, P_{\pi_{I}}\right)=\left(\Gamma_{\pi_{J}}, L_{\pi_{J}}, P_{\pi_{J}}\right)$ if and only if $I=J$, where $\pi_{I}$ and $\pi_{J}$ are respectively the minimal good resolutions which factors through the blow-ups of the maximal ideal and the Nash transform of $\left(X_{I}, 0\right)$ and $\left(X_{J}, 0\right)$.
In order to prove Theorem 5.3 we will need a preliminary result which gives a relationship between the inner rates and the integral closure of ideals (see [LJT08] for more knowledge on the integral closure of ideals).
Proposition 5.4. Let $(X, 0)$ be a complex surface germ and $I, J$ be two $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideals of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. If the inner rates functions $\mathcal{I}_{I}$ and $\mathcal{I}_{J}$ are equal then $\bar{I}=\bar{J}$.

To prove Proposition 5.4 we need the following Theorem
Theorem 5.5 (See [Lë09, Theorem 1.1] or [LJT08, Theorem 2.1]). Let $(X, 0)$ be a germ of complex space. Let $I$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$ and $h$ be an element of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. The following conditions are equivalent:
(i) $h \in \bar{I}$
(ii) The function $h \circ \pi$ is a section of $I \cdot \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X_{I}}}$, where $\overline{\mathrm{BL}_{I}}:\left(\overline{X_{I}}, \overline{E_{I}}\right) \longrightarrow(X, 0)$ is the normalized blow-up of $I$.

Proof of Proposition 5.4. By Proposition 3.7 there exists, up to isomorphism, a modification

$$
\pi_{I J}:\left(\overline{X_{I J}}, \overline{E_{I J}}\right) \longrightarrow(X, 0)
$$

which is the common normalized blow-up of the ideals $I$ and $J$. Let us prove that $\bar{I}=\bar{J}$, let $h$ be an element of $\bar{I}$. By Theorem 5.5 the function $h \circ \pi_{I J}$ is a section of $I \cdot \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X_{I J}}}$. By Proposition 3.7 we have $I . \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X_{I J}}}=J . \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X_{I J}}}$ and it implies that $h \circ \pi_{I J}$ is a section of $J . \mathcal{O}_{\overline{X_{I J}}}$. Again, by Theorem 5.5 we get that $h$ is an element of $\bar{J}$. We proved that $\bar{I} \subset \bar{J}$. Symmetrically, we prove that $\bar{J} \subset \bar{I}$.
Remark 5.6. The converse of Proposition 5.4 is false. Indeed, consider again the ideal $I$ of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0}$ generated by $\left(x^{2}, y^{2}\right)$. The integral closure $\bar{I}$ of the ideal $I$ is generated by $\left(x^{2}, y^{2}, x y\right)$ (see [Tei04, Proposition 3.4]). Let $\omega_{1}=\mathrm{d}\left(x^{2}\right) \wedge \mathrm{d}\left(y^{2}\right)$ and $\omega_{2}=\mathrm{d}\left(x^{2}\right) \wedge \mathrm{d}(x y)$. Consider the modification

$$
b:\left(X_{2}, E_{\nu_{1}} \cup E_{\nu_{2}}\right) \xrightarrow{b_{2}}\left(X_{1}, E_{\nu_{1}}\right) \xrightarrow{b_{1}}\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0\right)
$$

where $b_{1}$ is the blow-up of the origin of $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ and $b_{2}$ is the blow-up centered at the point $x^{*} \cap E_{\nu_{1}}$. A direct computation using the holomorphic forms $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ shows that $\nu_{\nu_{2}}(I)=5, m_{\nu_{2}}(I)=2$ and $\nu_{\nu_{2}}(\bar{I})=4, m_{\nu_{2}}(\bar{I})=2$. It follows that

$$
q_{\nu_{2}}^{I}=2 \neq \frac{3}{2}=q_{\nu_{2}}^{\bar{I}}
$$

In order to prove this Theorem 5.3, we will also need the following result by Spivalovsky, which characterizes the Nash transform.
Theorem 5.7 ([Spi90, Theorem 1.2]). A modification of $(X, 0)$ factors through the Nash transform of $(X, 0)$ if and only if it has no basepoints for the family of the polar curves associated to the linear projections on $\mathbb{C}^{2}$.

Before going through the proof, let us give a concrete example of the construction we will use to prove Theorem 5.3 .

Example 5.8. Let $(X, 0)=\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0\right)$ and consider the family of integrally closed m-primary ideal $\left\{I_{n}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}^{*}}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0}$ generated by $G_{n}=\left(x^{k} y^{n-k}, 0 \leq k \leq n\right)$. The set of generators $G_{n}$ is not complete. Indeed, the points $(1,0)$ and $(\sqrt[n]{1}, 0)$, where $\sqrt[n]{1}$ is a root of unity not equal to 1 , are sent to the point $(0,0, \ldots, 1)$ by the morphism $(x, y) \mapsto\left(y^{n}, x y^{n-1}, x^{2} y^{n-2}, \ldots, x^{n-1} y, x^{n}\right)$.

Let us consider the complete set of generators

$$
\widetilde{G}_{n}=\left(y^{n+1}, y^{n}, x y^{n-1}, x^{2} y^{n-2}, \ldots, x^{n-1} y, x^{n}, x^{n+1}\right)
$$

for the ideal $I_{n}$. By Theorem 4.1 the image of the germ $\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0\right)$ by the holomorphic map

$$
F_{n}(x, y)=\left(y^{n+1}, y^{n}, x y^{n-1}, x^{2} y^{n-2}, \ldots, x^{n-1} y, x^{n}, x^{n+1}\right)=\left(z_{0}, z_{1}, \ldots, z_{n+2}\right) \in \mathbb{C}^{n+3}
$$

is a complex surface germ $\left(X_{n}, 0\right)$ with an isolated singularity at the origin of $\mathbb{C}^{n+3}$ given by the equations:

$$
z_{n+1}^{k} z_{1}^{n-k} z_{k+1}=z_{n+2}^{k} z_{0}^{n-k}, 0 \leq k \leq n
$$

5.1. Application to Outer Lipschitz geometry. As a corollary of Theorem 5.3, we can construct infinitely many complex surface germs with an isolated singularity that are not metrically equivalent in the Bilipschitz sense but have a common normalization.

First, let us recall some definitions and results about the bilipschitz geometry of complex germs (See [Pic20] for more details).
Definition 5.9. Let $(X, 0)$ be a complex surface germ embedded in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$. The outer metric $\mathrm{d}_{o}$ on $X$ is the metric induced by the ambient Euclidian metric, i.e., for all $x, y \in X, \mathrm{~d}_{o}(x, y)=\|x-y\|_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}$. The inner metric $\mathrm{d}_{i}$ on $X$ is the arc length metric induced by the ambient riemannian metric.
Definition 5.10. Let $(M, d)$ and $\left(M^{\prime}, d^{\prime}\right)$ be two metric spaces. A map $f: M \longrightarrow M^{\prime}$ is a bilipschitz homeomorphism if $f$ is a homeomorphism and there exists a real constant $K \geq 1$ such that

$$
\frac{1}{K} d(x, y) \leq d^{\prime}(f(x), f(y)) \leq K d(x, y), \forall x, y \in M
$$

Definition 5.11. Two analytic germs $(X, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$ and $\left(X^{\prime}, 0\right) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{m}, 0\right)$ are inner Lipschitz equivalent (resp. outer Lipschitz equivalent) if there exists a germ of bilipschitz homeomorphism $\psi:(X, 0) \longrightarrow\left(X^{\prime}, 0\right)$ with respect to the inner (resp. outer) metric. The equivalence class of the germ $(X, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$ for this equivalence relation is called the inner Lipschiz geometry (resp. outer Lipschitz geometry) of $(X, 0)$.

One of the main motivations for studying complex surface germs up to bilipschitz equivalence is that the biholomorphic type of a complex germ determines its bilipschitz geometry. Another motivation follows from a theorem by Mostowski [Mos85], which states that the set of inner (resp. outer) Lipschitz geometries is countable. While a complete classification of complex surface germs with isolated singularities has been given in [BNP14] the classification of complex surface germs up to outer Lipschitz equivalence is still open.

The next result aims to understand the set of outer Lipschitz geometries of complex surface germs with isolated singularities.

Corollary 5.12 (Corollary B). Let $(X, 0)$ be a normal complex surface germ. Let $\Lambda_{X}$ be the infinite set of integrally closed $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideals of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. There exists a family of complex surface germs with an isolated singularity $\left\{\left(X_{I}, 0\right)\right\}_{I \in \Lambda_{X}}$ such that
(i) $(X, 0)$ is homeomorphic to $\left(X_{I}, 0\right)$ for all $I \in \Lambda_{X}$ and is the common normalization of the germs $\left\{\left(X_{I}, 0\right)\right\}_{I \in \Lambda_{X}}$.
(ii) For all $I, J \in \Lambda_{X}$ the surfaces $\left(X_{I}, 0\right)$ and $\left(X_{J}, 0\right)$ are outer Lipschitz equivalent if and only if $I=J$.

Corollary 5.12 is a direct consequence of Theorem 5.3 and the following result of Neumann and Pichon

Theorem 5.13 ([NP16, Theorem 1.2]). Let $(X, 0)$ be a complex surface germ with an isolated singularity. Then the outer Lipschitz geometry of $X$ determines the triple $\left(\Gamma_{\pi}, L_{\pi}, P_{\pi}\right)$ where $\pi$ is the minimal good resolution which factors through the blow-up of the maximal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$ and the Nash transform of $(X, 0)$.

question: Why is stress testing important for financial strategies?
answer: Stress testing evaluates how financial strategies perform under extreme market conditions. It helps identify potential vulnerabilities and ensures that a strategy can maintain its effectiveness even during challenging times, thereby demonstrating robustness.
