# 3- Emerging Technologies in Indusrty 4.0 

Emerging technologies in Industry 4.0 are revolutionizing manufacturing and industrial processes through the integration of advanced digital technologies like IIoT, AI and ML, Big data analytic, Edge computing and so on. Edge computing is one of these technologies that has been used in this work, the philosophy of edge computing focuses on executing computations nearby the data source. Edge computing resources may consist of a network or computer resources operated between end users and cloud data centers. IIoT devices generate enormous amounts of raw data that may exceed the capacity of the traditional cloud computing paradigm, this means that the majority of IIoT data will be consumed at the network edge rather than being transferred to the cloud. On the other hand, the cloud computing model may be insufficient for many reasons. For instance, the volume of data at the edge is excessive, using significant bandwidth and computational resources unnecessary. Moreover, the necessity for privacy protection obstructs cloud computing in IIoT. Therefore, the edge computing concept have been emerged to handle the mentioned cases[24]. Figure 3 illustrates the concept of Edge Computing.
![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

Fig -3- Edge Computing Concept

In this context, data compression is one approach that could be used based on edge computing concept to enhance system performance. The most prevalent form of data compression is video compression, which uses one of several regularly standards, H.264/AVC, VP9, AV1, or H.265/HEVC [25]. Using H.265/HEVC, streaming services can improve user experience and reduce data transmission costs by delivering higher-quality videos with manageable bandwidths. H. 265 is the codec that would replace H. 264 , where its compression ratio is up to $50 \%$ higher than H.264, making it useful in a lot of different places. Compression solutions that rely on edge computing do have some downsides, though one of these is the processing time required for encoding and compression, which is around 20 milliseconds per megapixel when using a 50:1 compression ratio[26].

# 5.2 Core-periphery detection 

We now compare the sub-sampling routines using the CP divide-and-conquer algorithm on real-world networks: Airport (Csárdi et al., 2025) is a network where nodes correspond to airports and edges to flights between airports $(n=755, m=4623)$; and Twitch (Rozemberczki et al., 2021; Leskovec and Krevl, 2014) has nodes which are users and edges represent friendships ( $n=168114, m=6797557$ ). Edge weights and directions were again removed, along with self-loops.

For each network, we report the size of the core, $k$, and corresponding Borgatti and Everett (BE) metric value for the optimal core returned by the algorithm, computed using (2). The BE values quantifies the strength of core-periphery structure detected by the algorithm, with larger values implying a better core was found. In the simulation settings, we simply used the core proportions as a measure of a node's coreness, but for the real data, we desire binary CP labels. To convert the core proportions to binary labels, we sort the nodes in descending order of their proportions. Then one by one, starting with the node with the largest proportion, we add this node to the core and compute the BE metric. We continue this process and select the core corresponding to the largest BE metric.

While the airport network is relatively small, this allows us to find the CP labels using the base algorithm without the divide-and-conquer step. Recall that the base algorithm is based on Algorithm 1 from Yanchenko (2022). We label this as "Full" in our results and provides us with a useful benchmark. Finally, we note the following values of $q$ and $B$ that were used for each network: Airport, $q=100 / n$ and $B=5000$; and Twitch, $q=500 / n$ and $B=25000$.

In Table 4, we report the core size and BE metric for the detected cores, and in Figure 5 , we compare the cores returned by the different algorithms. Specifically, for each subsampling pair, we compute the Jacaard coefficient ( JC ) between the returned core sets. If $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are two sets, then the JC is computed as

$$
J C\left(S_{1}, S_{2}\right)=\frac{\left|S_{1} \cap S_{2}\right|}{\left|S_{1} \cup S_{2}\right|}
$$

![table_3](table_3)

Table 4: Real data analysis results for core-periphery divide and conquer algorithm. $k$ refers to the number of nodes assigned to the core by the respective algorithms, and BE is the value of the Borgatti and Everett metric (2) corresponding to the optimal labels.

In words, the JC is the proportion of total elements in the two sets which are shared. It takes values from 0 to 1 with 1 indicating that $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are identical. In this way, the more similar the cores are, the larger the JC will be.

For Airport, all method return similar core sizes, cores and BE metric values as that of Full. Moreover, the cores for DN and RE are exactly the same ( JC of 1 ), supporting the results from Corollary 3.2. For Twitch, RE and RW yield the largest BE values, with RN, BFS and RNN also having similar values. DN yields a vastly different core size and BE value, while DFS does not perform as well. For this network, RW and RE have the most similar cores, which supports Lovász (1993). On the other hand, DN and RE's results are quite dissimilar, implying that the SBM assumption of Corollary 3.2 may be necessary for the results to hold.

question: What is a torsor under an affine group scheme over an algebraically closed field?
answer: A torsor under an affine group scheme over an algebraically closed field is necessarily trivial.

evidence.text:
# APPENDix A. A simple proof of triviality of torsors over an algebraically Closed field 

In this appendix we work in Vec, except in Remark A.2.
Wibmer [31] gave an elementary proof of the fact that a torsor under an affine group scheme over an algebraically closed field is necessarily trivial; this fact is the same as the uniqueness of the so-called Tannakian groups over a field such as above. We give a (hopefully) simpler proof of the triviality of torsors, which uses the same idea as was used to prove Theorem 1.4 (1); see Section 5.1.

Suppose that $k$ is an arbitrary field, and $\mathscr{G}=\operatorname{Spec} H$ is an affine group scheme represented by a Hopf algebra $H$. Every torsor under $\mathscr{G}$ is necessarily affine, and it is uniquely represented by an $H$-comodule algebra $A$, which is a twisted form of $H$, i.e., $A$ becomes isomorphic to $H$ after some base field extension. Such an $A$ is precisely what is called an $H$-Galois extension over $k$; it is by definition a non-zero $H$-comodule algebra $A=\left(A, \rho_{A}\right)$ such that the $A$-linear extension

$$
A \otimes A \rightarrow A \otimes H, \quad a \otimes b \mapsto a \rho_{A}(b)
$$

of the structure map $\rho_{A}: A \rightarrow A \otimes H$ is an isomorphism (of $H$-comodule algebras); the isomorphism, specialized through an algebra map $A \rightarrow L$ to some extension field $L$ of $k$, shows that $A$ is a twisted form of $H$, and conversely, for such a twisted

form, the map above is isomorphic since it turns so after some base field extension. Therefore, the above-mentioned triviality is translated as follows, and in fact, we are going to give a simple proof of this.
Proposition A.1. Suppose that $k$ is an algebraically closed field, and let $H$ be a Hopf algebra. Then an H-Galois extension over $k$ is necessarily trivial, i.e., it is isomorphic to $H$ as an $H$-comodule algebra.
Proof. Suppose that $A=\left(A, \rho_{A}\right)$ is an $H$-Galois extension over $k$. From (A.1) notice

$$
k=A^{\cos H}(:=\left\{x \in A \mid \rho_{A}(x)=x \otimes 1\right\})
$$

We may suppose that $H$ is not of finite type, since $A$ is trivial by Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, in case $H$ is of finite type; see [29, Section 18.3]. Given a Hopf subalgebra $J$ of $H$, define

$$
A_{J}:=\rho_{A}^{-1}(A \otimes J)
$$

This turns naturally into a $J$-comodule algebra, and is, in fact, a $J$-Galois extension over $k$. For the isomorphism (A.1) restricts to an isomorphism $A \otimes A_{J} \xrightarrow{\simeq} A \otimes J$ of $J$-comodule algebras, which shows by specialization that $A_{J}$ is a twisted form of $J$. In particular, we have $A_{J}^{\cos J}=k$; see (A.2). Suppose that we are given an $H$-colinear algebra map $f: J \rightarrow A$. Then we see that $f$ maps into $A_{J}$, and there results a $J$-colinear algebra map $J \rightarrow A_{J}$, through which $A_{J}$ is a $J$-module, and is, moreover, a $J$-Hopf module [22, Section 4.1]. It follows by the Hopf-module Theorem [22, Theorem 4.1.1] that the resulting is, in fact, an isomorphism

$$
J=A_{J}^{\cos J} \otimes J \xrightarrow{\simeq} A_{J}
$$

of $J$-comodule algebras; see the proof of Proposition 3.4.
Analogously to the proof of Theorem 1.4 (1), let us consider a pair $(J, f)$ of a Hopf subalgebra $J$ of $H$ and an $H$-colinear algebra map $f: J \rightarrow A$. A trivial example is $(k, k \hookrightarrow A)$. The set of all those pairs, into which we introduce the natural order defined by $\left(J_{1}, f_{1}\right) \leq\left(J_{2}, f_{2}\right)$ if $J_{1} \subset J_{2}$ and $f_{1}=f_{2} \mid J_{1}$, has a maximal pair, $\left(J_{\max }, f_{\max }\right)$, by Zorn's Lemma. As is seen from the cited proof, it remains to prove the following.
Claim. Given finite-type Hopf subalgebras $J$ and $K$ of $H$ such that $J \subset K$, every $H$-colinear algebra map $J \rightarrow A$ can extend to such a map $K \rightarrow A$.

Indeed, in order to see $J_{\max }=H$, which will complete the proof, we suppose on the contrary that $J_{\max } \varsubsetneqq H$, and choose arbitrarily a finite-type Hopf subalgebra $K$ of $H$ which is not included in $J_{\max }$. The claim applied to $J_{\max } \cap K$ and $K$ gives an $H$-colinear algebra map from $J_{\max } K\left(=J_{\max } \otimes_{J_{\max } \cap K} K\right.$, see (5.3)) to $H$ which extends $f_{\max }$; the extended map, paired with $J_{\max } K$, gives a pair properly greater than $\left(J_{\max }, f_{\max }\right)$. This contradiction shows the desired equality.

To prove the claim let us be given an $H$-colinear algebra map $f: J \rightarrow A$, which results in an isomorphism $J \xrightarrow{\simeq} A_{J}$ of $J$-comodule algebras such as in (A.4). As was seen in the first paragraph of the proof, one can choose an isomorphism $K \xrightarrow{\simeq} A_{K}$ of $K$-comodule algebras, which we identify with the identity map $\operatorname{id}_{K}$ of $K$. Then $f$ is identified with an automorphism $f: J \xrightarrow{\sim} J\left(=\Delta_{K}^{-1}(K \otimes J)\right.$, see (A.3)) of the $J$-comodule algebra $J$, which is necessarily in the form

$$
f: J \rightarrow J, \quad f(x)=g\left(x_{(1)}\right) x_{(2)}
$$

where $g=\varepsilon_{J} \circ f$, or $f=\bar{g}$ in the notation of (2.6). It remains to prove that this can extend to some automorphism $f^{\prime}: K \xrightarrow{\circ} K$ of the $K$-comodule algebra $K$. Since such an $f^{\prime}$ is necessarily in the form $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}\left(x_{(1)}\right) x_{(2)}$ with $g^{\prime}: K \rightarrow k$ an algebra map, we need to prove that the algebra map $g: J \rightarrow k$ can extend to an algebra map $K \rightarrow k$. Indeed, this is possible by Hilbert's Nullstellensatz since $K$ is faithfully flat over $J$ by [23, Theorem 3.1].

Remark A.2. Suppose $\mathscr{C}=\mathrm{sVec}$ or $\mathrm{Ver}_{p}^{\text {ind }}$, see (1.3). The result just proven holds more generally in $\mathscr{C}$. To see this, suppose that $H$ is a Hopf algebra in $\mathscr{C}$, and let $\mathfrak{G}=\operatorname{Spec} H$ be the corresponding affine group scheme. Since every nonzero algebra in $\mathscr{C}$ has a field as a non-zero quotient ordinary algebra, it follows that in $\mathscr{C}$, an $H$-Galois extension over the unit object $\mathbf{1}$ is the same as a twisted form of the $H$-comodule algebra $H$. Those forms are classified by the 1st Amitsur cohomology $H^{1}(\mathbf{1}, \mathfrak{G})_{\mathscr{C}}$ constructed in $\mathscr{C}$. But this is naturally identified with the ordinary $H^{1}\left(k, \mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}\right)$, or namely, we have

$$
H^{1}(\mathbf{1}, \mathfrak{G})_{\mathscr{C}}=H^{1}\left(k, \mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}\right)
$$

where $\mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}=\operatorname{Spec} \bar{H}$ is the affine group scheme corresponding to the ordinary Hopf algebra $\bar{H}$ (see (5.1), (5.5)) associated with $H$. For the complex for computing $H^{1}(\mathbf{1}, \mathfrak{G})_{\mathscr{C}}$, which is in the form

$$
\mathfrak{G}(L) \rightrightarrows \mathfrak{G}(L \otimes L) \rightrightarrows \mathfrak{G}(L \otimes L \otimes L)
$$

is naturally identified with the one

$$
\mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}(L) \rightrightarrows \mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}(L \otimes L) \rightrightarrows \mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}(L \otimes L \otimes L)
$$

for computing $H^{1}\left(k, \mathfrak{G}_{\mathrm{ev}}\right)$, where $L$ ranges through all extension-fields of $k$; see [17, Section 5.2]. Therefore, the proved Proposition A. 1 implies the generalized result in the categories.

# D Dynamics in the vicinity of the coarse-grained pattern 

We want to understand the local dynamics of the system. One would expect that when you are close to a coarse-grained pattern $\Xi^{*}$, the patterns that contribute to the dynamics, are precisely the ones that form the coarse-grained pattern. This is indeed the case as we will see below, for a parameter regime, which we will derive in this section.

As before suppose all patterns have a magnitude of unity and suppose we have two isolated patterns in our system, $\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}$, i.e. we have that for $l \neq r, s, \mu_{r, s} \ll \mu_{l, r}$ and $\mu_{r, s} \ll \mu_{l, s}$, where $\mu_{i j}$ is the angle between patterns $i$ and $j$. Let us also define $\mu_{m}$ to be the value, such that $\mu_{m}=\min _{l \neq r, s}\left\{\mu_{l, s}, \mu_{l, r}\right\}$, i.e. $\mu_{m}$ is the smallest angle of separation between the isolated patterns and the rest of the patterns. We are interested in the dynamics in the vicinity of the progenitor pattern of the two isolated patterns, that is, we consider $\mathbf{x}$ such that

$$
\mathbf{x}=\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}
$$

where $\mathbf{y}$ is some perturbation away from the coarse-grained pattern. The only restriction we place on $\mathbf{y}$ is that it must lie in the region "between" the two patterns $\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}$, i.e. for any non-isolated pattern $\Xi_{i}$, we must have $\angle\left(\Xi_{i}, \mathbf{y}\right) \geq \mu_{m}$, while for the isolated patterns we have $\angle\left(\mathbf{y}, \Xi_{r}\right) \leq \angle\left(\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}\right)$ and $\angle\left(\mathbf{y}, \Xi_{s}\right) \leq \angle\left(\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}\right)$. Then our dynamical system can be written as

$$
\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{Q}^{T} \operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+\mathbf{w}\right)-\mathbf{y}-\Xi^{*}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+\mathbf{w}\right)\right]_{i} } & =\frac{1}{Z} e^{\left(\beta\left(\Xi_{i} \cdot \Xi^{*}+\Xi_{i} \cdot \mathbf{y}\right)+w_{i}\right)} \\
& =\frac{1}{Z} e^{\beta\left(\frac{\cos \left(\mu_{i, r}\right) e^{w_{r}}+\cos \left(\mu_{i, s}\right) e^{w_{s}}}{e^{w_{r}}+e^{w_{s}}}+\Xi_{i} \cdot \mathbf{y}\right)+w_{i}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now consider in particular a pattern, $\Xi_{i}$, which is not one of the two isolated ones, so that $i \neq r, s$. Now $\mu_{m} \leq \mu_{r, s}$ and as such $\cos \left(\mu_{m}\right) \geq \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)$. Therefore we can bound the $i^{\text {th }}$ soft-max component, as follows

$$
\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+\mathbf{w}\right)\right]_{i} \leq \frac{1}{Z} e^{\beta\left(\cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)+\Xi_{i} \cdot \mathbf{y}\right)+w_{i}}
$$

Now recall we consider $\mathbf{y}$, such that the angle between $\mathbf{y}$ satisfies $\angle\left(\Xi_{i}, \mathbf{y}\right) \geq \mu_{m}$, and therefore $\cos \left(\angle\left(\Xi_{i}, \mathbf{y}\right)\right) \leq$ $\cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)$. From this we get the further bound

$$
\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+w\right)\right]_{i} \leq \frac{1}{Z} e^{\beta \cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)(1+| | \mathbf{y} \|)+w_{i}}
$$

If we consider (without loss of generality) the $r^{\text {th }}$ component of the soft-max (i.e. one corresponding to one of the isolated patterns), we get from Eq. 10 that

$$
\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)\right)\right]_{r}=\frac{1}{Z} e^{\beta\left(\frac{e^{w_{r}}+\cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right) e^{w_{r}}}{e^{w_{r}}+e^{w_{r}}}+\Xi_{r} \cdot \mathbf{y}\right)+w_{i}}
$$

Recall that we chose $\mathbf{y}$ above, such that we have $\angle\left(\mathbf{y}, \Xi_{r}\right) \leq \angle\left(\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}\right)$ and as such $\cos \left(\angle\left(\Xi_{r}, \Xi_{s}\right)\right) \geq \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)$. By further setting $p=e^{w_{r}} /\left(e^{w_{r}}+e^{w_{r}}\right)$, we get

$$
\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)\right)\right]_{r} \geq \frac{1}{Z} e^{\beta\left(p+(1-p) \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)+| | \mathbf{y} \| \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)\right)+w_{i}}
$$

With this preliminary calculation, we now look at the ratio of the soft-max components of a non-isolated pattern, compared to an isolated pattern. Let's call this ratio $\mathcal{S}$, i.e.

$$
\mathcal{S}=\frac{\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+w\right)\right]_{i}}{\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\beta \Xi\left(\Xi^{*}+\mathbf{y}\right)+w\right)\right]_{r}}
$$

The reason we are looking at this ratio is as follows. If $\mathcal{S} \ll 1$, then that would mean that the isolated pattern dominates the non-isolated one, and as such we are safe to ignore the contribution of the non-isolated patterns. While if $\mathcal{S} \ll 1$, then the non-isolated patterns do contribute to an extent, which we cannot ignore. With this we look at $\mathcal{S}$, and by combining Eq. 11 and Eq. 12 we get

$$
\mathcal{S} \leq \frac{e^{\beta \cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)(1+| | \mathbf{y} \|)+w_{i}}}{e^{\beta\left(p+(1-p) \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)+| | \mathbf{y} \| \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)\right)+w_{i}}}
$$

And thus simplifying we have

$$
\mathcal{S} \leq e^{\beta\left[\left\{\cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)-\cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)\right\}(1+| | \mathbf{y} \|)-p+p \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)\right]+\left(w_{i}-w_{r}\right)}
$$

Note when $\log (\mathcal{S}) \ll 0$, we in particular have $\mathcal{S} \ll 1$. We will look at the logarithmic inequality corresponding to Eq. 13,

$$
\log (\mathcal{S}) \leq \beta\left\{\cos \left(\mu_{m}\right)-\cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)\right\}(1+| | \mathbf{y} \mid|)-p+p \cos \left(\mu_{r, s}\right)+w_{i}-w_{r}
$$

To have a more explicit picture, let us consider an approximation for the angle between the isolated patterns, $\mu_{r, s}$, and for $\mu_{m}$. Proceeding via a Taylor expansion, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log (\mathcal{S}) & \leq \beta\left(\frac{\mu_{r, s}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\mu_{m}^{2}}{2}\right)(1+| | \mathbf{y} \mid|)-\frac{p \mu_{r, s}^{2}}{2}+w_{i}-w_{r}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu_{r, s}^{4}, \mu_{m}^{4}\right) \\
& \leq \beta\left(\frac{\mu_{r, s}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\mu_{m}^{2}}{2}\right)(1+| | \mathbf{y} \mid|)+w_{i}-w_{r}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu_{r, s}^{4}, \mu_{m}^{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that we assumed that $\mu_{r, s} \ll \mu_{m}$. As such, for sufficiently large $\beta$ (when $\beta \mu_{r, s}^{2}$ is of order unity, compared with $w_{i}, w_{r}$ that are of order unity), we will expect to have $\log (\mathcal{S}) \ll 0$ and the non-isolated patterns do not contribute to the dynamics in the vicinity of $\Xi^{*}$.

question: How does the multi-branch network architecture address imbalanced training?
answer: The multi-branch network shares parameters in shallow layers and splits into two branches with separate parameters for different phases, ensuring effective training of predictive and generative tasks.

evidence.text:
# 2.1.2 Training Strategies 

In our framework, the growth phase occupies a small portion of the overall training process, with the best-performing configuration being $t_{n} / T=0.01$. If we follow the standard diffusion training procedure and sample time steps uniformly, the number of iterations for the predictive task only takes $1 \%$ of the total training process, which will significantly degrade the model's performance on this task. Therefore, to ensure sufficient training for the predictive task, we oversample the time steps in the growth phase. Thus, the final loss can be written as the following equation:

$$
\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t \sim \frac{1}{2} U\left(1, t_{n}\right]+\frac{1}{2} U\left(t_{n}, T\right)}\left(\mathcal{L}_{t}^{(x)}+\mathcal{L}_{t}^{(h)}+\mathcal{L}_{t}^{(c)}\right)
$$

However, we observed that oversampling can lead to imbalanced training across the full range of time steps, which adversely affects the quality of the generative process. To address this issue, we propose a multi-branch network architecture. The network shares parameters in the shallow layers but splits into two branches in the deeper layers, with separate sets of parameters for each branch. These branches are activated in different phases of training: one branch is dedicated to the nucleation phase, while the other handles the growth phase, as shown in Figure 3. This design ensures that the predictive and generative tasks are trained effectively without negatively influencing each other.

question: Why is it important to test collision avoidance algorithms on physical robots after training them on synthetic data?
answer: Testing on physical robots ensures that the algorithms perform effectively in real-world conditions without further adjustments.

evidence.text:
## D. Real-World Experiments

In addition to the simulation experiments, we perform a set of collision avoidance experiments with a physical robot. For the experiments, we use a Continental delivery mobile robot which is modeled as the Dubins car model described by (13) in Section V-A. The robot uses a 3D LiDAR for local environment observations and wheel encoders for odometry. All computation is performed onboard with a mini PC Intel NUC11PHi7 (CPU: i7-1165G7 8x2.80GHz; RAM: 32GB; GPU: RTX2060 6GB).

As a representative scenario, we consider a task in which the local planner needs to avoid a static obstacle between two waypoints based only on the local observations. Like in the simulations, we conduct the experiments for different MPC methods and different lengths of the prediction horizon. The planners and the hypernetwork trained on synthetic data are directly transferred from the simulations to the real robot without any additional fine-tuning. The results of the experiments for different horizon lengths are presented in Table I, while Fig. 9 illustrates robot motion for the prediction horizon of 10 steps ( 1 s ). Our method successfully avoids collision for all tested horizon lengths while still achieving comparable real-time performance, which is consistent with our simulations and theoretical discussion. question: What does it mean for an element to be "rather below" another element in a bounded lattice?
answer: An element $a$ is rather below (well inside) another element $b$, written as $a \prec b$, if there exists $\mathrm{c} \in A$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.

evidence.text:
# 5. Regularity 

In this section we characterize when the four completions are regular. For distributive lattices, regularity is a natural strengthening of subfitness. As we saw above, subfitness of the canonical completion is equivalent to the lattice being Boolean. As we will see below, regularity yields the same result for the ideal completion. A more subtle result occurs for the Bruns-Lakser completion. The situation for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion is further complicated by the fact that the latter need not be distributive. Regular lattices behave very differently in the non-distributive setting; in particular, regularity no longer implies subfitness. This will be discussed in more detail in a forthcoming paper. Here we will restrict our attention to Dedekind-MacNeille completions that are distributive.

The next definition is well known for frames (see, e.g., [PP12, Sec. V.5]) and generalizes directly to bounded lattices.

Definition 5.1. Let $A$ be a bounded lattice.
(1) For $a, b \in A, a$ is rather below (well inside) $b$, written $a \prec b$, provided there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.
(2) $A$ is regular if $a \nless b$ implies the existence of $c \in A$ such that $c \prec a$ but $c \nless b$.

Remark 5.2.
(1) If $a$ has the pseudocomplement $a^{*}$, then $a \prec b$ iff $a^{*} \vee b=1$.
(2) A is regular iff every element is the join of elements rather below it. This is the usual definition of regularity in frames, but the above definition is more appealing for arbitrary bounded lattices. Observe that while arbitrary joins may not exist in $A \in$ DLat, if $A$ is regular then the join of $\{b \in A: b \prec a\}$ is $a$, so this join does exist for every $a \in A$.
(3) Every Boolean lattice is regular and in [BMPWW17, p. 360] it is shown that every regular distributive lattice is subfit. In a forthcoming paper we will show that this is no longer true for non-distributive lattices.

Our first goal is to characterize when distributive lattices are regular using Priestley duality. We do so by generalizing some existing results for frames, proved in [BGJ16, Lem. 3.3, 3.6]. Since pseudocomplements may not exist in an arbitrary distributive lattice, the proofs below are somewhat more involved. We start by characterizing the rather below relation.

Lemma 5.3. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X ,

$$
a \prec b \text { iff } \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})
$$

Proof. First suppose $a \prec b$. Then there is $c \in A$ such that $a \wedge c=0$ and $b \vee c=1$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ is an upset, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$. Thus, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$.

Conversely, suppose $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Since $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ is a closed downset, it is the intersection of clopen downsets containing it (see Fact 2.6). But then by compactness, there is a clopen downset D such that $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{D} \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Let $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ be such that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathrm{D}$. Then $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$, and hence $\mathfrak{a} \prec \mathfrak{b}$.

Following [BGJ16, Def. 3.4], for each $V \in L(X)$, define the regular part of $V$ to be

$$
\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{~V})=\bigcup\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{~L}(\mathrm{X}): \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{~V}\}
$$

For simplicity, we abbreviate the regular part of $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ by $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$.
Proposition 5.4. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X , the following are equivalent:
(1) A is regular.
(2) $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ for each $\mathfrak{a} \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $a \in A$. Take $x \in s(a)$ and let $U$ be a clopen neighborhood of $x$ in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. We must show that $U \cap R_{a} \neq \varnothing$. Since $U$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, there are $\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{x} \in \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \subseteq \mathrm{U}$ (see Fact 2.6(1)). Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ (by intersecting $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ with $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ ). Because $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \neq \varnothing$, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$, so $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{d}$. Since A is regular, there is $\mathrm{e} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{e} \prec \mathrm{c}$ and $\mathrm{e} \nless \mathrm{d}$. By Lemma 5.3, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$, so $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}} \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$. Thus, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}} \cap(\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})) \neq \varnothing$, so $R_{a} \cap U \neq \varnothing$, and hence $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1): Let $a \nless b$. Then $s(a) \nsubseteq s(b)$, so $R_{a} \nsubseteq s(b)$ since $R_{a}$ is dense in $s(a)$. Therefore, there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\downarrow \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{a})$ and $\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{b})$. Thus, $\mathrm{c} \prec \mathrm{a}$ (by Lemma 5.3) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, yielding that A is regular.

We next give a general characterization, akin to Theorem 4.2, of when regularity is preserved and/or reflected when moving between $A$ and $B$, where $A$ is a bounded sublattice of B. We write $\prec_{A}$ or $\prec_{B}$ to emphasize which rather below relation is being used. Clearly $a \prec_{A} b$ implies $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $a, b \in A$, however the converse is not true in general. Because of this, the proposition below requires an extra assumption. As in Theorem 4.2, distributivity plays no rôle.

Proposition 5.5. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B. Suppose that $a \prec_{A} b$ iff $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A}$.
(1) If A is join-dense in B and B is regular then A is regular.
(2) If A is both join- and meet-dense in B and A is regular then B is regular.

Proof. (1) Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $B$ is regular, there is $x \in B$ with $x \prec_{B} a$ and $x \nless b$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $B$, there is $c \in A$ with $c \leqslant x$ and $c \nless b$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \leqslant \mathrm{x} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, and hence $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Thus, A is regular.
(2) Let $x, y \in B$ with $x \nless y$. Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $B$, there are $a, b \in A$ such that $a \leqslant x, y \leqslant b$, and $a \nless b$. Because $A$ is regular, there is $c \in A$ with $c \prec_{A} a$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{x}$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{y}$. Thus, B is regular.

Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $\mathcal{D M A}$, one could expect that regularity is both preserved and reflected by the Dedekind-MacNeille completion, but this is not the case since the additional assumption in Proposition 5.5 may not be satisfied. We again emphasize that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is not always distributive and hence regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ need not imply subfitness. Thus, we make the blanket assumption that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive. While this does not necessarily imply that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, it is indeed the case provided $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.

Proposition 5.6. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. Then regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, and hence $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

Proof. If $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive, by [BMPWW17, p. 360] regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies subfitness of $\mathcal{D M A}$, and consequently subfitness of $A$ by Corollary 4.3. But then $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6. Hence, $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame and $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7.

The above proposition yields the following characterization of when a distributive Dede-kind-MacNeille completion is regular.

Proposition 5.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.
(2) A is subfit and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(3) A is proHeyting and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.

question: Are there any methods that integrate both HOLP and Ridge-HOLP formulas into their screening process?
answer: Yes, methods such as the group HOLP method, Dynamic Tilted Current Correlation method, and HOLP-DF method integrate both HOLP and Ridge-HOLP formulas into their screening process.

evidence.text:
### 2.2 HOLP and Ridge-HOLP

The HOLP method uses the Moore-Penrose inverse of $\boldsymbol{X}$ to estimate the vector of regression coefficients in the full regression model, that is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\right)^{-1} \boldsymbol{y}
$$

Then, the features are ranked by the absolute values of their estimated coefficients denoted by $\left|\hat{\beta}_{j}\right|, j=1, \ldots, p$. Then, a predetermined threshold $m$ is used to screen the top $m$ features. Wang and Leng (2016) showed that Equation (2) suffers from instability when $\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{X}^{\top}$ is close to degeneracy or when $n$ is close to $p$. To address this issue, Wang and Leng (2016) proposed Ridge-HOLP:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}=\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{X}^{\top}+r \mathbb{1}_{n}\right)^{-1} \boldsymbol{y}
$$

where $r$ is the ridge tuning parameter and $\mathbb{I}_{n}$ denotes the identity matrix.
The Ridge-HOLP formula in Equation (3) is equal to the standard ridge formula but is more efficient when $p>n$ as the computational complexity of Ridge-HOLP is $O\left(n^{3}+n^{2} p\right)$, while the standard ridge formula is $O\left(p^{3}+p^{2} n\right)$. This is because RidgeHOLP requires an $(n \times p)$ by $(p \times n)$ multiplication $O\left(n^{2} p\right)$ and an $(n \times n)$ matrix inverse $O\left(n^{3}\right)$, while standard ridge requires a $(p \times n)$ by $(n \times p)$ multiplication $O\left(p^{2} n\right)$ and a $(p \times p)$ matrix inverse $O\left(p^{3}\right)$. When $n$ is close to $p$, Wang and Leng (2016) recommend using Ridge-HOLP with a fixed tuning parameter $r=10$.

The penalty in the Ridge-HOLP formula in Equation (3) also helps to handle multicollinearity. When features are highly correlated, then estimated regression coefficients have large variances (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970), which leads to poor ranking accuracy and thus lower screening performance. The penalty in Ridge-HOLP reduces the estimation sensitivity. However, selecting an appropriate tuning parameter $r$ is crucial to balance the bias-variance trade-off and to maximize the screening performance of Ridge-HOLP.

Multiple feature screening methods have integrated the HOLP and Ridge-HOLP formulas (2) and (3) into their screening process. Examples of this include the group HOLP method of Qiu and Ahn (2020), the Dynamic Tilted Current Correlation method of Zhao et al. (2021), and the HOLP-DF method of Samat et al. (2022). In these methods, the HOLP and Ridge-HOLP formulas are an integral part of the screening process.

question: Are validators required to stake tokens to participate in AlArena?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
## 2 AlArena System Design
### 2.1 Participants

Fig. 1 shows the overview of AlArena system. There are various categories of participants in the AlArena system:

- Task Creators: Task creators are responsible for defining training tasks and their specific requirements, including selecting and designing appropriate learning algorithms for model training and validation. To promote decentralization, the created tasks can be reviewed and verified by the stakeholders within AlArena.
- Training Nodes: Given a created task, training nodes are responsible for training the model on their service using public data. To participate, training nodes must stake blockchain assets or tokens to establish their eligibility. Training nodes will receive rewards based on their stake amount and performance.
- Validators: Validators are responsible for assessing the work completed by training nodes and submitting validation scores that influence the distribution of rewards. To participate, validators must stake tokens, which not only allows them to validate assigned tasks but also ensures fair task allocation.

[^0]- Delegators: Delegators contribute to the AlArena system by supporting the staking process of other participants without directly engaging in task training or validation. They stake tokens on behalf of other participants, boosting the delegates' capacity to earn greater rewards. In return, delegators share in the rewards earned by their delegatees, according to predefined algorithms that reflect their staked contributions.

question: Why is it challenging to create effective policies based on general principles for AI behavior?
answer: Challenges arise from determining when principles are upheld and handling conflicting principles. While values guide discussions, they may not provide concrete solutions for policy development.

evidence.text:
# 3d. Extracting Values 

One of the most 'scalable' solutions, and the one employed by most of the teams is constitutional Al [26] which relies on a fine-tuned Al 'teaching' other Al models to ensure that the outputs are aligned to some desired behavior - defined through a written list of principles given by human experts. The AI is trained to follow these principles through a reinforcement learning process - in which the feedback is provided by a 'teacher AI' tasked with recognizing transgressions of principles. This process has had remarkable success in protecting AI outputs trained in the process against red-teaming attacks or attacks that can be classified more neatly into categories of well-documented societal harms, such as explicit manifestations of racist hate speech (among other examples).

Naturally then, most of the teams aimed to produce general statements or principles (or values) for Al to follow. This is probably because Open AI's call explicitly states that 'Laws encode values and norms to regulate behavior' suggesting that laws are what is needed [2]. This in line with AI Ethics and AI policy discussions which have amassed a host of values or principles like Fairness, Accountability, Transparency and Privacy which Al systems should aspire to.

It seems ideal to be able to simply give Al a list of agreed-upon principles to follow but it is not self-evident when a principle is being upheld or not or what to do when two different principles contradict [27]. As Carl Miller of the Recursive Public project put it to us: 'values or principles are a good starting point for discussions but on their own are not satisfying or efficient material for developing policy from.'

$$

$$

$$

$$

The Kuratowski-Painlevé upper limit of the sequence of sets $\left\{A_{n}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, denoted $\mathrm{Ls}_{n \rightarrow \infty} A_{n}$, is the set of points $x$ for which there exists a subsequence $\left\{x^{\left(n_{k}\right)}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of points such that $x^{\left(n_{k}\right)} \in A_{n_{k}}$ for all $k$ and $x=\lim _{k \rightarrow \infty} x^{\left(n_{k}\right)}$. A sequence $\left\{A_{n}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is said to converge, in the Kuratowski-Painlevé sense, to a set $A$ if $\mathrm{Ls}_{n \rightarrow \infty} A_{n}=A=\operatorname{Li}_{n \rightarrow \infty} A_{n}$, in which case we write $A=\operatorname{Lim}_{n \rightarrow \infty} A_{n}$.

In [8] it was shown that for all $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$ we have:

$$
\lim _{p \rightarrow+\infty} \lambda \stackrel{p}{+} \mu= \begin{cases}\lambda & \text { if } \quad|\lambda|>|\mu| \\ \frac{1}{2}(\lambda+\mu) & \text { if } \quad|\lambda|=|\mu| \\ \mu & \text { if } \quad|\lambda|<|\mu|\end{cases}

# 4 An application in the cryptocurrency market 

In this section, risk measures proposed in Section 3 are applied for cryptocurrency market dataset to quantify the relative spillover effects. We employ a static methodology to quantify the relative risk contributions of cryptocurrencies using the multivariate risk measures discussed in this paper. The static approach offers several distinct advantages that align with the goals of this study. Firstly, it delivers clear and interpretable results, allowing for a straightforward comparison of risk contributions among different assets. This clarity is essential for both theoretical validation and practical application, as it provides actionable insights for investors and regulators. Secondly, the static method is computationally efficient, enabling the analysis of large datasets and the application of complex risk measures without excessive resource demands. This efficiency is particularly valuable in the context of cryptocurrencies, where data volumes are substantial and market dynamics are intricate. Lastly, the static approach provides a stable framework for initial exploration and validation of new risk measurement tools, ensuring that the core properties of these tools can be assessed reliably before extending to more complex dynamic analyses.

The analysis utilizes three cryptocurrencies (CCs): Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Monero

(XMR). The data contains daily closing prices in USD stemming from the Community Network Data provided by CoinMetrics. ${ }^{3}$ The sample includes $N=3226$ observations from 01/09/2015 to 30/06/2024 as CCs are traded every day, including weekends. For ease of our subsequent analysis, the prices are transformed in log-losses, that is,

$$
X_{i, t}=-100 \cdot \ln \left(p_{i, t} / p_{i, t-1}\right)
$$

where $X_{i, t}$ represents the percentage-based log-losses ${ }^{4}$ on day $t$ with $i \in\{1,2,3\}$ for BTC, ETH, and XRP and $p_{i, t}$ denotes the closing price for cryptocurrency $i$ on day $t$. For each cryptocurrency $i, N$ observations $\left(x_{i, 1}, \ldots, x_{i, N}\right)$ are obtained. A statistical summary for these percentage-based log-loss samples is shown in Table 1, and their Spearman and Kendall correlation matrices are provided in Table 2. From Table 1, it can be observed that both BTC and XMR have relatively low mean losses, with BTC showing the smallest standard deviation, indicating a more stable performance. The elevated standard deviations observed for Ethereum and Monero relative to Bitcoin may reflect heightened exposure to volatility inherent in the cryptocurrency market, particularly during discrete events or periods of acute market stress. Ethereum, for instance, has demonstrated sensitivity to regulatory scrutiny and protocol upgrades (e.g., transitions to Ethereum 2.0), while Monero's volatility has been amplified by debates over privacy regulations and network congestion. These idiosyncratic factors, coupled with broader market uncertainty, likely contribute to the pronounced fluctuations seen in both assets compared to Bitcoin. The results from Table 2 indicate that all the three cryptocurrencies enjoy positive dependence structure in losses, and the correlation between BTC and ETH is relatively stronger compared with the correlation between ETH and XMR.

We use the method of inference function for margins (IFM) proposed in Joe (2005), which has been also widely applied by many research papers such as Shi \& Yang (2018) and Zhu et al. (2023). Interested readers can refer to Joe (2005) for more efficiency properties of IFM. To calculate the co-risk measures introduced both in Sections 2 and 3, the following empirical procedure is adopted:

- Step 1: Estimate the respective marginal model for each group of samples separately.
- Step 2: Estimate the copula based on the pseudo-sample observations obtained from the parametric probability integral transformation on the samples.
- Step 3: Calculate the respective risk measures.

question: How does Koszul duality contribute to understanding curved Morita deformations?
answer: Koszul duality helps in analyzing curved Morita deformations by providing constructions that demonstrate how equivalent deformations map to the same Hochschild class, aiding in proving injectivity within this framework.

evidence.text:
# 2. Curved Morita Deformations 

2.1. Cdg algebras and modules. We now give the basic definitions of cdg algebras and modules; for a more detailed introduction, see [LL24] and the references therein. Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A cdg algebra $\mathcal{A}$ over $R$ is given by a graded $R$-algebra $\mathcal{A}^{\#}$ equipped with a derivation $d_{\mathcal{A}} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{R}\left(\mathcal{A}^{\#}, \mathcal{A}^{\#}\right)$ of degree 1 and an element $c \in A^{2}$ such that $d_{\mathcal{A}}(c)=0$

and $d_{\mathcal{A}}^{2}=[c,-]$; the derivation $d$ is called predifferential and the element $c$ curvature of the algebra. A right cdg module over a cdg algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a graded right $\mathcal{A}^{\#}$-module $M^{\#}$ equipped with an $\mathcal{A}^{\#}$-derivation $d_{M} \in$ $\operatorname{Hom}_{R}\left(M^{\#}, M^{\#}\right)^{1}$ such that $d_{M}^{2} m=-m c$ for all $m \in M$; if $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are cdg algebras, a $\operatorname{cdg} \mathcal{A}-\mathcal{B}$ bimodule is a graded $\mathcal{A}-\mathcal{B}$ bimodule $M$ equipped with a degree 1 derivation $d_{M}$ for which the identity $d_{M}^{2} m=c_{\mathcal{A}} m-m c_{\mathcal{B}}$ holds. For us, a morphism of cdg algebras is a morphism of graded algebras which preserves the curvature and commutes with the multiplications and predifferentials. Any morphism of cdg algebras $\mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}$ endows $\mathcal{B}$ with the structure of a $\operatorname{cdg} \mathcal{A}-\mathcal{B}$ bimodule. Note that, unlike in the dg case, a $\operatorname{cdg} \mathcal{A}-\mathcal{B}$ bimodule does not have an underlying structure of a $\operatorname{cdg} \mathcal{A}$ or $\mathcal{B}$ module; in particular the $\operatorname{cdg} \mathcal{A}$-bimodule $\mathcal{A}$ is not, in general, a cdg $\mathcal{A}$-module.
2.2. Hochschild cohomology and Morita bimodules. Let $A, B$ be dg algebras over $k$ and $X$ an $A-B$ bimodule. Recall that $X$ is said to be a (derived) Morita bimodule if the functor

$$
-\otimes_{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathrm{L}} X: D(A) \rightarrow D(B)
$$

is an equivalence. Following [KL09], we will use the arrow category $\mathfrak{c}_{X}$ associated to the bimodule $X$, which is a dg-category with two distinct objects $P$ and $Q$ and
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{c}_{X}}(P, P)=A, \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{c}_{X}}(Q, Q)=B, \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{c}_{X}}(Q, P)=X$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak{c}_{X}}(P, Q)=0$.
with composition defined in the obvious way. The category $\mathfrak{c}_{X}$ comes equipped with two fully faithful dg functors

$$
j: A \rightarrow \mathfrak{c}_{X} \text { and } i: B \rightarrow \mathfrak{c}_{X}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are seen as dg-categories with one object, which are identified respectively with $P$ and $Q$. In [Kel03], Keller introduced for any Morita bimodule $X$ a bijection ${ }^{1}$

$$
\varphi_{X}: \mathrm{HH}^{\bullet}(B) \rightarrow \mathrm{HH}^{\bullet}(A)
$$

between the Hochschild cohomologies of $B$ and $A$ which is functorial with respect to the (derived) tensor product of bimodules. By construction of $\varphi_{X}$, the diagram
![img-1.jpeg](img-1.jpeg)

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ In fact $\varphi_{X}$ is shown to give an isomorphism in the homotopy category of $B_{\infty}$ algebras between the Hochschild complexes, but we'll only need the result at the homotopy level.

is a commutative diagram of isomorphisms, where $j^{*}, i^{*}$ are the maps induced by the restrictions along the fully faithful functors $A \rightarrow \mathfrak{c}_{X}$ and $B \rightarrow \mathfrak{c}_{X}$.
2.3. Curved Morita deformations. Denote with $k[\varepsilon]$ the algebra of the dual numbers. Let $A$ be a dg algebra over $k$. In the following, we will just say $k[\varepsilon]$-free to mean free as a graded $k[\varepsilon]$-module.

Definition 2.1. A curved Morita deformation of $A$ is a $k[\varepsilon]$-free $\operatorname{cdg} k[\varepsilon]$ algebra $B_{\varepsilon}$ equipped with, setting $B:=B_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k$, a $B-A$ Morita bimodule $X$. Two curved deformations $\left(B_{\varepsilon}, X\right)$ and $\left(C_{\varepsilon}, Y\right)$ are equivalent if there exists a $\operatorname{cdg} B_{\varepsilon}-C_{\varepsilon}$ bimodule $Z_{\varepsilon}$ that is free as a graded $B_{\varepsilon}$-module and as a graded $C_{\varepsilon}$-module (in particular, it is $k[\varepsilon]$-free) and such that, setting $C=C_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k$, the $B-C$ bimodule $Z=Z_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k$ is cofibrant as a bimodule and there exists an isomorphism $X \cong Z \otimes_{C} Y$ in the derived category of $B-A$ bimodules.

We will denote with $\operatorname{cDef}_{A}(k[\varepsilon])$ the set of curved Morita deformations of $A$ up to equivalence.

Lemma 2.2. Equivalence of curved deformations is an equivalence relation, so the set $\operatorname{cDef}_{A}(k[\varepsilon])$ is well defined.

Proof. Transitivity is easy, since if a deformation $B_{\varepsilon}$ is equivalent via $X_{\varepsilon}$ to $C_{\varepsilon}$ and $C_{\varepsilon}$ is equivalent to $D_{\varepsilon}$ via $Y_{\varepsilon}$ then one can check that $X_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{C_{\varepsilon}} Y_{\varepsilon}$ gives an equivalence between $B_{\varepsilon}$ and $D_{\varepsilon}$. Symmetry is less immediate: let $Z_{\varepsilon}$ be a morphism between deformations $B_{\varepsilon}$ and $C_{\varepsilon}$. Then $Z$ is a Morita bimodule, thus there exists a cofibrant $C-B$ Morita bimodule $W$ such that $Z \otimes_{C} W \cong B$ and $W \otimes_{B} Z \cong C$. Denoting with $\mathfrak{c}_{W}$ the arrow category of $W$, by definition of $\varphi_{W}$ there is a commutative diagram of isomorphisms
![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

Since $\varphi_{W}$ is an inverse to $\varphi_{Z}$ and by Proposition 2.3 the map $\varphi_{Z}$ carries the class that defines $B_{\varepsilon}$ to the one defining $C_{\varepsilon}$, reasoning exactly as in the proof of Proposition 2.5 we can conclude that there exists a graded $B_{\varepsilon}$-free and $C_{\varepsilon}$-free $C_{\varepsilon}-B_{\varepsilon}$ cdg bimodule $\dot{W}_{\varepsilon}$ such that its reduction $\dot{W}$ is cofibrant and isomorphic in the derived category of bimodules to $W$, which is a Morita equivalence. We have thus proved that equivalence of curved deformations is a symmetric relation. Reflexivity is proven in the same way: for any deformation $B_{\varepsilon}$ we have the $\operatorname{cdg} B_{\varepsilon}$-bimodule $B_{\varepsilon}$ whose reduction

$B$ is manifestly a Morita bimodule; resolving this via the same procedure as before, we are done.

Remark. It is clear that the set $\operatorname{cDef}_{A}(k[\varepsilon])$ is really just the set of connected components of a (higher) groupoid. A satisfactory construction of the whole groupoid would require a generalization to curved categories of the Morita theory of [Toë07] where the weak equivalences are, at least on $k[\varepsilon]$-free categories, the morphisms inducing weak equivalence on the (uncurved) reductions. In this generalization, the mapping spaces would be given by (an enhancement of) some version of the semiderived category of bimodules, following constructions in [Pos18]; indeed our condition of graded $C_{\varepsilon}$-freeness and cofibrancy of the reduction is implied by the natural cofibrancy condition for the semiderived category of [Pos18]. This is also related to the 1-derived category of [LL24], since its subcategory given by the $k[\varepsilon]$-free modules coincides with the semiderived category. At the moment, this theory does not exist so we have to define our objects "by hand". In particular, we have no intrinsic definition of the left derived functor of the reduction $-\otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k$ from (weakly) curved $\operatorname{dg} k[\varepsilon]$-algebras to $\operatorname{dg} k$-algebras; we solve this issue by restricting to $k[\varepsilon]$-free algebras to begin with.
2.4. Curved deformations and Hochschild cohomology. It is wellknown (see [Low08; KL09]) that there is a correspondence between the set of Hochschild 2-cocycles and that of deformations of $A$ as a $c A_{\infty}$ algebra, i.e. $k[\varepsilon]$-free $c A_{\infty}$ algebras $A_{\varepsilon}$ equipped with an isomorphism of dg algebras $A_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k \cong A$. Define a map

$$
\nu: \operatorname{cDef}_{A}(k[\varepsilon]) \rightarrow \mathrm{HH}^{2}(A)
$$

in the same way as in [KL09]: if $\left(B_{\varepsilon}, X\right)$ is a curved deformation of $A$, then $B_{\varepsilon}$ is a $c A_{\infty}$ deformation of $B$, so defines a cocycle $\eta$ and a class $[\eta]$ in $\mathrm{HH}^{2}(B)$. The class $\nu\left(B_{\varepsilon}\right) \in \mathrm{HH}^{2}(A)$ is given by definition by $\varphi_{X}([\eta])$.

Proposition 2.3. The map $\nu$ is well defined.
Proof. The proof of [KL09, Proposition 3.3] applies verbatim.
Proposition 2.4. The map $\nu$ is surjective.
Proof. Let $[\eta] \in \mathrm{HH}^{2}(A)$ be an Hochschild class; then any cocycle $\eta$ representing the class defines a $c A_{\infty}$ deformation $A_{\varepsilon}$ of $A$. Assume for now that there exists a $k[\varepsilon]$-free cdg algebra $B_{\varepsilon}$ equipped with a $c A_{\infty} B_{\varepsilon}-A_{\varepsilon}$ bimodule $Z_{\varepsilon}$ such that the reduction $Z$ is a Morita $B-A$ bimodule (in particular, cannot have higher components). It is clear that $\left(B_{\varepsilon}, Z\right)$ is an element of

$\operatorname{cDef}_{A}(k[\varepsilon])$. By definition of $\varphi_{Z}$, the diagram
![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)
commutes, and $\mathfrak{c}_{Z_{\varepsilon}}$ defines a $c A_{\infty}$ deformation of $\mathfrak{c}_{Z}$ which defines an Hochschild cocycle $\mu \in \mathrm{HH}^{2}\left(\mathfrak{c}_{Z}\right)$. Moreover by construction, $j^{*}[\mu]=[\eta]$; therefore, $\nu\left(B_{\varepsilon}\right)=j^{*}[\mu]=[\eta]$. We are left to prove that such $B_{\varepsilon}$ exists. Consider the cdg algebra $\mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right)$ given as the image via the curved Yoneda embedding (see [DL18] for a complete description of the curved Yoneda embedding and of the category of $q A_{\infty}$ modules) of the $c A_{\infty}$ algebra $A_{\varepsilon}$. This is isomorphic to the cdg algebra $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{\varepsilon}-\operatorname{Mod}}\left(A_{\varepsilon}, A_{\varepsilon}\right)$ where the hom is taken in the cdg category of $q A_{\infty} A_{\varepsilon}$-modules. Since $A_{\varepsilon}$ is $k[\varepsilon]$-free, the same holds for $\mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right)$ since, as a graded $k[\varepsilon]$-module, it is a product of homs between $k[\varepsilon]$-free modules. There is a natural map of $c A_{\infty}$ algebras $A_{\varepsilon} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{Y}} \mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right)$ given by the curved Yoneda embedding. Its higher components are killed by reduction, so setting $\mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right)_{0}:=\mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right) \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k$, we have a morphism of dg algebras $A \xrightarrow{\mathcal{Y}_{0}} \mathcal{Y}\left(A_{\varepsilon}\right)_{0}$. This coincides with the $A_{\infty}$ Yoneda embedding which, by [DL18, Theorem 4.15] is a quasi-isomorphism and we are done.

Proposition 2.5. The map $\nu$ is injective.
Proof. Suppose that $\left(B_{\varepsilon}, X\right)$ and $\left(C_{\varepsilon}, Y\right)$ are cdg deformations of $A$ such that $\nu\left(B_{\varepsilon}\right)=\nu\left(C_{\varepsilon}\right)$. Let $Z$ be a cofibrant Morita $B-C$ bimodule such that there is an isomorphism $Z \otimes_{C} Y \cong X$ in the derived category - such a bimodule always exists by the standard Morita theory of dg-algebras, see e.g. the proof of [KL09, Proposition 3.7]. Then by definition of $\varphi_{Z}$ the diagram
![img-4.jpeg](img-4.jpeg)
is commutative. Denoting with $\eta_{B}$ and $\eta_{C}$ the Hochschild cocycles of $B$ and $C$ defining their $c A_{\infty}$ deformations $B_{\varepsilon}$ and $C_{\varepsilon}$, since they map to the same element in $\mathrm{HH}^{2}(A)$ and all arrows are isomorphisms, there must be

an element $[\gamma] \in \mathrm{HH}^{2}\left(\mathfrak{c}_{Z}\right)$ such that

$$
i^{*}([\gamma])=\left[\eta_{\mathcal{B}}\right] \text { and } j^{*}([\gamma])=\left[\eta_{\mathcal{C}}\right]
$$

By [KL09, Lemma 3.8], it is actually possible to find a 2-cocycle $\gamma$ mapping to $\eta_{\mathcal{A}}$ and $\eta_{\mathcal{B}}$ before passing to cohomology. Now $\gamma$ defines a $c A_{\infty}$ deformation of $\mathfrak{c}_{Z}$ which is immediately seen to be itself an arrow category for some $B_{\varepsilon}-C_{\varepsilon} c A_{\infty}$ bimodule $Z_{\varepsilon}$. By construction of $Z_{\varepsilon}$ it is $k[\varepsilon]$-free and its reduction modulo $\varepsilon$ is the $B-C$ Morita bimodule $Z$.

We are almost done, except that we need to rectify $Z_{\varepsilon}$ to a cdg - and not $c A_{\infty}$ - bimodule. This is an application of Koszul duality, for which we employ the notations and constructions of [Pos10, Sections 6 and 8] ${ }^{2}$. Using the fact that the (co)bar construction is appropriately monoidal, a $c A_{\infty} B_{\varepsilon}-C_{\varepsilon}$ bimodule corresponds to a $c A_{\infty}$ module over the cdg algebra $E_{\varepsilon}=B_{\varepsilon}{ }^{\mathrm{op}} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} C_{\varepsilon}$. This by definition is a cdg comodule $\operatorname{Bar}_{v}\left(E_{\varepsilon}, Z_{\varepsilon}\right)$ over the cdg coalgebra $\operatorname{Bar}_{v}\left(E_{\varepsilon}\right)$ (for a similar construction, see the curved bar construction of [Pos18]). Consider then the $\operatorname{cdg} E_{\varepsilon}$-module $\tilde{Z}_{\varepsilon}=E_{\varepsilon} \otimes^{r}$ $\operatorname{Bar}_{v}\left(E_{\varepsilon}, Z_{\varepsilon}\right)$. This is graded $E_{\varepsilon}$-free - its underlying graded module is $E_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} \operatorname{Bar}_{v}\left(E_{\varepsilon}, Z_{\varepsilon}\right)$ - so it is both graded $C_{\varepsilon}$-free and graded $B_{\varepsilon}$-free. Moreover, denoting $E=E_{\varepsilon} \otimes_{k[\varepsilon]} k \cong B^{\text {op }} \otimes_{k} C$, the reduction $\tilde{Z}$ of $\tilde{Z}_{\varepsilon}$ is the $\mathrm{dg} E$-module $E \otimes^{r} \operatorname{Bar}_{v}(E, Z)$, where now the tensors are over the base field $k$. By the proof of [Pos10, Theorem 6.3], this coincides with the (reduced) bar resolution of the $\mathrm{dg} E$-module $M$, which is therefore both cofibrant and, being isomorphic to $Z$ in the derived category of bimodules, a Morita equivalence.

question: How do normal, Laplace, and Cauchy distributions affect the performance of step size selectors in MCMC simulations?
answer: These distributions represent different tail behaviors that challenge the selectors. The symmetric selector maintains higher acceptance probabilities across all, while the asymmetric one struggles near modes and tails.

evidence.text:
### 5.1. Symmetric step size selection criterion

We first assess the benefit of using the symmetric step size criterion in Algorithm 2 versus the asymmetric criterion from Biron-Lattes et al. (2024) on three synthetic targets with varying tail behavior: $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, Laplace $(0,1)$, and $\operatorname{Cauchy}(0,1)$. For each $\|x\| \in\left\{10^{-5}, 10^{-4}, \ldots, 10^{2}\right\}$, we simulated $10^{7}$ draws from the target and renormalized them to the specified value. Then, for each draw, we simulated one step of AutoStep RWMH/MALA $\left(\theta_{0}=1\right)$, and recorded the acceptance probability.

The average of these acceptance probabilities is shown in Fig. 1 for AutoStep RWMH, showing that the asymmetric step size selector can get stuck for extended periods near the mode of the target (small $\|x\|$ ) and in the tails (large $\|x\|$ ). This behavior particularly problematic in practice for Bayesian inference, which is often initialized in the tails. In contrast, the proposed symmetric step size selector

![img-0.jpeg](img-0.jpeg)

Figure 1: Comparison of the symmetric (this work, blue) versus asymmetric ((Biron-Lattes et al., 2024), orange) step size criteria in Algorithm 2, in terms of the move acceptance probability of AutoStep RWMH as a function of the state norm $\|x\|$. Note that the asymmetric criterion yields very low acceptance probabilities for states near the mode (left side of the plot) and in the tails (right side of the plot).
is more robust, exhibiting an acceptance probability that is greater than $10 \%$ for the entire range of norms from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{2}$. This result aligns with our theoretical results (Proposition 4.5 and Corollary 4.6) on the irreducibility of AutoStep with the symmetric step size selection criterion.

question: What is the purpose of using bootstrap and quasi-Bayesian methods in treatment choice?
answer: Bootstrap and quasi-Bayesian methods are used for optimal treatment choice to minimize maximum regret over the identified set for the ATE, conditional on $p$.

evidence.text:
# 4.4 Optimal Treatment Assignment with Interval-Identified ATE 

In recent work, Christensen et al. (2023) note that "plug-in" rules for determining treatment choice can be sub-optimal when ATEs are not point-identified since the bounds on the ATE are not smooth functions of the reduced-form parameter $p$. Using an optimality criterion that minimizes

maximum regret over the identified set for the ATE, conditional on $p$, they advocate bootstrap and quasi-Bayesian methods for optimal treatment choice. More specifically, they consider settings for which the ATE of a treatment is identified via intersection bounds:

$$
b_{L}(p) \equiv \max _{j \in\left\{1, \ldots, J_{L}\right\}}\left\{\tilde{\ell}_{j}+\ell_{j} p\right\} \leq A T E \leq \min _{j \in\left\{1, \ldots, J_{U}\right\}}\left\{\tilde{u}_{k}+u_{k} p\right\} \equiv b_{U}(p)
$$

for some fixed and known $J_{L}, J_{U}, \tilde{\ell}_{1}, \ldots, \tilde{\ell}_{J_{L}}, \tilde{u}_{1}, \ldots, \tilde{u}_{J_{U}}, \ell_{1}, \ldots, \ell_{J_{L}}$ and $u_{1}, \ldots, u_{J_{U}} \cdot{ }^{4}$ Therefore, Assumption 3.1 trivially holds for the ATE.

Christensen et al. (2023) advocate a quasi-Bayesian implementation of their optimal treatment choice rule taking the form

$$
\hat{d}=\mathbf{1}\left(\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\max \left\{b_{U}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right), 0\right\}+\min \left\{b_{L}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right), 0\right\}\right] \geq 0\right)
$$

for some large $m$, where $\varepsilon_{1}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{m}{ }^{\text {i.i.d. }} \mathcal{N}(0, \widehat{\Sigma})$ are independent of $\hat{p}$. As the following proposition shows, this form of $\hat{d}$ satisfies Assumption 3.2 when $\hat{\gamma}_{L}(d)=\hat{\gamma}_{U}(d)$ are specified properly.

Proposition 4.1. Suppose $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=\{\hat{d}\}$, where $\hat{d}$ is defined by (4.6). Then Assumptions 3.2 and 3.3 are satisfied for

$$
\hat{\gamma}_{L}(d)=\hat{\gamma}_{U}(d)=\left(\varepsilon_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{m}^{\prime}, \underline{k}_{1}, \ldots, \underline{k}_{m}, \bar{k}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{k}_{m}, s_{1}^{\ell}, \ldots, s_{m}^{\ell}, s_{1}^{u}, \ldots, s_{m}^{u}\right)^{\prime}
$$

where $\underline{k}_{i} \equiv \operatorname{argmin}_{k \in\left\{1, \ldots, J_{U}\right\}}\left\{\tilde{u}_{k}+u_{k}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right)\right\}, \bar{k}_{i} \equiv \operatorname{argmax}_{k \in\left\{1, \ldots, J_{L}\right\}}\left\{\tilde{\ell}_{k}+\ell_{k}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right)\right\}, s_{i}^{\ell} \equiv$ $\operatorname{sign}\left(\tilde{\ell}_{\bar{k}_{i}}+\ell_{\bar{k}_{i}}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right)\right)$ and $s_{i}^{u} \equiv \operatorname{sign}\left(\tilde{u}_{\underline{k}_{i}}+u_{\underline{k}_{i}}\left(\hat{p}+\varepsilon_{i}\right)\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, m$.

question: What are Hurwitz algebras and how do they relate to vector product algebras?
answer: Hurwitz algebras are a class of normed division algebras over the real numbers, including real numbers, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions. They relate to vector product algebras (G2-algebras) through their algebraic structures and properties within symmetric ribbon categories.

evidence.text:
# 6.2.2. Classical G2 family. 

Definition 6.28. The classical G2(d) family is the symmetric ribbon category generated by a trivalent vertex modulo the following relations:
![img-48.jpeg](img-48.jpeg)

Following the PhD thesis of Boos [Boo98] in German, and its several English language expositions [Wes10, Str19, Bae01], the classical G2 family is closely related to Hurwitz algebras. We summarize this as follows.

Definition 6.29. A vector product algebra is a (non-unital) $k$-algebra $A$ with a symmetric bilinear form with a symmetric monoidal functor $G 2(d) \rightarrow \mathrm{Vec}_{k}$ sending the object to $A$ and the trivalent vertex to the multiplication. We will also call it a G2-algebra. Similarly we will refer to an object $A$ in a symmetric ribbon category $\mathcal{C}$ together with a functor $G 2(d) \rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ as a G2-algebra object in $\mathcal{C}$.

Example 6.30. $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with the standard bilinear form and multiplication given by the cross product is a vector product algebra (or G2-algebra) over $\mathbb{R}$. For this example $d=3$. If we endow $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with the defining action of $S O(3)$ then the standard bilinear form and the cross product are $S O(3)$ equivariant. Thus the defining representation of $S O(3)$ is a G2-algebra object in $\operatorname{Rep}(S O(3))$.

Definition 6.31. A Hurwitz algebra over $k$ is a unital (not necessarily associative) algebra $A$ over $k$ with a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form $\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle: A \otimes A \rightarrow k$ such that the norm map $N(v):=\langle v, v\rangle$ satisfies $N(\mathbb{1})=1$ and $N(u v)=N(u) N(v)$.

Hurwitz algebras are also called unital composition algebras. Often you will see composition algebras and Hurwitz algebras defined directly using a quadratic norm map $N$ in the definition instead of a bilinear form, but this is not necessary outside of characteristic 2.

In any Hurwitz algebra we can define an involution $\tilde{\cdot}$ via $\tilde{v}=2\langle v, \mathbb{1}\rangle-v$, and it follows that $N(v) \mathbb{1}=\widetilde{v} v$.

Example 6.32. The real numbers, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions, with their standard norms, are Hurwitz algebras over $\mathbb{R}$. Moreover, in these examples the bilinear form is positive definite, from which it follows that they're all division algebras with the inverse of $x$ given by $\bar{x} / N(x)$. Their complexifications $\left(\mathbb{C}, \mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{C}, M_{2}(\mathbb{C})\right.$, and the bi-octonions) are Hurwitz algebras over $\mathbb{C}$. (Since the quadratic form is no longer definite, they are not division algebras.)

We would like to give a definition of Hurwitz algebra objects in symmetric ribbon categories, but there's a difficulty in generalizing directly, since the construction of $N$ implicitly uses a diagonal map. In order to remedy this situation we take the "polarization" of the identity $N(u v)=$ $N(u) N(v)$ as follows. Substitute $u=a+b$ and $v=c+d$ and then take the terms that are homogeneous of degree $(1,1,1,1)$, yielding (after dividing by 2 ):

$$
\langle a c, b d\rangle+\langle a d, b c\rangle=2\langle a, b\rangle\langle c, d\rangle
$$

Conversely Equation (26) implies the usual composition identity $N(u v)=N(u) N(v)$ by setting $a=b=u$ and $c=d=v$ and dividing by 2 .

Definition 6.33. If $C$ is a symmetric ribbon category, then a Hurwitz algebra object in $C$ is an object $A$ which is symmetrically self-dual, endowed with a multiplication $\mu: A \otimes A \rightarrow A$ and a unit $u: \mathbf{1} \rightarrow A$, satisfying the unit axioms, and such that $\langle\mathbb{1}, \mathbb{1}\rangle=1$ and $\langle a c, b d\rangle+\langle a d, b c\rangle=2\langle a, b\rangle\langle c, d\rangle$.

In this definition we have used the convention from Remark 6.20 to interpret these algebraic expressions as morphisms in $C$. We could also express these identities using diagram notation as follows:
![img-49.jpeg](img-49.jpeg)

Warning 6.34. The multiplication map on a Hurwitz algebra is typically not rotationally invariant (i.e., the inner product is typically not associative).

Remark 6.35. We could treat vector product algebras in a similar way, and get the axioms in Definition 6.29 from polarizing the natural identities for the cross product and dot product, namely $\langle x, x y\rangle=0=\langle x y, y\rangle$ and $\langle x y, x y\rangle=\langle x, x\rangle\langle y, y\rangle-\langle x, y\rangle^{2}$ [Wik22].

If $A$ is a Hurwitz algebra object, then we have a trace map which is dual to the unit map. Moreover, the first axiom of a Hurwitz algebra object tells you that $\operatorname{tr}(\cdot) \mathbb{1}: A \rightarrow A$ is an idempotent, and so in the idempotent completion of $C$, we have $A \cong \mathbf{1} \oplus X$ for some sub-object $X$. The restriction of multiplication composed with projection onto $X$ gives a map $M: X \otimes X \rightarrow X$.

Proposition 6.36 ([Str19, Thm. 25]). Suppose $C$ is an idempotent complete symmetric ribbon category with a Hurwitz algebra object $A \cong \mathbf{1} \oplus X$ and $\operatorname{dim} X=d$. Then $C$ takes a symmetric monoidal functor from $G 2(d)$ sending the strand to $X$ and the trivalent vertex to the restricted multiplication $M$ (i.e., $X$ is a G2-algebra object in C).

Conversely, in the additive completion of $G 2(d)$, the direct sum of the unit and the strand admits a unique structure of a Hurwitz algebra such that its traceless part agrees with the G2(d)-algebra structure on $X$.

Remark 6.37. Explicitly, the multiplication on the Hurwitz algebra $1 \oplus X$ is given by $(a, x)(b, y)=$ $(a b-\langle x, y\rangle, a y+b x+x y)$. In particular, the component of the multiplication map in $X \otimes X \rightarrow \mathbf{1}$ is not the pairing $X \otimes X \rightarrow \mathbf{1}$ induced by the symmetric self-duality of $A$, but instead those two maps are negatives of each other. One good way to think about this is that $\langle x, y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x \bar{y})$ and so they're negatives of each other when restricted to $X$, since $\bar{x}=-x$ in $X$. In general, there are some parameters involved in turning a non-unital algebra $X$ into a unital algebra $1 \oplus X$; see the proof of Proposition 6.51.

The following lemma proves sufficiency for the classical G2 family.
Lemma 6.38. The Hom spaces for G2(d) are spanned by planar non-elliptic diagrams and thus are bounded by the dimensions of the Hom spaces for the category of representations of $G_{2}$.

Proof. First, use the last (defining) identity to remove any crossings to reduce to planar diagrams. By [Wes10, Eq. 15], these relations imply a relation simplifying the square into a sum of planar terms with no faces, and by the same argument as [Wes10, §3.1] the pentagon also simplifies into

a sum of planar terms with no faces. Thus, by Euler characteristic (see [Kup96, §4]) every Hom space is spanned by the non-elliptic diagrams.

The following propositions show that consistency at generic values of the parameter is false, and show specialization at the points that are consistent; together they give a generalization of the classification of Hurwitz algebras due to Hurwitz.
Proposition 6.39 ([Wes10]). G2(d) is the zero category unless $d=0,1,3$, or 7 .
If $A$ is one of the four real Hurwitz algebras from Example 6.32, then let $G_{A}$ denote the group of unital algebra automorphisms of the real Hurwitz algebra $A$ which preserve the bilinear form, as in $\S 6.1$. (It's not difficult to see that these groups can also be described as the groups of automorphisms of the corresponding real vector product algebra $X$ which preserve the bilinear form.) Since the inner product on the real Hurwitz algebras are positive definite, it follows that $G_{A}$ is a compact group, and that its category of complex representations has a unitary structure. The groups $G_{A}$ are trivial, $S_{2}, S O(3)$, and the compact form of $G_{2}$, respectively, as shown in Table 9 on page 87 .
Proposition 6.40. If $d=0,1,3$, or 7 , take $A$ to be $\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{H}$, or $\mathbb{O}$, respectively and define $G_{A}$ as above. Then at these four values of $d$, the category $G 2(d)$ has a full and dominant functor to the category $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{A}\right)$.
Proof. Since $A$ is a real Hurwitz algebra of dimension $d+1$ we have a functor $\mathcal{F}: G 2(d) \rightarrow$ $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{A}\right)$.

This functor is full and dominant by Proposition 6.5 and Remark 6.6.
Note that when $A=\mathbb{R}$ the image of the strand in $G 2(0)$ is the zero object in $\operatorname{Rep}\left(G_{A}\right)$ and when $A=\mathbb{C}$ the image of the trivalent vertex in $G 2(1)$ is the zero map.
