# 3. Preliminaries on double Segal spaces 

In this section, we will review and study a selection of types of Barwick's double and 2-fold Segal spaces with different completeness conditions. We will then proceed to show that their ambient $\infty$-categories are cartesian closed by using the theory of exponential ideals that was discussed in Section 2.
3.1. Double Segal spaces. Double Segal spaces arise as certain presheaves on $\Delta^{\times 2}$. Throughout, we will write

$$
[n, m] \in \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

for the image of $([n],[m])$ under the Yoneda embedding $\Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$.
Definition 3.1. The presheaves $[0,0],[1,0],[0,1]$ and $[1,1]$ are called the free-living object (or 0-cell), the free-living horizontal and vertical arrow (or 1-cell), and the free-living 2-cell, respectively.

Definition 3.2. A double Segal space is a presheaf on $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ that is local with respect to the class of following maps:
(Seg) the spine inclusions

$$
[1, m] \cup_{[0, m]}[1, m] \cdots \cup_{[0, m]}[1, m] \rightarrow[n, m]
$$

and

$$
[n, 1] \cup_{[n, 0]}[n, 1] \cdots \cup_{[n, 0]}[n, 1] \rightarrow[n, m]
$$

for $n, m \geq 0$.
We will write

$$
\operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \subset \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

for the reflective full subcategory of double Segal spaces.
Remark 3.3. Unraveling the definitions, we observe that a double Segal space $\mathcal{P}$ contains:

- a space $\mathcal{P}_{0,0}$ of objects,
- a space $\mathcal{P}_{0,1}$ of vertical arrows,
- a space $\mathcal{P}_{1,0}$ of horizontal arrows,
- and a space $\mathcal{P}_{1,1}$ of 2-cells.

In general, the Segal condition for $\mathcal{P}$ tells us that we may view $\mathcal{P}_{n, m}$ as a grid of compatible cells. The 2-cells and the compatible arrows of $\mathcal{P}$ that have the same direction may be composed in a mutually compatible and coherently associative fashion. A 2-cell may be pictured as a square
![img-7.jpeg](img-7.jpeg)
where the horizontal/vertical directed arrows are horizontal/vertical arrows of $\mathcal{P}$.
Remark 3.4. Double Segal spaces are generalizations of Rezk's Segal spaces [Rez01]. Recall that the $\infty$-category

$$
\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{S}) \subset \operatorname{PSh}(\Delta)
$$

of Segal spaces is defined to be the reflective subcategory generated by the spine inclusions $[1] \cup_{[0]}[1] \cup_{[0]} \cdots \cup_{[0]}[1] \rightarrow[n]$ for $n \geq 0$. Here, we implicitly view every $[n] \in \Delta$ as an object of $\operatorname{PSh}(\Delta)$ via the Yoneda embedding.

Construction 3.5. We will use three involutive operations on $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ :

$$
(-)^{\mathrm{t}},(-)^{\mathrm{hop}},(-)^{\mathrm{vop}}: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

called the transpose, horizontal opposite, and vertical opposite respectively. They are defined by restricting along the functors

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{t}: \Delta \times \Delta \rightarrow \Delta \times \Delta:([n],[m]) \mapsto([m],[n]) \\
\text { hop }: \Delta \times \Delta \xrightarrow{\text { op } \times \text { id }} \Delta \times \Delta, \quad \text { vop }: \Delta \times \Delta \xrightarrow{\text { id } \times \text { op }} \Delta \times \Delta
\end{gathered}
$$

Here op : $\Delta \rightarrow \Delta$ denotes the usual opposite involution, i.e. it is restricted from the involution functor $(-)^{\text {op }}$ for categories.

One readily verifies that these involutions restrict to involutions

$$
(-)^{\mathrm{t}},(-)^{\mathrm{hop}},(-)^{\mathrm{vop}}: \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

on the $\infty$-category of double Segal spaces.
3.2. Two-fold Segal spaces. As will be dicussed later in further detail, double Segal spaces may be used to obtain Barwick's model of ( $\infty, 2$ )-categories. To this end, we will need to consider the double Segal spaces with only degenerate vertical arrows.

Definition 3.6. A double Segal space $X$ is called a 2-fold Segal space if the structure map

$$
\left(\text { id, } s_{0}\right)^{\star}: X_{0,0} \rightarrow X_{0,1}
$$

is an equivalence. In other words, a presheaf $X \in \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ is a 2 -fold Segal space if it is local with respect to (Seg) of Definition 3.2, and additionally to:
$($ deg $)$ the degeneracy map $[0,1] \rightarrow[0,0]$.
We will write

$$
\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \subset \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

for the reflective subcategory of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ spanned by those 2 -fold Segal spaces.
Note that every 2 -fold Segal space $X \in \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ has the feature that the restriction $X_{0, \bullet}$ is an essentially constant simplicial space. It will be convenient to consider the subcategory of such presheaves.

Definition 3.7. We will write

$$
(-)_{h}: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

for the inclusion of the full subcategory of those presheaves $X \in \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ so that $X_{0, \bullet}$ is essentially constant. This is called the horizontal inclusion functor. Note that this is a inclusion of a reflective subcategory, with generating local maps given by the degeneracy maps $[0, n] \rightarrow[0,0]$ for all $n$.

Construction 3.8. There is also a vertical inclusion functor

$$
(-)_{v}: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

given by the composite

$$
\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}} \xrightarrow{(-)_{h}} \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \xrightarrow{(-)^{1}} \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \xrightarrow{(-)^{1 \text { dop }}} \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

Note that this restricts to a functor $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\delta) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\delta)$.
Construction 3.9. Let Gaunt ${ }_{2}$ be the full subcategory of the category of 2-categories that is spanned by the gaunt 2-categories. Then one can write down the bicosimplicial object

$$
\Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \text { Gaunt }_{2}:([n],[m]) \mapsto[n ; m, \ldots, m]
$$

where $[n ; m \ldots, m]$ denotes the globular 2-category that may be pictured as
![img-8.jpeg](img-8.jpeg)

The restriction to $\{[0]\} \times \Delta$ is constant, so that the we obtain an induced functor

$$
N: \text { Gaunt }_{2} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}}
$$

so that the image of a gaunt 2 -category $G$ is level-wise described by the set

$$
N G_{n, m}=\operatorname{Hom}([n ; m, \ldots, m], G)
$$

of functors from $[n ; m, \ldots, m]$ to $G$. One readily verifies that the functor $N$ is fully faithful; we will leave the inclusion $N$ implicit throughout this chapter.

Remark 3.10. The obvious commutative square
![img-9.jpeg](img-9.jpeg)
of bisimplicial spaces is a pushout square in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$, as one readily verifies. If $X$ is a presheaf in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$, then $X$ is local with respect to the left map in this square. Consequently, $X$ is also local to the right (quotient) map in the square. It follows that the we obtain a natural equivalence

$$
\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}\left([n ; m \ldots, m]_{h}, X\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}([n, m], X)=X_{n, m}
$$

This observation implies that $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$ is a presheaf $\infty$-topos. Namely, let $\Theta_{2}^{\prime} \subset$ Gaunt ${ }_{2}$ be the full subcategory spanned by the 2 -categories $[n ; m, \ldots, m], n, m \geq 0$. Then we obtain an adjunction

$$
\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Theta_{2}^{\prime}\right) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\mathrm{deg}}
$$

where the left adjoint is the cocontinuous extension of the restricted nerve $N \mid \Theta_{2}^{\prime}$, and the right adjoint is induced by restriction along the bicosimplicial object $\Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \Theta_{2}^{\prime}$. Using the above, one readily concludes that this sets up an adjoint equivalence.

In turn, this can be used to recover the comparison of [BR20] between 2-fold Segal spaces and $\Theta_{2}$-spaces. Namely, the subcategory $\Theta_{2} \subset$ Gaunt $_{2}$ of loyal disks $\left[n ; m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}\right]$ (see [Rez10]) is generated by $\Theta_{2}^{\prime}$ under retracts. So the inclusion $\Theta_{2}^{\prime} \subset \Theta_{2}$ induces an equivalence $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Theta_{2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Theta_{2}^{\prime}\right)$. A direct verification shows that the composed equivalence

$$
\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Theta_{2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Theta_{2}^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\mathrm{deg}}
$$

derives to an equivalence between $\Theta_{2}$-spaces and 2 -fold Segal spaces.
Remark 3.11. One may picture the horizontal and vertical inclusions of the image of the 2-globe $[1 ; 1]$ as

Construction 3.12. Note that there is an adjunction $\Delta \times \Delta \rightleftarrows \Delta$, where the left adjoint is given by projection onto the first coordinate, and the right adjoint is given by the inclusion of the subcategory $\Delta \times\{[0]\}$. This gives rise to an adjunction $\operatorname{PSh}(\Delta) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ between presheaf $\infty$-categories, that in turn restricts to an adjunction

$$
\operatorname{PSh}(\Delta) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\mathrm{deg}}:(-)^{(1)}
$$

We will leave the fully faithful left adjoint implicit throughout this chapter; every simplicial space is viewed as a presheaf in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$ via this functor. The above adjunction also restricts to give an adjunction

$$
\operatorname{Seg}(\delta) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\delta):(-)^{(1)}
$$

as well.
We will use the following special names for the vertical and horizontal opposites of 2 -fold Segal spaces:

Definition 3.13. If $X$ is a 2 -fold Segal space, then its 1 -opposite and 2 -opposite are defined by respectively $X^{1-\mathrm{op}}:=X^{\text {hop }}$ and $X^{2-\mathrm{op}}:=X^{\text {vop }}$.

Moreover, we recall the definition of the associated mapping Segal spaces of a 2 -fold Segal space:

Definition 3.14. If $x$ and $y$ are objects of a 2 -fold Segal space $X$, then we will write $X(x, y)$ for the Segal space of maps from $x$ to $y$ that is defined by the pullback square
![img-10.jpeg](img-10.jpeg)

3.3. Horizontal and vertical fragments. On account of [Hau18, Proposition 4.12], the inclusion $(-)_{h}: \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$ admits a right adjoint. We will give an alternative short proof of this here.

Construction 3.15. We will write

$$
\operatorname{Hor}(-): \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}}
$$

for the functor that is induced by the bicosimplicial object

$$
\Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right):([n],[m]) \mapsto[n ; m, \ldots, m]_{h}
$$

Proposition 3.16. The functor $\operatorname{Hor}(-)$ is right adjoint to $(-)_{h}$.
Proof. Let us write $L: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$ for the left adjoint to $(-)_{h}$. Recall from Remark 3.10 that we have a quotient map $[n, m] \rightarrow[n ; m, \ldots, m]_{h}$ that is natural in $\Delta^{\times 2}$ and is carried to an equivalence by $L$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be presheaves on $\Delta^{\times 2}$. Then we now obtain natural equivalences

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}(X, \operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})) & \simeq \lim _{[n, m] \in\left(\Delta^{\times 2} / X\right)^{n}} \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}([n, m], \operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})) \\
& \simeq \lim _{[n, m] \in\left(\Delta^{\times 2} / X\right)^{n}} \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}([n ; m \ldots, m]_{h}, \mathcal{P}) \\
& \simeq \lim _{[n, m] \in\left(\Delta^{\times 2} / X\right)^{n}} \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}\left((L[n, m])_{h}, \mathcal{P}\right) \\
& \simeq \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}\left((L X)_{h}, \mathcal{P}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

In the last step, we used that $(-)_{h}$ preserves colimits, which follows from the easily verifiable fact that $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$ is closed under colimits in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$.

Remark 3.17. Note that the functor $\operatorname{Hor}(-)$ carries double Segal spaces to 2-fold Segal spaces. Consequently, we obtain a restricted adjunction

$$
(-)_{h}: \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}): \operatorname{Hor}(-)
$$

If $\mathcal{P}$ is a double Segal space, then $\operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})$ is called the horizontal fragment of $\mathcal{P}$. This 2-fold Segal space may be described by the pullback squares
![img-11.jpeg](img-11.jpeg)
level-wise. This follows from Remark 3.10; see also [Hau18, Remark 4.13].
Definition 3.18. It now directly follows that the vertical inclusion $(-)_{v}: \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$ admits a right adjoint as well. We will write

$$
\operatorname{Vert}(-): \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}): \mathcal{P} \mapsto \operatorname{Hor}\left(\left(\mathcal{P}^{\text {hop }}\right)^{\mathrm{t}}\right)
$$

for its right adjoint. This is called the vertical fragment functor.
Remark 3.19. One may show that the functors $\operatorname{Hor}(-)$ and $\operatorname{Vert}(-)$ are compatible with taking opposites as follows: there are natural equivalences

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Hor}\left(\mathcal{P}^{\text {hop }}\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})^{1-\mathrm{op}}, \quad \operatorname{Hor}\left(\mathcal{P}^{\text {vop }}\right) \simeq \operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})^{2-\mathrm{op}} \\
& \operatorname{Vert}\left(\mathcal{P}^{\text {hop }}\right) \simeq \operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})^{2-\mathrm{op}}, \quad \operatorname{Vert}\left(\mathcal{P}^{\text {vop }}\right) \simeq \operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})^{1-\mathrm{op}}
\end{aligned}
$$

for every double Segal space $\mathcal{P}$.

Note that $\operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P}) \simeq \operatorname-Hor}\left(\mathcal{P}^{t}\right)^{2-\mathrm{op}}$ and $X_{v} \simeq\left(X^{2-\mathrm{op}}\right)_{h}^{t}$. One could also have defined the vertical inclusion and vertical fragments in such a way that there would not appear 2opposites in these descriptions. However, our introduced convention seems more natural regarding the material that will follow.
3.4. Completeness conditions. So far, we have not talked about completeness conditions for 2-fold and double Segal spaces. We will start by recalling the situation for Segal spaces [Rez01].

Definition 3.20. We define $J \in \operatorname{PSh}(\Delta)$ to be the simplicial set defined by the pushout square
![img-12.jpeg](img-12.jpeg)
of simplicial spaces.
Definition 3.21. A Segal space $X$ is called complete if it is local with respect to the map $J \rightarrow[0]$.

Remark 3.22. It is a celebrated result of Joyal and Tierney [JT07] that complete Segal spaces are a model for $\infty$-categories. Precisely, the functor

$$
\operatorname{Cat}_{\infty} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}(\Delta): \mathcal{C} \mapsto([n] \mapsto \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}}([n], \mathcal{C}))
$$

obtained by restricting the Yoneda embedding, is fully faithful, with image given by the complete Segal spaces.

To discuss the two-dimensional completeness conditions, we will need an additional suspended version of $J$.

Notation 3.23. We will write $[1 ; J]$ for the object that fits in the pushout square
![img-13.jpeg](img-13.jpeg)
in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$. Note that there is a canonical map $[1 ; J] \rightarrow[1]$.
Notation 3.24. We will consider the following labeled families of maps:
$(h c)[1]_{h} \times J_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{h}$,
$(v c) J_{h} \times[1]_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{v}$,
$(l h c)[1 ; J]_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{h}$,
$(l v c)[1 ; J]_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{v}$.
Remark 3.25. In light of Remark 3.10, we have a pushout square
![img-14.jpeg](img-14.jpeg)
in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. Consequently, the map $(h c)$ is contained in the saturated class generated by (lhc) and the map $J_{v} \rightarrow[0]$. Conversely, the map $J_{v} \rightarrow[0]_{v}$ is a retract of $(h c)$, so that $(l h c)$ and $J_{v} \rightarrow[0]_{v}$ are contained in the saturation of $(h c)$.

The following result appears in greater generality in [Hau18, Section 7] as well.
Proposition 3.26. Let $X$ be a 2-fold Segal space. Then the following assertions are equivalent:
(1) for every two objects $x, y \in X$, the Segal space $X(x, y)$ is complete,
(2) $X$ is local with respect to the map (hc),
(3) $X$ is local with respect to the map (lhc).

Proof. It follows from Remark 3.25 that (2) and (3) are equivalent, since $J_{v} \rightarrow[0]_{v}$ is contained in the saturation of (Seg) and (deg). To show that (1) and (2) are equivalent, we use that the map $[1]_{h} \times J_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{h}$ is cofibered under $\{0,1\}_{h}$. So, we obtain a commutative triangle
![img-15.jpeg](img-15.jpeg)

Now, (2) holds if and only if the top arrow is an equivalence. This can be checked fiberwise, which precisely recovers condition (1).
Definition 3.27. Let $X$ be a 2 -fold Segal space. Then $X$ is called locally complete if the equivalent conditions of Proposition 3.26 are met. We will write

$$
\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c} \subset \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

for the reflective subcategory of locally complete 2-fold Segal spaces.
Proposition 3.28. Let $X$ be a 2-fold Segal space. Then the following are equivalent:
(1) $X^{(1)}$ is a complete Segal space,
(2) $X$ is local with respect to (vc).

Proof. This follows from the dual form of Remark 3.25 and the fact that (lvc) is contained in the saturation of (Seg) and (deg).
Definition 3.29. We say that a 2 -fold Segal space $X$ is complete if it is locally complete and the equivalent conditions of Proposition 3.28 are met.

The reflective subcategory of $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$ that is spanned by the complete 2 -fold Segal spaces meets the characterization of [BSP21] of the $\infty$-category of ( $\infty, 2$ )-categories; see [BSP21, Theorem 4.16]. We will write

$$
\operatorname{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)} \subset \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

for this full subcategory, and also refer to complete 2-fold Segal spaces as ( $\infty, 2$ )-categories. There are concrete comparisons between complete 2 -fold Segal spaces and other models for ( $\infty, 2$ )-categories in [Lur09b], [BR13] and [BR20].
Remark 3.30. Note that the adjunction $\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{S}) \rightleftarrows \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}):(-)^{(1)}$ restricts to an adjunction $\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}:(-)^{(1)}$.

Remark 3.31. One easily verifies that the nerve functor that was constructed in Construction 3.9 has image contained in $\mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}$, so it defines an inclusion

$$
\operatorname{Gaunt}_{2} \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}
$$

Although we will not use it in this chapter, it is worth mentioning that this functor has been extended to a fully faithful functor defined on the whole of $\mathrm{Cat}_{2}$ by Moser [Mos20]. Here, Cat ${ }_{2}$ denotes the underlying $\infty$-category (actually, a weak (3,1)-category) of the canonical model structure on 2-categories [Lac02].

We will now discuss several completeness conditions for double Segal spaces in terms of completeness of their vertical and horizontal fragments.
Definition 3.32. A double Segal space $\mathcal{P}$ is called locally complete if $\operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})$ and $\operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})$ are locally complete, i.e. whenever it local with respect to (lhc) and (vhc). We will write

$$
\operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c} \subset \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

for the full subcategory spanned by the locally complete double Segal spaces.
Remark 3.33. Note that locally complete double Segal spaces are closed under horizontal and vertical oppposites, and transposes.
Definition 3.34. A double Segal space $\mathcal{P}$ is called a double $\infty$-category if it is local with respect to (hc), i.e. if $\operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})^{(1)}$ is complete and $\operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})$ is locally complete (see Remark 3.25). We will write

$$
\operatorname{DblCat}_{\infty} \subset \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

for the reflective subcategory spanned by the double $\infty$-categories.
Remark 3.35. We may view double $\infty$-categories as simplicial objects in $\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}$ as follows. Applying Fun $\left(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}},-)\right.$ to the embedding that was discussed in Remark 3.22, we will obtain a fully faithful functor

$$
i: \operatorname{Fun}\left(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

that carries a simplicial $\infty$-category $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ to the bisimplicial space

$$
i\left(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\right)_{n, m}=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}}([m], \mathcal{P}_{n}^{\prime})
$$

One readily verifies that this restricts to an equivalence between:
(1) the Segal objects in Cat $_{\infty}$, i.e. simplicial objects $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}: \Delta^{\text {op }} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}$ so that each functor $\mathcal{P}_{n}^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{1}^{\prime} \times_{\mathcal{P}_{n}^{\prime}} \cdots \times_{\mathcal{P}_{n}^{\prime}} \mathcal{P}_{1}^{\prime}$ is an equivalence for every $n \geq 0$,
(2) the double $\infty$-categories.

We will leave this identification implicit, and view every double $\infty$-category as a Segal object in Cat $_{\infty}$.
Remark 3.36. The subcategory $\mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}$ is not closed under transposition, as one may readily check. The involutions $(-)^{\text {hop }}$ and $(-)^{\text {vop }}$ do restrict to an endofunctor on $\mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}$. Suppose that $\mathcal{P}$ is a double $\infty$-category, viewed as a simplicial $\infty$-category. Then the vertical opposite $\mathcal{P}$ is described level-wise by

$$
\left(\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{vop}}\right)_{n}=\mathcal{P}_{n}^{\mathrm{op}}
$$

Example 3.37. In [Rui23], we discuss the double $\infty$-category

$$
\mathfrak{C a t}_{\infty}
$$

which is loosely described as follows:

- its objects are are $\infty$-categories,
- its vertical arrows are functors,
- its horizontal arrows are profunctors, i.e. a horizontal arrow $F: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}$ is given by a functor $\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathcal{S}$,
- its 2-cells are given as follows: a 2-cell
![img-16.jpeg](img-16.jpeg)

corresponds to a natural transformation
![img-17.jpeg](img-17.jpeg)

More generally, we construct in [Rui23] a double $\infty$-category

$$
\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}(\mathcal{E})
$$

for every suitable $\infty$-category $\mathcal{E}$, whose objects are $\infty$-categories internal to $\mathcal{E}$. In [Hau16], Haugseng constructs a similarly described double $\infty$-category

$$
\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}^{\mathcal{V}}
$$

of $\infty$-categories enriched in a suitably monoidal $\infty$-category $\mathcal{V}$.
In practice, double $\infty$-categories, such as these in Example 3.37, are usually more conviently constructed as Segal objects in Cat $_{\infty}$. We will briefly discuss how one may verify the completeness of double $\infty$-categories when viewed as simplicial $\infty$-categories.

Notation 3.38. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a double $\infty$-category, viewed as a Segal object in Cat $_{\infty}$. Then we write $\mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$ for the $\infty$-category defined by the pullback square
![img-18.jpeg](img-18.jpeg)

Proposition 3.39. Suppose that $\mathcal{P}$ is a double Segal space. Then the following assertions are equivalent:
(1) $\operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})$ is complete and $\operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})$ is locally complete,
(2) $\mathcal{P}$ is a double $\infty$-category and the canonical functor $\mathcal{P}_{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$ is fully faithful.

Proof. We must show that a double $\infty$-category $\mathcal{P}$ is local with respect to ( $v h c$ ) if and only if $\mathcal{P}_{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$ is fully faithful. This functor is fully faithful if and only if it is left orthogonal to the inclusion $\{0,1\} \rightarrow[1]$, i.e. if and only if the induced square
![img-19.jpeg](img-19.jpeg)
is a pullback square. This can be identified with the commutative square
![img-20.jpeg](img-20.jpeg)

In light of the pushout square that appears in Remark 3.25, this square is a pullback square if and only if the restriction map

$$
\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\kappa 2}\right)}([1]_{v}, \mathcal{P}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\kappa 2}\right)}([1 ; J]_{v}, \mathcal{P})
$$

induced by ( $v h c$ ) is an equivalence.

Example 3.40. In [Rui23], we show that $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(\mathcal{E})$ is locally complete for every suitable $\infty$-category $\mathcal{E}$. In particular, $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}$ is locally complete. Throughout this article, we will denote its vertical fragment by

$$
\mathrm{CAT}_{\infty}:=\operatorname{Vert}\left(\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}\right)
$$

It is our preferred model for the $(\infty, 2)$-category of $\infty$-categories.
Proposition 3.41. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a double Segal space. Then the following assertions are equivalent:
(1) $\operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})$ and $\operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P})$ are complete,
(2) $\mathcal{P}$ is local with respect to (hc) and (vc),
(3) $\mathcal{P}$ is a double $\infty$-category and the functor $\mathcal{P}_{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$ is an equivalence.

Proof. It is readily verified that (1) and (2) are equivalent using Remark 3.25. To show that (2) and (3) are equivalent, we must show that a double $\infty$-category $\mathcal{P}$ is local with respect to (vc) if and only if $\mathcal{P}_{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$ is an equivalence. But this readily follows from Proposition 3.39, and the observation that one recovers the map $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}\left([0]_{h}, \mathcal{P}\right) \rightarrow$ $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}\left(J_{h}, \mathcal{P}\right)$ if one applies $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}}([0],-)$ to the functor $\mathcal{P}_{0} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}_{\text {eq }}$.
Definition 3.42. A double Segal space is called complete if it meets the equivalent conditions of Proposition 3.41. We will write

$$
\mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}^{\mathcal{E}} \subset \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}
$$

for the full and reflective subcategory spanned by the complete double Segal spaces.
Remark 3.43. The complete double $\infty$-categories are closed under horizontal and vertical opposites, and transposes.

We conclude this subsection by summarizing the reflective subcategory of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$ that were constructed above:

3.5. Exponentiability of double Segal spaces. We will now show the following:

Proposition 3.44. The reflective subcategories listed in Table 3.4.1 are exponential ideals of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. In particular, all these subcategories are cartesian closed and inherit the internal homs from $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$.

In order to prove Proposition 3.44, we will use the following result of Rezk:

Lemma 3.45 (Rezk). Suppose that $K=[0]$ or $J$ and consider the the pushout square
![img-21.jpeg](img-21.jpeg)
in $\operatorname{PSh}(\Delta)$. Then the canonical map $P(K) \rightarrow[1] \times K$ is is contained in the saturated class of morphisms generated by the spine inclusions.
Proof. This is essentially the content of [Rez01, Subsection 12.3].
Proof of Proposition 3.44. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be one of these full subcategories of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. Write $S$ for the generating local maps of the localization $\mathcal{C}$, as listed in the table in Subsection 3.1. Let $X$ be a bisimplicial space. Then Lemma 2.12 asserts that we have to show that the functor

$$
X \times(-): \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)
$$

carries each map $f \in S$ to a map in the saturation of $S$. Since the product preserves colimits in each variable, we may reduce to showing this for $X=[n, m]$. But one can readily verify that $[n, m]$ is a retract of $[1,0]^{\times n} \times[0,1]^{\times m}$. Thus it suffices to handle the cases that $X=[1,0]$ and $X=[0,1]$.

Now, in any of the cases that $f$ is of type (Seg), the desired result can directly be obtained from the 1-dimensional case [Rez01, Proposition 10.3].

Suppose that $f$ is of the form $(h c)$. If $X=[1]_{h}$, the result readily follows. Hence, it remains to show that

$$
[1]_{v} \times\left([1]_{h} \times J_{v}\right)=[1]_{h} \times\left([1]_{v} \times J_{v}\right) \rightarrow[1]_{h} \times[1]_{v}=[1]_{v} \times[1]_{h}
$$

sits in the saturation of (Seg) and (hc). Let $P(K) \rightarrow[1] \times K$ be the map of Lemma 3.45 for $K=[0]$ and $J$. It follows from this lemma that the vertical arrows in the commutative square
![img-22.jpeg](img-22.jpeg)
are contained in the saturation of (Seg). The upper map is a pushout along $[1]_{h} \times\{0,1\}_{v} \times$ $J_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{h} \times\{0,1\}_{v}$, so it lies in the saturation of $(h c)$. Consequently, by 2 -out-of-3, the bottom map lies in the saturation generated by (Seg) and ( $h c$ ), as desired.

Let us now handle the map $f$ of type $(l h c)$ and the case that $X=[1]_{h}$. One can check that the map

$$
\left([1] \times[1 ; J]\right)_{h} \rightarrow\left([1] \times[1]\right)_{h}
$$

is obtained by taking pushouts of the rows in the commutative diagram
![img-23.jpeg](img-23.jpeg)

The middle vertical map is precisely (lhc). Consequently, it suffices to check that the outer vertical maps are contained in the saturation of (Seg) and (lhc). But this readily follows from the observation that the canonical inclusions

$$
[1 ; J]_{h} \cup_{[0]_{h}}[1]_{h} \rightarrow[2 ; J, 0]_{h}, \quad \text { and } \quad[1]_{h} \cup_{[0]_{h}}[1 ; J]_{h} \rightarrow[2 ; 0, J]_{h}
$$

are contained in the saturation (Seg).

Next, we handle the case that $f$ is of type (lhc) and $X=[1]_{v}$. We have to verify that

$$
[1]_{v} \times[1 ; J]_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{v} \times[1]_{h}
$$

sits in the saturation of (lhc) and (Seg). Let $(-)$ ㅂ $(-)$ denote the pushout-product for arrows in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. We can then write

$$
[1]_{v} \times[1 ; K]_{h}=\left(\{0,1\}_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{h}\right) \boxtimes\left(\left([1] \times K\right)_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{v}\right)
$$

for $K=[0]$ and $J$. Using the pushout-product, we define

$$
Q(K):=\left(\{0,1\}_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{h}\right) \boxtimes\left(P(K)_{v} \rightarrow[1]_{v}\right)
$$

and obtain a commutative square
![img-24.jpeg](img-24.jpeg)

The vertical arrows lie in the saturation of (Seg) on account of Lemma 3.45. The top arrow is a pushout along

$$
\left(\{0,1\}_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{h}\right) \boxtimes\left(\left(\{0,1\} \times J\right)_{v} \rightarrow\{0,1\}_{v}\right) \rightarrow\left(\{0,1\}_{h} \rightarrow[1]_{h}\right) \boxtimes\left(\{0,1\}_{v} \rightarrow\{0,1\}_{v}\right)
$$

and this is precisely the map $\{0,1\}_{v} \times[1 ; J]_{h} \rightarrow\{0,1\}_{v}$, which is contained in the saturation of (lhc). Thus the result follows from 2-out-of-3.

The cases (vc) and (lvc) formally follow from the above cases, and this finishes the proof.
Definition 3.46. The double Segal space of functors between a bisimplicial space $X$ and a double Segal space $\mathcal{P}$ is defined to be

$$
\mathbb{F} \operatorname{un}(X, \mathcal{P}):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}(X, \mathcal{P})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}(X, \mathcal{P})
$$

Definition 3.47. The vertical and horizontal cotensor products of a 2-fold Segal space $X$ with a double Segal space are defined as

$$
[X, \mathcal{P}]:=\mathbb{F} \operatorname{un}\left(X_{v}, \mathcal{P}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad(X, \mathcal{P}):=\mathbb{F} \operatorname{un}\left(X_{h}, \mathcal{P}\right)
$$

respectively.
Note that $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$ is not an exponential ideal of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. However, it is still cartesian closed since it is a presheaf $\infty$-topos (see Remark 3.10). The following can be readily deduced from Proposition 3.44:
Corollary 3.48. The full subcategories $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}), \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c}$ and $\mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}$ are exponentiable ideals of $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$.
Notation 3.49. The 2-fold Segal space of functors between 2-fold Segal spaces $X$ and $Y$ is denoted by

$$
\operatorname{FUN}(X, Y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}(X, Y)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}}(X, Y)
$$

The following result asserts that the defined cotensor products are compatible with fragments:
Proposition 3.50. Let $X$ and $\mathcal{P}$ be a 2-fold and double Segal space respectively. There are canonical equivalences of 2-fold Segal spaces

$$
\operatorname{Vert}(\{X, \mathcal{P}\}) \xrightarrow{\simeq} \operatorname{FUN}(X, \operatorname{Vert}(\mathcal{P})), \quad \operatorname{Hor}(\{X, \mathcal{P}\}) \xrightarrow{\simeq} \operatorname{FUN}(X, \operatorname{Hor}(\mathcal{P}))
$$

Proof. This follows immediately from the fact that the inclusions $(-)_{h}$ and $(-)_{v}$ preserve products.

Remark 3.51. Let $X$ be an $\infty$-category and suppose that $\mathcal{P}$ is a double $\infty$-category. Then the vertical cotensor double $\infty$-category $[X, \mathcal{P}]$ is given by the composite

$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{op}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}_{\infty} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)} \mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}
$$

as a simplicial $\infty$-category (see Remark 3.35). To see this, we note that $X_{v}$ is always a double $\infty$-category and $\left(X_{v}\right)_{n}=X$ for all $n$. Since the functor $[X,-]: \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty} \rightarrow \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}$ is right adjoint to the functor

$$
X_{v} \times(-): \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty} \rightarrow \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}
$$

the observation follows.
Example 3.52. Let $X$ be an $\infty$-category and $\mathcal{C}$ be an $\infty$-category with finite limits. Then we may apply the vertical cotensor construction to the double $\infty$-category $\operatorname{Span}(\mathcal{C})$ of spans that is constructed in [Hau18]. One readily deduces using Remark 3.51 that there is a canonical equivalence of double $\infty$-categories

$$
[X, \operatorname{Span}(\mathcal{C})] \simeq \operatorname{Span}(\operatorname{Fun}(X, \mathcal{C}))
$$

Example 3.53. Let $T$ be an $\infty$-category. We may apply the above construction to the double $\infty$-category $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}$ (see Example 3.37) so that we obtain a (locally complete) double $\infty$-category

$$
\left[T^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}\right]
$$

whose objects are called $T$-indexed $\infty$-categories. Its vertical fragment is given by the $(\infty, 2)$-category of functors $\operatorname{FUN}\left(T^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathrm{CAT}_{\infty}\right)$. It is shown in [Rui23] that $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty} \simeq \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(\mathcal{S})$, so there is an equivalence

$$
\left[T^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}\right] \simeq\left[T^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(\mathcal{S})\right]
$$

See Example 3.37 for the notation. The right hand-side can be identified with the double $\infty$-category $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(\operatorname{PSh}(T))$, as may be concluded directly from the construction of $\mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(-)$ in [Rui23], so that we obtain an equivalence

$$
\left[T^{\mathrm{op}}, \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}\right] \simeq \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}(\operatorname{PSh}(T))
$$

More generally, one can consider the vertical cotensor product

$$
\left[\mathcal{X}^{1-\mathrm{op}}, \mathbb{C a t}_{\infty}\right]
$$

where $\mathcal{X}$ is an $(\infty, 2)$-category. The objects of this double $\infty$-category are functors $\mathcal{X}^{1-\mathrm{op}} \rightarrow$ $\mathrm{CAT}_{\infty}$, and these are usually called 2-presheaves.
3.6. The squares construction. We will make use of the squares functor for 2-fold Segal spaces in this article. In the strict context, this construction goes back to Ehresmann [Ehr63]. It has been studied by Grandis and Paré [GP04], and recently by Guetta-Moser-Sarazola-Verdugo [GMSP23] as well. In the $\infty$-categorical context, it was introduced in the work of Gaitsgory-Rozenblyum on derived algebraic geometry, where it plays an important role in setting up the $(\infty, 2)$-categorical foundations for their treatment of sixfunctor formalisms. It has also been studied recently by Abellán [Abe23].

To define the squares functor, we make use of the gaunt 2-categories
![img-25.jpeg](img-25.jpeg)
which are obtained by taking the oplax Gray tensor product of $[n]$ and $[m]$; see [Gra74] for the original definition. These 2-categories can be organized into a bicosimplicial object

$$
[\cdot] \otimes[\cdot]: \Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\operatorname{deg}}:([n],[m]) \mapsto[n] \otimes[m]
$$

We will need the following result:
Proposition 3.54. Let $n, m \geq 1$. Then the canonical maps
(i) $[1] \otimes[m] \cup_{[0] \otimes[m]} \cdots \cup_{[0] \otimes[m]}[1] \otimes[m] \rightarrow[n] \otimes[m]$,
(ii) $[n] \otimes[1] \cup_{[n] \otimes[0]} \cdots \cup_{[n] \otimes[0]}[n] \otimes[1] \rightarrow[n] \otimes[m]$,
are equivalences of 2-fold Segal spaces.
Instead of giving a direct proof of Proposition 3.54 here, we will show how it can be leveraged from the literature. We will make use of the following observation:
Lemma 3.55. Suppose that $f: X \rightarrow Y$ is a map between 2-fold Segal spaces so that:
(1) $f_{0,0}$ is an equivalence of spaces,
(2) $f^{(1)}$ is carried to an equivalence by the reflector $\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}_{\infty}$,
(3) $f$ is carried to an equivalence by the reflector $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}$.

Then $f$ is an equivalence of 2-fold Segal spaces.
Proof. In light of the Segal condition and assumption (1), we have to verify that $f_{1,0}$ and $f_{1,1}$ are equivalences of spaces. Since (2) holds, the map

$$
X_{1,0} \rightarrow Y_{1,0} \times_{Y_{0,0}^{\times 2}} X_{0,0}^{\times 2}
$$

induced by $f_{1,0}$ must be an equivalence; see [Lur09b, Theorem 1.2.13] for instance. Hence $f_{1,0}$ is an equivalence. In light of [Hau18, Remark 7.19], assumption (1) implies that

$$
X(x, y)_{1} \rightarrow Y(f(x), f(y))_{1} \times_{Y(f(x), f(y))_{0}^{\times 2}} X(x, y)_{0}^{\times 2}
$$

is an equivalence for all objects $x, y \in X$. Recall that the map $X(x, y)_{n} \rightarrow Y(f(x), f(y))_{n}$ is precisely the comparison map

$$
X_{1, n} \rightarrow Y_{1, n} \times_{Y_{0,0}^{\times 2}} X_{0, n}^{\times 2}
$$

on fibers above $(x, y) \in X_{0,0}^{\times 2} \xrightarrow{\simeq} X_{0, n}^{\times 2}$. Since $f_{1,0}$ is an equivalence, it follows that $X(x, y)_{0} \rightarrow$ $Y(x, y)_{0}$ is an equivalence. Thus $X(x, y)_{1} \rightarrow Y(f(x), f(y))_{1}$ must be an equivalence. Since this holds for all $x, y$ in $X$, this in turn implies that $f_{1,1}$ is an equivalence.

Proof. We will just treat map (1); the other one is handled similarly. Let us consider the inclusion

$$
i:[1] \otimes[m] \cup_{[0] \otimes[m]} \cdots \cup_{[0] \otimes[m]}[1] \otimes[m] \rightarrow[n] \otimes[m]
$$

of bisimplicial sets, where the iterated pushout on the left is computed in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)$. Then one readily verifies that $i_{0,0}$ is the identity. Moreover, one can readily show that $i^{(1)}$ lies in the saturated class spanned by the 1-dimensional spine inclusions (see Remark 3.4). Let us consider the reflectors

$$
L: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\mathrm{deg}} \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}), \quad L^{\prime}: \operatorname{PSh}(\Delta) \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{S})
$$

One can verify that the (colimit-preserving) functor $(-)^{(1)}: \operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }} \rightarrow \operatorname{PSh}(\Delta)$ carries maps in (Seg) to the saturated class of 1-dimensional spine inclusions. So it follows that $L^{\prime}(L i)^{(1)} \simeq L^{\prime} i^{(1)}$ is an equivalence. A similar argument shows that $(L i)_{0,0}$ is an equivalence, as every map in (Seg) is carried to an equivalence by the evaluation functor $(-)_{0,0}$.

Now, Lemma 3.55 asserts that it is sufficient to check that $L i$ is carried to an equivalence by the reflector $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)}$. This follows from the work of Gagna-HarpazLanari [GHL21] and [HHLN21, Proposition 5.1.9].

Construction 3.56. Since $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$ is cocomplete, the bicosimplicial object

$$
[\cdot] \otimes[\cdot]: \Delta^{\times 2} \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}):([n],[m]) \rightarrow[n] \otimes[m]
$$

extends to a colimit preserving functor $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$. On account of Proposition 3.54, there exists a unique dotted extension in the diagram
![img-26.jpeg](img-26.jpeg)

The horizontal functor admits a right adjoint, which restricts to a right adjoint

$$
\mathrm{Sq}: \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})
$$

for Gr. This is called the squares functor. For a 2-fold Segal space $X$, it is level-wise given by

$$
\operatorname{Sq}(X)_{n, m}:=\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}([n] \otimes[m], X)
$$

Construction 3.57. There is a canonical functor

$$
\iota_{h}^{n, m}:[n] \otimes[m] \rightarrow[n ; m, \ldots, m]
$$

between gaunt 2-categories that is natural in $([n],[m]) \in \Delta^{\times 2}$. The functor $\iota_{h}^{n, m}$ selects the non-degenerate oplax $n \times m$ grid in $[n ; m, \ldots, m]$ where all the vertical arrows in the grid are identities, pictured as
![img-27.jpeg](img-27.jpeg)

There is also a similarly defined functor

$$
\iota_{v}^{n, m}:[n]^{\mathrm{op}} \otimes[m] \rightarrow[m ; n \ldots, n]
$$

between gaunt 2-categories. The functor $\iota_{v}^{n, m}$ selects the non-degenerate oplax $n \times m$ grid in $[m ; n \ldots, n]$ where all horizontal arrows in the grid are identities, pictured as
![img-28.jpeg](img-28.jpeg)

Let $X$ be a 2-fold Segal space. Then Remark 3.10 implies that $X_{h}$ and $X_{v}$ are (naturally) described by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(X_{h}\right)_{n, m} \simeq \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}([n ; m \ldots, m]_{h}, X_{h}) \\
& \left(X_{v}^{\text {hop }}\right)_{n, m} \simeq \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)}([m ; n \ldots, n]_{v}, X_{v})
\end{aligned}
$$

In light of these descriptions, we can construct maps

$$
X_{h} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X), \quad X_{v} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X)
$$

using the natural transformations $\iota_{h}$ and $\iota_{v}$.
Proposition 3.58. Let $X$ be a 2-fold Segal space. The functors $X_{h} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X)$ and $X_{v} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X)$ are adjunct to equivalences $X \rightarrow \operatorname-Hor}(\operatorname{Sq}(X))$ and $X \rightarrow \operatorname{Vert}(\operatorname{Sq}(X))$.
Proof. We will just show the statement for the horizontal case; the other case is handled similarly. We have to show that the map

$$
\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}([n ; m \ldots, m], X) \rightarrow \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}([n ; m, \ldots, m], \operatorname{Hor}(\operatorname{Sq}(X)))
$$

is an equivalence for all $n, m \geq 0$. Note that this map can be identified with the map

$$
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}([n ; m \ldots, m]_{h}, X_{h}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}([n ; m, \ldots, m]_{h}, \operatorname{Sq}(X))
$$

induced by $X_{h} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X)$. In light of Remark 3.10, this is an equivalence if and only if the square
![img-29.jpeg](img-29.jpeg)
is a pullback square. By construction of the map $X_{h} \rightarrow \operatorname{Sq}(X)$, this square is obtained from the commutative square
![img-30.jpeg](img-30.jpeg)
of gaunt 2-categories by applying $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})}(-, X)$. But this square is a pushout square in $\operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})$, as argued in [HHLN21, Lemma 5.1.11]. Namely, to show that it is a pushout,

one may reduce to $n, m \in[0,1]$ using the co-Segal condition. The only left-over non-trivial case is $n=m=1$, where it follows from the fact that the canonical map $[1 ; 1] \cup_{[1]^{c}}[2] \rightarrow$ $[1] \otimes[1]$ is an equivalence - already in $\operatorname{PSh}\left(\Delta^{\times 2}\right)_{\text {deg }}$.
Corollary 3.59. The squares functor restricts to right adjoints $\mathrm{Sq}: \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c} \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c}$ and $\mathrm{Sq}: \mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)} \rightarrow \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}^{\mathrm{c}}$ as well.
Proof. It readily follows from Proposition 3.58 that the squares functor restricts as such. The left adjoints are then given by the composites

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c} \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Gr}} \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S})^{l c} \\
& \operatorname{Cat}_{(\infty, 2)} \rightarrow \operatorname{Seg}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Gr}} \operatorname{Cat}^{2}(\mathcal{S}) \rightarrow \mathrm{DblCat}_{\infty}^{\mathrm{c}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the functors that appear first and last in the composites are inclusions and localizations respectively.

question: How do umbrella sampling and trajectory reweighting contribute to determining $T_m$ in DNA studies?
answer: Umbrella sampling helps explore a range of configurations by applying biases, while trajectory reweighting adjusts these results for different temperatures. Together, they provide accurate estimates of melting temperatures by correcting for finite size effects and local concentration fluctuations.

evidence.text:
## F. 1 Duplex Melting Temperature Calculation

The melting temperature $\left(T_{m}\right)$ of a DNA duplex is defined as the temperature at which $50 \%$ of the DNA strands are bound in a duplex and $50 \%$ of the DNA strands remain unbound as single-stranded DNA. In general, binding and unbinding events occur on long timescales and therefore require enhanced sampling methods to calculate via simulation.

At a high level, melting temperature calculations are performed in oxDNA as follows. Given a DNA duplex, a discrete order parameter is assigned to each base pair indicating whether or not the two nucleotides are bound. Thus, a global order parameter indicating the total number of base pairs for a given state can be defined; a state is defined as bound if it has at least one base pair and unbound otherwise. Next, a biased simulation is run at a single temperature in which an umbrella weight is assigned to each possible number of base pairs. The simulation results are then unbiased to obtain the number of states visited in the bound and unbound states. These counts are then extrapolated to a range of temperatures and a finite size correction is applied to the extrapolated counts. Finally, a melting curve is fit to the ratio of bound to unbound counts at each temperature and the melting temperature is determined as the temperature at which there are $50 \%$ bound and $50 \%$ unbound states.
Formally, consider a system of two complimentary sequences of single-stranded DNA of length $n$ that can base pair to form a duplex. The $i^{t h}$ base pair is comprised of the $i^{t h}$ and the $(2 n-i+1)^{t h}$ nucleotides with the first and second strands represented by nucleotides indexed by $[1, n]$ and $[n+1,2 n]$, respectively. Given a configuration $R \in \mathbb{R}^{2 n \times 3}$, assume the existence a base-pair level order parameter

$$
B(i)= \begin{cases}1 & \text { if } R_{i} \text { and } R_{2 n-i+1} \text { are bonded } \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

We can then define a state-level order parameter that computes the total number of base pairs,

$$
N(R)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} B(i)
$$

Since there are $n$ possible base pairs, $N(R) \in[0, n]$. We then define a vector of umbrella weights $\omega \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ where $\omega_{i}$ denotes the umbrella weight applied to a state with $i$ base pairs. If $U: \mathbb{R}^{2 n \times 3} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ denotes the oxDNA energy function, umbrella sampling via these weights will sample states from the following probability distribution:

$$
p(R)=\frac{\omega_{N(R)} \exp (-\beta U(R))}{Z}
$$

where

$$
Z=\int \omega_{N\left(R^{\prime}\right)} \exp \left(-\beta U\left(R^{\prime}\right)\right) d R^{\prime}
$$

Next, we sample a trajectory of $T$ states $\vec{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times 2 n \times 3}$ from this distribution via virtual-move Monte Carlo (VMMC) at temperature $\tau$. Given this trajectory, we can compute the biased number of states with $i$ base pairs, $S_{i}$ :

$$
S_{i}^{\text {biased }}=\sum_{t=1}^{T} \delta\left(N\left(\vec{R}_{t}\right)=i\right)
$$

For an arbitrary state-level observable $A$, the expected value with respect to a set of states sampled from an umbrella sampling simulation can be computed as

$$
\langle A\rangle=\frac{\langle A / \omega\rangle_{\vec{R}}}{\langle 1 / \omega\rangle_{\vec{R}}}
$$

where $\omega$ denotes the umbrella weight for a given state. Thus, we can obtain an unbiased value of $S_{i}$,

$$
S_{i}^{\text {unbiased }}=\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{\omega_{i}} \delta\left(N\left(\vec{R}_{t}\right)=i\right)
$$

where we ignore the normalization factor as we only care about ratios of counts when computing $T_{m}$. In the same manner, given a simulation at temperature $\tau$, one can treat this simulation as a biased sample of the ensemble at another temperature $\tau^{\prime}$ and the expected value of an observable $A$ can be corrected in the same way as in umbrella sampling [60]:

$$
\langle A(x)\rangle_{\tau^{\prime}}=\left\langle A(x) \exp \left(U(x, \tau) / k \tau-U\left(x, \tau^{\prime}\right) / k \tau^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle
$$

Note that in oxDNA $U\left(x, \tau^{\prime}\right)$ is different than $U(x, \tau)$ due to the temperature-dependence of the stacking term in the interaction energy. Thus, given our set of states sampled at temperature $\tau$ with our umbrella weights $\vec{\omega}$, we can obtain an unbiased value of $S_{i}$ at temperature $\tau^{\prime}$ :

$$
S_{i, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }}=\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{\omega_{i}} \exp \left(\Delta U\left(\vec{R}_{t}\right)_{\tau^{\prime}}\right) \delta\left(N\left(\vec{R}_{t}\right)=i\right)
$$

![img-14.jpeg](img-14.jpeg)

Figure S9: Sensitivity analysis for the A. duplex and B. hairpin $T_{m}$ optimizations, represented by the five most significant parameters ranked by the absolute value of their gradients.
where

$$
\Delta U\left(\overrightarrow{R}_{t}\right)_{r^{\prime}}=U\left(\overrightarrow{R}_{t}, \tau\right) / k \tau-U\left(\overrightarrow{R}_{t}, \tau^{\prime}\right) / k \tau^{\prime}
$$

Again, we omit the normalizing factor. Given $S_{i, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }}$ for $i \in[0, n]$ for a given temperature $\tau^{\prime}$, we then compute the total number of bound and unbound states as

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{\text {bound, } \tau^{\prime}} & =\sum_{i=1}^{n} S_{i, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }} \\
S_{\text {unbound, } \tau^{\prime}} & =S_{0, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }}
\end{aligned}
$$

and define the relative probability with which bound and unbound states are observed as

$$
\Phi_{\tau^{\prime}}=\frac{S_{\text {bound, } \tau^{\prime}}}{S_{\text {unbound, } \tau^{\prime}}}
$$

The fraction of bound pairs can then be expressed as

$$
f_{1, \tau^{\prime}}=\frac{\Phi}{1+\Phi}
$$

Importantly, $f_{1, \tau^{\prime}}$ is computed using states sampled from a simulation of two DNA strands in a finite-sized box with periodic boundaries. In practice, this quantity is affected by fluctuations in the local concentration of reactants and therefore $f_{1, \tau^{\prime}} \neq f_{\infty, \tau^{\prime}}$ where $f_{\infty, \tau^{\prime}}$ is the bulk equilibrium bonding fraction at the same temperature and concentration. To account for this source of error, we apply the correction introduced by Ouldridge [69]:

$$
f_{\infty, \tau^{\prime}}=\left(1+\frac{1}{2 \Phi}\right)-\sqrt{\left(1+\frac{1}{2 \Phi}\right)^{2}-1}
$$

For a set of evenly-spaced temperatures $\left\{\tau_{l o}, \cdots, \tau_{h i}\right\}$, we apply Equations 82-88 to compute $\left\{f_{\infty, \tau_{l o}}, \cdots, f_{\infty, \tau_{h i}}\right\}$. Finally, we interpolate to find the temperature $\tau^{*}$ at which $f_{\infty, \tau^{*}}=0.5$. We can similarly interpolate to compute the width of the melting curve where

$$
T_{\text {width }}=\tau_{0.2}-\tau_{0.8}
$$

where $\tau_{0.2}$ and $\tau_{0.8}$ are the temperatures at which the bulk equilibrium bonding fraction is 0.2 and 0.8 , respectively.
Given a set of reference states sampled at a single temperature $\tau$ subject to umbrella weights $\omega$, the calculation of the melting temperature (and melting curve width) are differentiable via trajectory reweighting and implicit differentiation. Consider the calculation of $S_{i, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }}$ via Equation 82. As this quantity is a sum rather than an expected value and therefore the contribution of each state is scaled by 1 rather than $1 / N$ in the case where $\theta=\tilde{\theta}$, we rewrite Equation 82 as

$$
S_{i, \tau^{\prime}}^{\text {unbiased }}=\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{T}{w_{i}} \frac{1}{\omega_{i}} \exp \left(\Delta U\left(\overrightarrow{R}_{t}\right)_{\tau^{\prime}}\right) \delta\left(N\left(\overrightarrow{R}_{t}\right)=i\right)
$$

where $w_{i}$ is the DiffTRE weight for the $i^{\text {th }}$ state. Importantly, $\frac{N}{w_{i}}=1$ when $\theta=\tilde{\theta}$. Additionally, as $\nabla_{\theta} \omega=0$, such prefactors can be computed. However, given the temperature dependent stacking term in the oxDNA potential, $\nabla_{\theta} \exp \left(\Delta U\left(\vec{R}_{t}\right)_{r^{\prime}}\right) \neq 0$ in the general case where $\theta$ includes stacking parameters. The oxDNA standalone code uses an energy threshold for computing $B(i)$ and therefore $\nabla_{\theta} B(i) \neq 0$ but as this quantity is thresholded (and not continuous) we neglect this term; we find that this is a reasonable approximation in practice. Given our differentiable formulation of $S_{i, r^{\prime}}^{\text {nobscued }}$ in Equation 90, the remaining calculation of the melting temperature and width require elementary differentiable operators, including the process of one-dimensional linear interpolation.
Above, we describe our method of differentiable melting curve calculation via a single order parameter (i.e. number of base pairs). In practice, we use a second order parameter, the inter-strand center of mass distance, to accelerate sampling. Equation 90 can flexibly accomodate an arbitrary number of order parameters as the delta function can be evaluated for an arbitrary subset of order parameters while the weight for a given state $\omega_{i}$ depends on all biased order parameters used in sampling.
Computing $T_{m}$ values requires sampling many uncorrelated states. To sample reference states, we perform 34 individual simulations of $5 \times 10^{7}$ virtual-move Monte Carlo (VMMC) steps, sampling snapshots every $2.5 \times 10^{5}$ steps. We perform biased simulations at 307.15 K . We resample reference states with $\lambda=0.95$ or after three gradient updates. All duplex $T_{m}$ calculations are done with the oxDNA 1.0 force field rather than oxDNA 2.0.

question: What is the time-dependent Aharonov-Bohm effect?
answer: The time-dependent Aharonov-Bohm effect involves a scenario where the magnetic flux inside a solenoid changes over time. This variation introduces complexities in theoretical analysis, as it requires considering line-integrals of the vector potential in four-dimensional space, leading to ongoing debates about its implications.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

The time-dependent Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect considers the situation in which the magnetic flux inside the solenoid changes time-dependently. Different from the standard AB-effect, the problem is unexpectedly subtle and not easy to solve without any doubt, which is the reason why it is still in a state of unsettlement even theoretically. The difficulty originates from the fact that its theoretical analysis requires line-integrals of the time-dependent vector potential along paths in the 4-dimensional Minkowski space. Owing to the 4-dimensional Stokes theorem, this closed line-integral of the vector potential can be related to the integral of the electric and magnetic fields over the 2-dimensional area, the boundary of which is given by the above-mentioned closed path. The central controversy concerns the success or failure of the claim by Singleton and collaborators based on the 4-dimensional Stokes theorem, which states that the time-dependent part of the AB-phase shift due to the magnetic vector potential is precisely cancelled by the effect of induced electric field generated by the time-variation of the magnetic flux. In the present paper, we carefully reanalyze their cancellation argument by going back to the basic quantum mechanical analysis of the charged particle motion under the presence of the time-dependent external electromagnetic potential combined with more careful treatment of the 4-dimensional Stokes theorem. Careful analysis of the 4-dimensional Stokes theorem shows that the cancellation argument by Singleton et al. is partially correct but their central claim that only the time-independent part of the magnetic field contributes to the AB-phase shift so that there is no time-dependent AB-effect is not justified, thereby supporting likely existence of the time-dependent AB-effect.


Keywords: Time-dependent Aharonov-Bohm effect, 4-dimensional Stokes theorem, quantum mechanics, gauge transformation

question: How does air pollution affect under-5 child mortality in China?
answer: Air pollution, particularly from pollutants such as SO2 and PM2.5 emitted by coal power plants, increases susceptibility to respiratory infections among children under five, leading to higher mortality rates.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

This paper evaluates the impact of a mandatory shutdown policy of small-capacity coal power plants during China's $11^{\text {th }}$ 5-Year Plan pe-$\operatorname{riod}(2006-2010)$ on under-5 mortality. We collect capacity and location information on 2181 coal power plants that operated during 2000-2010 and compile a unique data set that combines coal power plants, county-level under-5 mortality and socioeconomic variables, high spatial resolution data of $\mathrm{PM}_{2.5}$ and $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ and meteorological conditions. We model the impacts of air pollution on under-5 mortality using the IV-Lasso method, with distance-weighted sums of retired capacity and high-altitude wind status as instrumental variable candidates for air pollution. Our estimates imply that the phase-out policy saved around 46,000 lives during the $11^{\text {th }}$ 5-Year Plan period. We also find heterogeneity in the policy effects across regions. (JEL I10, I18, P25, P28, Q52, Q53, Q58)


Coal-generated electricity in China accounts for $62 \%$ of the country's total electricity supply (IEA, 2024a) and has been a key driver of economic growth over the past four decades. However, burning coal also generates air pollutants, such as $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{PM}_{2.5}$. Over the three decades following 1990, the Chinese government implemented a series of regulations aimed at improving air quality, particularly by reducing $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ emissions, while still meeting coal demand and sustaining economic growth. As a result, total SO2 emissions peaked in 2006 and have steadily decreased since then (Figure 1). Understanding the contribution of these $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ emission control policies to public health, especially for children as the most vulnerable population, is of considerable interest, not only to China, but also to other fast-growing countries.

Although the effects of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ on human health have been studied extensively in the public health field, there are still areas that require further investigation. One such area is the impact of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ on under-5 mortality, a topic that has rarely been explored specifically. Understanding this effect is particularly important for The United Nations' sustainable development goals, especially the target to end preventable deaths of newborns and children under 5 years of age by 2030, with the goal of reducing under-5 mortality to at least 25 per 1,000 live births (UNECE, 2024). Many developing and under-developed countries are still far from reaching this target, including India (World Bank Group, 2024b), which also relies heavily on coal for energy supply and is consistently increasing coal demand (IEA, 2024b). Burning coal releases various toxic pollutants including

[^0]
[^0]:    * Xiaoying Liu: Affiliate researcher at Population Studies Center, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, United States, xiaoyliu@sas.upenn.edu. Heng Yu: University of Chicago, 5757 S University Ave, Chicago, IL 60637, hyu8@uchicago.edu. Acknowledgements: we thank Jing Wei for sharing ChinaHighPM2.5 dataset. We also thank Jere Behrman, Emily Hannum, Shiqiu Zhang, Jo Van Biesebroeck and other participants at Development Economics seminar at KU Leuven for comments.

mercury, lead, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter and heavy metals into the air (Gasparotto and Da Boit Martinello, 2021). These pollutants are known to increase susceptibility to respiratory infections by disrupting immune functions, imparing macrophage activity, altering cellular receptors used by pathogens, and disturbing the microbiome (see Monoson et al. (2023) for an extensive review of epidemiological evidence and laboratory mechanisms), particularly among vulnerable populations such as children and the elderly. According to a 2015 global study on the causes of under-5 mortality, pneumonia accounts for nearly one-sixth of deaths and is the leading cause of death among children aged 1-59 month period (Liu et al., 2016), surpassing both diarrhoea and malaria combined (Watkins and Sridhar, 2018). Although epidemiological studies over the past three decades have focused on the associations between $S O_{2}$ and public health, limited attention has been given to evaluating sulfur control policies and addressing bias from omitted variables that are linked to both air pollution and mortality.

This paper examines the impacts of $S O_{2}$ and $P M_{2.5}$ on under-5 mortality in China, leveraging a policy that mandated the replacement of inefficient coal power plants with more efficient ones (also called "big-up, small-down" policy) and installation of flue gas desulfurization (FGD) system during the $11^{\text {th }}$ 5-Year Plan (FYP) period (2006-2010). The "big-up, small-down" policy and FGD installation policy, issued by the central government in 2006, required local governments to phase out low-efficiency power plants (particularly those with a capacity of less than 50 megawatts (MW)) and to ensure installation of FGD in other coal power plants over the course of the five-year period. Our identification strategy exploits the exogenous shocks (or improvements) to air pollution levels ( $S O_{2}$ and $P M_{2.5}$ ) caused by this policy. We compile a unique national-scale dataset that links annual county-level under-5 mortality rates and socio-economic development, individual coal power plant operations and closures, high spatial and temporal resolution air pollution and meteorological conditions from remote sensing, all using geocoding. Specifically, we geocode all power plants that were operating or shut down between 2000 and 2010. We calculate the total capacity of power plant units that were shut down or required to install FGD each year within a certain radius from the geographic center of each county. Additionally, we obtain annual under-5 mortality rates at the county level and calculate monthly mean concentrations of $S O_{2}$ and $P M_{2.5}$ within each county boundary using high-resolution remote sensing data. We then estimate the impacts of $S O_{2}$ and $P M_{2.5}$ on under-5 mortality, using the closed-down capacities and capacities with installed FGD as instrumental variables to create exogenous variation in air pollution levels.

This paper makes four contributions to the literature. Firstly, it contributes to the economic literature that examines the health effects of air pollution in quasi-experimental settings. Unlike studies that examine spontaneous natural events (e.g., a volcanic eruption(Halliday, Lynham and De Paula, 2019) or natural forest fire (Jayachandran, 2009)) leading to short-term air quality deterioration, we evaluate a national policy that resulted in sustained improvements in air quality within the context of a highly polluted country. The period from 2006 to 2010 in China provides an ideal natural experiment for policy evaluation, offering two key advantages: 1) the national air quality policy during the

$11^{\text {th }}$ FYP period focused solely on sulfur control, allowing us to disentangle the effects of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ from other pollutants; 2) the policy was enforced in a top-down manner, which helps address potential endogeneity issues in estimation. Secondly, this study contributes to the literature on the health impacts of coal power plants specifically. While previous research has examined the health effects of coal power plant expansion or regulations in different countries (Gupta and Spears, 2017; Luechinger, 2014; DeCicca and Malak, 2020), this is the first study to focus on the impacts of coal power plants on child mortality in China. Thirdly, our study utilizes high spatial- and temporal-resolution satellite remote sensing data to measure air pollution during a period when ground-level monitoring data were unavailable, and it makes use of detailed information on individual coal power plants to measure policy exposure at county level. Our last contribution is methodological. This study adds to the few literature that implements the IV-Lasso method in selecting instrumental variables using machine learning. In addition to anthropogenic factors, air quality is affected by atmospheric conditions such as thermal inversions, planetary boundary layer height, altitude winds and altitude pressures (Deryugina et al., 2019; Godzinski and Suarez Castillo, 2021) that are completely unrelated to local anthropological activities. Given the interdisciplinary nature of these studies involving high-frequency air quality observations, there may exist a large set of instrumental variable candidates available for use. Estimating with Lasso-IV method, we are able to efficiently select a smaller set of instrumental variables (Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen, 2014).

More broadly, evaluating the health impacts of sulfur control policies in China has important implications for other developing countries conducting cost-benefit analyses of environmental policies. As coal remains the primary source of energy driving economic growth and the main contributor to $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ emissions, sulfur control policies may potentially slow economic growth. On the other hand, economic development can fund investments in public health, reducing mortality from malnutrition or lack of medical care. Given the ongoing rise in coal demand to support economic growth in India, Indonesia, Viet Nam and the Philippines (IEA, 2024b), is it still feasible to reduce the under-5 mortality in these countries? What can be learned from China, the world's largest coal consumer and once the most polluted country, which has successfully reduced $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ significantly in the last two decades and achieved a very low under-5 mortality rate?

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section I, we introduce the background of air quality control policies in the $11^{\text {th }}$ FYP in China; Section II introduces the data, which is followed by Section III that introduces the empirical model and identification strategy; Section IV presents our main results; Section V presents heterogeneity analysis results by subsamples; Section VI discusses the results and concludes.

question: How does Amortized Bayesian Inference transform posterior sampling during the inference phase?
answer: Posterior sampling is transformed into an almost instantaneous forward pass through the neural network.

evidence.text:
## A. 2 Amortized Bayesian Inference

While performing Bayesian inference for high-dimensional models on a single data set is already challenging, the computational burden increases considerably when the same model must be applied to multiple data sets. Achieving accurate posterior inference can quickly become too computationally expensive in such cases. This issue is most apparent when fitting the same statistical model to several or sometimes millions (von Krause et al., 2022) of mutually independent data sets.
Amortized Bayesian Inference (ABI) (ABI; Gershman and Goodman, 2014; Ritchie et al., 2016; Le et al., 2017; Radev et al., 2020a) offers a promising solution to the problem of repeated refits for models with or without tractable likelihood functions. ABI decouples estimation into two phases: (1) a training phase, during which a neural network learns a posterior functional from model simulations, and (2) an inference phase, where posterior sampling is transformed into an almost instantaneous forward pass through the neural network. The term amortized emphasizes that the computational demand from the initial training phase amortizes over subsequent rapid model fits, typically within a fraction of a second when using invertible neural networks (Kruse et al., 2021).
Towards amortized Bayesian inference, several methods have been developed that amortize the evaluation of certain model or algorithm components in combination with other non-amortized components. Examples include amortized approximate ratio estimators (Hermans et al., 2020) and the likelihood approximation networks of Fengler et al. (2021) which can be used within (non-amortized) MCMC, as well as amortized methods to improve proposal distributions within (non-amortized) sequential Monte-Carlo.

question: How does the performance of the Two-Stage Least Squares (TSLS) estimator compare to the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator in terms of bias and variance when estimating peer effects?

question: How does the Edgeworth expansion technique contribute to studying implied volatility surfaces?
answer: The Edgeworth expansion technique is employed to analyze the at-the-money skew and curvature of implied volatility surfaces. It allows for a detailed examination of these features by expanding on traditional methods, offering a more nuanced understanding within various financial models.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

We introduce a novel cumulant-based method for approximating the shape of implied volatility smiles, applicable to the widely-used stochastic volatility models and distribution-based asset pricing models. We adopt an Edgeworth expansion technique to study the at-the-money (ATM) skew and curvature of the implied volatility surface. We propose cumulant conditions to derive their short-term asymptotics. Then we show that the conditions are satisfied by a wide scope of regular stochastic volatility models, rough volatility models and distribution-based models.


Keywords: Implied volatility; ATM Skew; ATM Curvature; Asymptotic approximation

question: What is RMS used for in the context of video-to-sound generation?
answer: RMS is used as a temporal feature to shape the audio in alignment with video, serving as the temporal event condition in RMS-ControlNet.

evidence.text:
## B. RMS as a Temporal Event Condition

We propose to use RMS over timestamps as a temporal feature to shape the audio in alignment with video. RMS serves as the temporal event condition in RMS-ControlNet, guiding the audio generation process. Here, RMS serves as an effective intermediate feature to shape audio temporally corresponding to video. We define RMS $R(x)=\left[R_{1}, \ldots, R_{i}, \ldots\right]$ as a framelevel amplitude envelope feature of audio waveform defined
as follows: for the i-th frame,

$$
R_{i}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\omega} \Sigma_{t=i h}^{i h+\omega} x^{2}(t)}
$$

where $x(t)(t \in[0, T])$ is the audio waveform, $\omega$ is a window size and $h$ is a hop size.

There are two main reasons for selecting RMS. First, timestamps capture only the start and end points of sound events, overlooking crucial audio characteristics such as volume dynamics-for instance, the gradual intensity shift of a moving car, which is difficult to describe in text. RMS effectively represents these aspects, from transient event-based sounds to continuous ambient sounds [14]. Additionally, human annotation for timestamp is costly and highly subjective, as further discussed in the next paragraph. Moreover, Heller et al. [24] demonstrated that listeners perceive hybrid sounds-Foley sounds combined with the temporal envelope of real recordings-as more realistic than either Foley or real recordings alone. This finding underscores the importance of intensity dynamics in sound generation.

Onset annotation is inherently subjective and lacks a systematic definition, making it prone to inconsistencies. For certain sound events-such as scratching sounds with multiple adjacent attacks or sounds with slow gradual attacks including water, wind, and musical instrument sound-defining an exact onset timestamp is challenging, as it may not align with both the waveform envelope and human perception. In other words, the moment a sound begins physically does not always match how humans perceive its onset [25]. Fig. 5 demonstrates examples from the Greatest Hits dataset [26], highlighting the subjectivity of onset annotations. This subjectivity is critical in video-to-sound generation, where precise temporal synchrony is essential. Inaccurate timestamp annotations can degrade model performance and make timestamp-based evaluations unreliable.

question: How does fragment-based drug discovery work?
answer: Fragment-based drug discovery involves screening small chemical compounds, known as fragments, to see if they bind effectively to biological targets. These fragments are then combined into larger molecules for potential therapeutic use.
