# 3.3 Handling composite nulls in one-sided testing problems 

An even more common testing setup in practice is

$$
H_{0}: \theta^{*} \leqslant \theta_{0} \quad \text { vs. } \quad H_{1}: \theta^{*}>\theta_{0} \quad\left(\theta_{0} \in \Theta\right)
$$

meaning we have a composite null hypothesis and a composite alternative. Throughout this section, we assume that for all $\theta_{1} \in \Theta$ with $\theta_{1} \geqslant \theta_{0}$,

$$
\lambda(x)=\frac{p_{\theta_{1}}(x)}{p_{\theta_{0}}(x)} \text { is nondecreasing in } x
$$

Robbins and Siegmund [22] showed that under this assumption the process $\left(\Lambda_{t}^{\text {plugin }}\right)$ defined in Equation (18) also provides a valid sequential test for the composite null hypothesis above. In the following, we show that the same holds for our boosted process.

Proposition 3.1. Consider the one-sided testing problem (20) under the monotone likelihood ratio property (21) and let $\lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right)=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}\left(X_{t}\right)}{p_{\theta_{0}}\left(X_{t}\right)}$ for some predictable parameter $\theta_{t} \geqslant \theta_{0}$. Then,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}}\left[T_{\alpha}\left(b_{t} \lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right) ; M\right) \mid \Lambda_{t-1}^{\text {boost }}\right] \leqslant 1 \Longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[T_{\alpha}\left(b_{t} \lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right) ; M\right) \mid \Lambda_{t-1}^{\text {boost }}\right] \leqslant 1 \quad\left(\theta \leqslant \theta_{0}\right)
$$

To summarize, for the composite testing problem above and under the monotone likelihood ratio property, we can do exactly the same as described in Section 3.2 for the simple null hypothesis without inflating type I error.

Remark 3. An important class satisfying property (21) is the one-parameter exponential family, where each density is given by $p_{\theta}(x)=h(x) \exp (T(x) \eta(\theta)-A(\theta))$ with $h, T, \eta$ and $A$ being known functions. It is easy to see that (21) is fulfilled for the sufficient statistic $T(x)$, if $\eta(\theta)$ is nondecreasing in $\theta$.

question: What are trace-invariants in the context of tensor components?
answer: Trace-invariants are homogeneous local-unitary invariant polynomials in tensor components, represented graphically as edge-colored graphs. They help describe the symmetries and properties of tensors.

evidence.text:
### 4.1.1 Trace-invariants

Similarly to invariant matrix functions, a function $f$ of the tensor $A$ is said to be local-unitary invariant (LU-invariant), if for any $U_{1}, \ldots, U_{D} \in U(N)$,

$$
f(A)=f\left(\left(U_{1} \otimes \cdots \otimes U_{D}\right) A\left(U_{1}^{\dagger} \otimes \cdots \otimes U_{D}^{\dagger}\right)\right)
$$

We call trace-invariants the homogeneous local-unitary invariant polynomials in the tensor components [11] such that all the output indices $i^{c}$ are identified and summed (contracted) with input indices $j^{c}$ respecting the color $c=1, \ldots D$.

Graphical representation. The trace-invariants can be represented as edge colored graphs. In the mixed case we represent a tensor $A$ by a pair consisting in a white and a black vertex connected by a thick edge to which we assign a color $D+1$. The input (resp. output) indices of color $c, j^{c}$ (resp. $i^{c}$ ) are represented by half-edges of color $c$ connected to the black (resp. white) vertex. This is depicted in Fig. 2, on the left. In the pure case we represent a tensor $T$ as a white vertex with output half-edges $i^{c}$, and a tensor $\bar{T}$ as a black vertex with input half-edges $j^{c}$, as depicted in Fig. 2, on the right.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{7}$ Note that even in the latter situation, these variables behave as independent ones, for instance when deriving saddle point or Schwinger-Dyson equations involving differentiation with respect to $T_{i^{1} \ldots i^{D}}$ and $\bar{T}_{i^{1} \ldots i^{D}}$.

![img-1.jpeg](img-1.jpeg)

Figure 2: Left: a mixed tensor $A_{i^{1} \ldots i^{D} ; j^{1} \ldots j^{D}}$ with input indices $j^{c}$ (resp. output $i^{c}$ ) represented as half-edges of color $c$ attached to the black (resp. white) vertex. Right: the pure case with $T_{i^{1} \ldots i^{D}}$ and $\bar{T}_{j^{1} \ldots j^{D}}$.

The pairing of a half-edge of color $c$ on a white vertex with a half-edge of color $c$ on a black one to form an edge of color $c$ represents the identification and summation of the two corresponding indices $i^{c}$ and $j^{c}$.

As illustrated in Fig. 3, the resulting graphs are bipartite $(D+1)$-edge-colored graphs in the mixed case (simply $(D+1)$-colored graphs below), while in the pure case they are $D$-colored, as there are no thick edges.
![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

Figure 3: Left: a trace-invariant for a mixed tensor $A$ with $D=3$ inputs and 3 outputs. Right: a similar invariant for the pure case with two tensors, $T$ with $D=3$ outputs and $\bar{T}$ with 3 inputs.

The trace-invariants are in one-to-one correspondence with the non-isomorphic non-labeled bipartite edge colored graphs with $n$ white and $n$ black vertices. Due to the presence of the extra edges, the invariance under relabeling in the mixed case differs from the one of the pure case.

Encoding via permutations. Trace-invariants are encoded by permutations. In the mixed case we label 1 to $n$ the copies of the tensor $A$, and we consider the $D$ permutations $\boldsymbol{\sigma}=$ $\left(\sigma_{1}, \ldots, \sigma_{D}\right), \sigma_{c} \in S_{n}$ obtained by setting $\sigma_{c}(s)=s^{\prime}$ if the output index $i^{c}$ of the tensor labeled $s$ is identified and summed with the input index $j^{c}$ of the tensor labeled $s^{\prime}$. Denoting $\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(A)$ the labeled trace-invariants, we have:

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(A)=\sum_{\text {all indices }}\left(\prod_{s=1}^{n} A_{i_{\sigma}^{1} \ldots i_{\sigma}^{D} ; j_{\sigma}^{1} \ldots j_{\sigma}^{D}}\right) \prod_{c=1}^{D}\left(\prod_{s=1}^{n} \delta_{i_{\sigma}^{c} ; j_{\sigma_{c}(s)}^{c}}\right)
$$

In the pure case we label 1 to $n$ the tensors $T$ and $\overline{1}$ to $\bar{n}$ the tensors $\bar{T}$, and we set $\sigma_{c}(s)=s^{\prime}$ if the output index $i^{c}$ on the white vertex $s$ is connected with the input index $j^{c}$ on the black vertex $\overline{s^{\prime}}$ :

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(T, \bar{T})=\sum_{\text {all indices }}\left(\prod_{s=1}^{n} T_{i_{\sigma}^{1} \ldots i_{\sigma}^{D}} \bar{T}_{j_{\sigma}^{1} \ldots j_{\sigma}^{D}}\right) \prod_{c=1}^{D}\left(\prod_{s=1}^{n} \delta_{i_{\sigma}^{c} ; j_{\sigma_{c}(s)}^{c}}\right)
$$

The summation convention is represented in Fig. 4. Remark that if $A=T \otimes \bar{T}$, then $\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(A)=$ $\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(T, \bar{T})$.

![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)

Figure 4: Convention adopted for encoding index summations with permutations, mixed on the left and pure on the right.

The connected components of the $(D+1)$-edge colored graph obtained in the mixed case correspond to the blocks of the partition $\Pi(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\Pi\left(\sigma_{1}\right) \vee \cdots \vee \Pi\left(\sigma_{D}\right)$, and we denoted their number by $K_{\mathrm{m}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\# \Pi(\boldsymbol{\sigma})$. This follows by observing that the cycles of the permutation $\sigma_{c}$ correspond to the bi-colored cycles of edges with colors $(c, D+1)$ in the graph. We call these the mixed connected components of $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$.

The connected components of the $D$-edge colored graph obtained in the pure case (also called pure connected components) correspond to the blocks of the bipartite partition $\Pi_{\mathrm{p}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=$ $\bigvee_{1 \leqslant c \leqslant D} \Pi_{\mathrm{p}}\left(\sigma_{c}\right)$ discussed in Sec. 2, whose number we denoted by $K_{\mathrm{p}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})$. If $K_{\mathrm{p}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=1$, we say that $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is purely connected.

Relabeling. We let for $\eta, \nu \in S_{n}$ :

$$
\eta \boldsymbol{\sigma} \nu=\left(\eta \sigma_{1} \nu, \ldots, \eta \sigma_{D} \nu\right)
$$

The trace-invariants do not depend on the labels of the tensors. The mixed and pure cases behave slightly differently:

- The mixed case. In the mixed case a relabeling of the $n$ tensors $A$ corresponds to a simultaneous conjugation of all the $\sigma_{c}$ by the same permutation $\eta \in S_{n}$, that is:

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\eta \boldsymbol{\sigma} \eta^{-1}}(A)
$$

In this case a non-labeled trace-invariant is an equivalence class (orbit in $S_{n}^{D} / \sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ ) of labeled bipartite $(D+1)$-edge colored graphs with the equivalence relation:

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim_{\mathrm{m}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \exists \eta \in S_{n} \mid \boldsymbol{\sigma}=\eta \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime} \eta^{-1}
$$

- The pure case. In the pure case the white and black vertices can be relabeled independently, that is for any $\eta, \nu \in S_{n}$ :

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(T, \bar{T})=\operatorname{Tr}_{\eta \boldsymbol{\sigma} \nu}(T, \bar{T})
$$

In this case a non-labeled trace-invariant is an equivalence class (orbit in $S_{n}^{D} / \sim_{\mathrm{p}}$ ) of labeled bipartite $D$-edge colored graphs (with no thick edges) with the equivalence relation:

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim_{\mathrm{p}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \exists \eta, \nu \in S_{n} \mid \boldsymbol{\sigma}=\eta \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime} \nu
$$

Remark 4.1. It is obvious that $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim_{\mathrm{m}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime}$ implies $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim_{\mathrm{p}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime}$, but the converse is not true in general. What holds however is the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim_{\mathrm{p}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\prime} \text { in } S_{n}^{D} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} \sim_{\mathrm{m}} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{\prime} \text { in } S_{n}^{D-1}
$$

where $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}=\left(\sigma_{1} \sigma_{D}^{-1}, \ldots, \sigma_{D-1} \sigma_{D}^{-1}\right) \in S_{n}^{D-1}$, that is one can treat a pure invariant like a mixed one with one less color by declaring the edges of color $D$ of the pure invariant to be thick.

Matrices. The $D=1$ mixed case reproduces the matrix trace-invariants discussed in Sec. 3.1. Indeed, for $D=1$ a mixed trace-invariant is a collection of cycles with thick edges of color 2 and thin edges of color 1. Labeling the matrices $M$ corresponds to labeling the thick edges and (4.2) becomes $\operatorname{Tr}_{\sigma}(M)$. Relabeling the matrices corresponds to conjugating $\sigma$ by some permutation and a non-labeled trace-invariant corresponds to the conjugacy class of $S_{n} / \sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ of permutations of fixed cycle type.

The $D=2$ pure case is also matricial: one has matrices $X$ and $\bar{X}$, typically the conjugate of $X$. A trace-invariant corresponds to a collection of alternating cycles with white and black vertices and thin edges of color 1 and 2. The trace-invariants are functions of $X X^{\dagger}$.

question: How are trades validated in a constant function market maker (CFMM)?
answer: Trades are valid if they do not decrease the CFMM's utility and do not require more assets than the AMM holds, i.e., $u(\Pi) \leq u(\Pi+\delta)$ and $\Pi+\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$.

evidence.text:
### 2.1 Background on Automated Market Maker

An AMM is, in brief, a pool of assets against which any individual trader can transact. The key innovation of these types of asset pools within decentralized finance is that they permit investors to add their own assets to the AMM in exchange for a fraction of the fees collected by the AMM. The most common AMM construction is that of the constant function market maker (CFMM) which is defined by a multivariate utility function $u: \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{+}$and the size of the asset pool $\Pi \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ (such that $u(\Pi)>0$ ). As summarized in, e.g., [4], the CFMM then permits trades $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ that do not decrease the CFMM's utility nor does it require more assets than the AMM holds, i.e., $\delta$ is a valid trade if:

$$
u(\Pi) \leq u(\Pi+\delta) \quad \text { and } \quad \Pi+\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}
$$

These AMMs are called constant function market makers because, under mild assumptions (see, e.g., [6]), the utility before and after a transaction are equal $(u(\Pi)=u(\Pi+\delta))$.

Based on the constant function construction, the marginal price of asset $i$ in terms of the numéraire asset $j$ can be determined via the relation $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=\frac{\partial}{\partial \Pi_{i}} u(\Pi) / \frac{\partial}{\partial \Pi_{j}} u(\Pi)$. This mapping is often called the pricing oracle. As is clear from the construction, $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=P_{j}^{i}(\Pi)^{-1}$ for any $\Pi \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$; this makes clear that there do not exist fees within this construction. In practice, fees are charged on a fraction of the assets being sold to the AMM, i.e., $\gamma \in(0,1)$ of the incoming assets (asset $i$ such that $\delta_{i}>0$ ) are taken to compensate the market maker for its service as a counterparty. Mathematically this modifies the CFMM construction so that $u(\Pi)=u\left(\Pi+\left[I-\gamma \operatorname{diag}\left(\mathbb{I}_{\{\delta>0\}}\right)\right] \delta\right)$.

Finally, investors are able to deposit their assets into the AMM in exchange for a fraction of

the fees collected; these depositors are often referred to as liquidity providers (LPs). This is done following the constant pricing oracle construction so that the prices before and after the liquidity provision remain equal, i.e., $\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ is deposited if $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=P_{i}^{j}(\Pi+\delta)$ for any pair of assets $(i, j)$; in practice, and as presented explicitly in the preceding equation, no fees are charged on these deposits. Similarly, LPs can later withdraw their assets at any time taking from the AMM the same fraction of the asset pool that they initially deposited. The fraction of fees collected by any individual LP is equal to the fraction of the assets that they hold at the AMM. Throughout this work, and as implemented within Uniswap v3 [1], the fees are distributed immediately upon collection to the liquidity providers.

Assumption 2.1. For the remainder of this work, we will consider the constant product market maker (CPMM) in the $n=2$ asset setting as is utilized by Uniswap and Sushiswap pools (i.e., $u(x, y):=x y)$. In addition, throughout, we take the second asset as the numéraire (i.e., $P(x, y):=$ $\left.P_{1}^{2}(x, y)\right)$.

In practice, AMMs exist as smart contracts that operate in a decentralized manner directly on a blockchain. This means that transactions are only processed at the block-writing times. By construction of the blockchain, this occurs at discrete times. For the Bitcoin blockchain, which utilizes a proof-of-work construction, each block is processed in approximately 10 minute intervals. However, more modern blockchains - using, e.g., proof-of-stake consensus - have nearly constant inter-block times $\Delta t>0$. For the Ethereum blockchain, the inter-block time is $\Delta t=12$ seconds; for the Polygon blockchain, the inter-block time is $\Delta t=2$ seconds.

Assumption 2.2. For the remainder of this work, we will assume that the inter-block time is fixed at $\Delta t>0$. Therefore the realized price process is $P_{i \Delta t}$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

question: What is the stable length of a loxodromic element $g$ in a $\delta$-hyperbolic space?
answer: The stable length of $g$, denoted as $\tau(g)$, is defined as $\lim _{n} \frac{d\left(g^{n} o, o\right)}{n}$.

evidence.text:
# Appendix A. Quantitative version of Wenyuan Yang's admissible path lemma 

The aim of this section is to prove a quantitative version of W. Yang's admissible path lemma [68, Corollary 3.4], which applies to our setting. For our purposes, we will take a fixed action on a hyperbolic space but vary the loxodromic element and thus the quasi-geodesic constants $\lambda$. So throughout, we track dependence on $\lambda$. The following quantitative version of the Morse lemma is present in [29, Section 5.2]; see [62, Theorem 1.1]) for an explicit polynomial.
Lemma A.1. [Quantitative Morse Lemma] Let $X$ be a $\delta$-hyperbolic space, and let $\gamma$ be a $(\lambda, 0)$ -quasi-geodesic. Let $\sigma$ be a geodesic with the same endpoints as $\gamma$. Then $\gamma$ is contained in a $Q_{1}(\lambda)$ neighborhood of $\sigma$ with $Q_{1}$ a quadratic polynomial (which depends on $\delta$ ).

We continue with some notation. Let $(G, S) \curvearrowright X$ be a group $G$ with a finite generating set $S$ acting acylindrically on a $\delta$-hyperbolic space $X$. Fix an origin $o \in X$. Let $g \in G$ be a loxodromic element. Let $\tau(g)=\lim _{n} \frac{d\left(g^{n} o, o\right)}{n}$ denote the stable length of $g$. We observe that $\tau(g)$ is independent of the choice of base point and is stable under conjugation. Let $[g]$ denote the displacement (or translation length) of $g$, defined by

$$
[g]=\inf _{x \in X} d(g x, x)
$$

This infimum is in fact achieved at some point $x_{0} \in X$. We let $L_{g}=\cup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\left[g^{n} x_{0}, g^{n+1} x_{0}\right]$. Let $\gamma=\cup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\left[g^{n} o, g^{n+1} o\right]$ be the axis of $g$ going through $o$. Let $\lambda=\frac{d(g o, o)}{\tau(g)}$ so that $\gamma$ is a $(\lambda, 0)$-quasiaxis; i.e., if $m<n$ are integers then

$$
\ell(\gamma)=\sum_{i=m}^{n-1} d\left(g^{i} o, g^{i+1} o\right) \leq \lambda d\left(\gamma^{-}, \gamma^{+}\right)=\lambda d\left(g^{n-m} o, o\right)
$$

Note that clearly $[g] \leq d(g o, o)=\tau(g) \lambda$. Let $E(g)$ denote the maximal elementary (i.e., virtually cyclic) subgroup of $G$ containing $g$. For sets $Y, Z \subset X$, let $\pi_{Y}(Z)$ denote the projection of $Z$ onto $Y$. More precisely, $y \in \pi_{Y}(Z)$ if and only if $y \in Y$ and there exists $z \in Z$ such that $d(y, z)=$ $\min \left\{d\left(y^{\prime}, z\right): y^{\prime} \in Y\right\}$. For a set $Y \subset X$ let $\|Y\|$ denote its diameter; i.e., the smallest real number such that $d\left(y, y^{\prime}\right) \leq\|Y\|$ for all $y, y^{\prime} \in Y$.

The following is due to Delzant. We note that the constant $D_{0}$ below depends only on the action $G \curvearrowright X$.

Proposition A.2. ( [21, Proposition 5]) Let $G \curvearrowright X$ be an acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space and let $g \in G$ be a loxodromic element (i.e. a hyperbolic isometry). Then for all $h \notin E(g)$,

$$
\left\|\pi_{L_{g}}\left(h L_{g}\right)\right\| \leq D_{0}(1+[g])
$$

The following lemma is the quantitative version of [64, Lemma 2.23].
Lemma A. 3 (Quantitative Bounded Projection). There is a quadratic $Q_{2}$ such that whenever a loxodromic element $g$ and a point $x \in X$ gives a $(\lambda, 0)$-quasi-axis $\gamma=\cup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\left[g^{n} x, g^{n+1} x\right]$ and $h \notin E(g)$, then

$$
\left\|\pi_{\gamma}(h \gamma)\right\| \leq Q_{2}(\lambda)(1+[g])
$$

Proof. The quasi-axes $\gamma$ and $L_{g}$ both converge to the same points on the Gromov boundary of $X$. We may, therefore, apply the quantitative Morse lemma to transfer the inequality from Proposition A. 2 to $\gamma$, up to a quadratic in $\lambda$.

The following theorem, the main theorem of this section, is essentially a reproduction of [68, Corollary 3.4] but where we have tracked all of the constants and dependencies to verify they grow polynomially.

Theorem A. 4 (Quantitative Admissible Path Theorem). Let $(G, S) \curvearrowright X$ be a group $G$ with a finite generating set $S$ acting acylindrically on a $\delta$-hyperbolic space $X$. Fix a constant $C>0$. There is a degree 6 polynomial $P$ (depending on $G, S, X, \delta, C$ ) such that if $g$ is loxodromic with $\tau(g)=C$, then for all group elements $h_{1}, \ldots, h_{m} \notin E(g)$ such that $\left|h_{i}\right|_{S} \leq|g|_{S}$, the product $h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{n_{2}} \cdots h_{m} g^{n_{m}} \neq e$ whenever $\left|n_{i}\right| \geq P\left(|g|_{S}\right)$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$ (with $n_{m}$ also being allowed to equal 0 ).

Proof. Set $\lambda=\frac{d(g o, o)}{\tau(g)}$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the collection of $(\lambda, 0)$-quasi-geodesics in $X$; in particular, $\mathcal{L}$ includes all geodesics since (without loss of generality) $\lambda \geq 1$. Let $\mathbb{X}$ be defined by $\mathbb{X}=$ $\left\{\cup_{n=k}^{\ell}\left[h g^{n}, 0, h g^{n+1} o\right]: h \notin E(g)\right\}$ and note that $\mathbb{X} \subset \mathcal{L}$. By Lemma A. 1 and [9, Section 3], we have that $\mathbb{X}$ is $(\mu, \varepsilon)$-contracting with respect to $\mathcal{L}$ where $\mu, \varepsilon$ are uniformly bounded above by a quadratic $Q_{3}(\lambda)$. That is, whenever $q \in \mathcal{L}$ and $p \in \mathbb{X}$ such that $d(q, p) \geq Q_{3}(\lambda)$ then $\left\|\pi_{p}(q)\right\|<Q_{3}(\lambda)$. (In the notation of [68], $\mu\left(\lambda^{\prime}, c^{\prime}\right), \varepsilon\left(\lambda^{\prime}, c^{\prime}\right) \leq Q_{3}(\lambda)$ for all $\left.\lambda^{\prime}, c^{\prime} \in \mathbb{R}\right)$

We now obtain that for each $p \in \mathbb{X}, p$ is $\sigma$-quasiconvex where $\sigma(U)=\frac{3}{2} Q_{3}(\lambda)+2 U$. Indeed, let $q$ be a geodesic in $X$ such that its endpoints $q^{+}$and $q^{-}$are in the $U$-neighborhood $N_{U}(p)$ of $p$. Since $p$ is $(\mu, \varepsilon)$-contracting, either $d(q, p)<\mu$ (and we are done) or $\left\|\pi_{p}(q)\right\|<\varepsilon$. In particular, we have $d\left(q^{+}, q^{-}\right) \leq \varepsilon+2 U$. Since $q$ is a geodesic, for any $x \in q$ we have $d\left(q^{+}, x\right)+d\left(q^{-}, x\right)=d\left(q^{+}, q^{-}\right)$. Therefore without loss of generality $d\left(q^{+}, x\right) \leq \varepsilon / 2+U$, implying that $d\left(x, \pi_{p}(x)\right)<2 U+\frac{3}{2} \varepsilon$. Thus $q \subset N_{\sigma(U)}(p)$.

By Lemma A.3, if $p, p^{\prime} \in \mathbb{X}$ are quasi-geodesics corresponding to $h, h^{\prime}$ in different left cosets of $E(g)$, then $p, p^{\prime}$ have bounded projection $T$ where $T=Q_{2}(\lambda)(1+[g])=O\left(\lambda^{3}\right)$ since $[g] \leq$ $d(g o, o)=\tau(g) \lambda$ (and the stable length $\tau(g)$ is fixed). We note that in [68], the symbol $\tau$ is used for bounded projection but we have already used $\tau$ for stable length. By [68, Lemma 2.7], $p, p^{\prime}$ also have $\nu$-bounded intersection where $\nu(U)=2 U+O\left(\lambda^{3}\right)$.

Now let $n_{1}, \ldots, n_{k}$ be integers and consider the path

$$
\begin{aligned}
P= & {\left[o, h_{1} o\right] \cup\left[h_{1} o, h_{1} g o\right] \cup \ldots \cup\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}-1} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} o\right] \cup\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}} o, h_{1}, g^{n_{1}} h_{2} o\right] \cup \ldots } \\
& \ldots \cup\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}} \cdots h_{k} g^{n_{k}-1} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} \cdots h_{m} g^{n_{m}} o\right],
\end{aligned}
$$

and set

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{1} & =\left[o, h_{1} o\right] \\
q_{2} & =\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} g h_{2} o\right] \\
q_{3}, \ldots, q_{m} & =\ldots \\
p_{1} & =\left[h_{1} o, h_{1} g^{\operatorname{sgn}\left(n_{1}\right)} o\right] \cup \ldots \cup\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}-\operatorname{sgn}\left(n_{1}\right)} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} o\right] \\
p_{2} & =\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{\operatorname{sgn}\left(n_{2}\right)} o\right] \cup \ldots \cup\left[h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{n_{2}-\operatorname{sgn}\left(n_{2}\right)} o, h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{n_{2}} o\right] \\
p_{3}, \ldots, p_{m} & =\ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

$P$ is a path from $o$ to $h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{n_{2}} \cdots h_{m} g^{n_{m}} o$ in $X$. We note that each $p_{i}$ is a $(\lambda, 0)$-quasi-geodesic in $\mathbb{X}$ (and thus has two endpoints in some $p^{\prime} \in \mathbb{X}$ ), each $p_{i}$ has length at least $\tau(g)\left|n_{i}\right|$, each $q_{i}$ has $C^{\prime}|g|_{S}$-bounded projection to $p_{i}$ and $p_{i-1}$ (since $q_{i}$ is a geodesic of length at most $\left.C^{\prime}|h|_{S} \leq C^{\prime}|g|_{S}\right.$ where $C^{\prime}=\max _{k \in S} d(k o, o)$; note that $C^{\prime}$ is a constant dependent only on the group action and the choice of generating set), and any two $p_{i}, p_{i+1}$ have $\nu$-bounded intersection since each $h_{i} \notin E(g)$ so $p_{i}, p_{i+1}$ lie in different quasi-axes of $g$. We note that $\lambda=\tau(g) d(g o, o) \leq \tau(g) C^{\prime}|g|_{S}$ so that $\lambda=O\left(|g|_{S}\right)$.

We are now ready to analyze the constants in the proof of [68, Proposition 3.3]. We have $c=0$ everywhere.

$$
C_{\lambda, 0}=\lambda(\mu(\lambda, 0)+\epsilon(\lambda, 0)+C^{\prime}|g|_{S})
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
= & O\left(|g|_{S}^{3}\right) \\
& B_{\lambda, 0}=2 \varepsilon(1,0)+2 \mu(1,0)+\nu(\mu(1,0)+\sigma(0))+|g|_{S} \\
= & O\left(|g|^{2}\right) \\
R= & \max \left(C^{\prime}|g|_{S}+2 \varepsilon(1,0)+4 \mu(1,0)+1\right. \\
& \mu(1,0)+5 \varepsilon(1,0)+B_{\lambda, 0}+1) \\
= & O\left(|g|_{S}^{2}\right) \\
& \Lambda=\lambda(6 R+1) \\
= & O\left(|g|_{S}^{3}\right) \\
D= & \max \left(\mu(1,0)+\varepsilon(1,0)+C^{\prime}|g|_{S}+C_{\lambda, 0}\right. \\
& 2 T+3 \varepsilon(1,0)+6 \mu(1,0) \\
& \left.\Lambda(R+\sigma(\mu(1,0))\right) \\
& 13 \varepsilon(1,0)+6 \mu(1,0)+2 B_{\lambda, 0}\right) \\
= & O\left(|g|_{S}^{5}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if we choose all of the $n_{i}$ so that $\left|n_{i}\right|$ are larger than $\lambda D=O\left(|g|_{S}^{6}\right)$, we can apply [68, Corollary 3.4] to obtain that our path $P$ is a $(\Lambda, 0)$-quasi-geodesic. In particular, $P$ is nontrivial and so it must be that $h_{1} g^{n_{1}} h_{2} g^{n_{2}} \cdots h_{m} g^{n_{m}} \neq e$. (Note that in the case $n_{m}=0$, we can still apply [68, Corollary 3.4].) This finishes the proof.

question: Is the quadratic form $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}$ of the regression coefficient vector identifiable from the system of moment equations?
answer: Yes, the quadratic form $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \boldsymbol{\beta}$ is simultaneously identifiable from the system of moment equations.

## D Proofs Related to Identifications under Gaussian Designs
## D. 1 GLMs with non-zero covariate mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$

In this section, we first prove Lemma 3, which states that the linear form $\lambda_{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\mu}$ and the quadratic form $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \boldsymbol{\beta}$ of the regression coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ in Model GLM are simultaneously identifiable from the system of (population) moment equations (5).

Proof of Lemma 3. Let $Z \sim \mathrm{~N}\left(\lambda_{\beta}, \gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)$. Recall that we reduce the first four moment equations (5) as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{f}_{0}\left(\lambda_{\beta}, \gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)-m_{1}=0 \\
& \gamma_{\beta}^{2} \mathrm{f}_{1}^{2}\left(\lambda_{\beta}, \gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)-m_{2}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

and denote the forward map as $\Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$.
We first compute the Jacobian $\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta} & =\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) & 2 \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right) \\
\frac{1}{2 \gamma_{\beta}^{2}} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right) & \frac{1}{\gamma_{\beta}^{2}} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right)^{2}
\end{array}\right) \\
& =\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) & 2 \gamma_{\beta}^{2} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime \prime}(Z) \\
\frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime \prime}(Z) & \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)+\gamma_{\beta}^{2} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime \prime \prime}(Z)\right)
\end{array}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Without loss of generality, we take the link function $\phi$ to be monotonically strictly increasing. The determinant of $\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}\right| & =\frac{1}{\gamma_{\beta}^{2}} \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left\{\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right)^{2}-\left(\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right)\right)^{2}\right\} \\
& =\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left\{\mathbb{E}^{2} \phi^{\prime}(Z)+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\left(\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime \prime \prime}(Z)-\mathbb{E}^{2} \phi^{\prime \prime}(Z)\right)\right\} \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\left|\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}\right| \geq 0$ follows from applying Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to the first line of the above display and $\phi$ monotonically increasing. Here, we note that monotonicity is but a sufficient condition for the above inequality to hold - which leaves the door open to extend our approach to SIMs with general non-monotonic link functions.

Lemma 9 implies that we are only left to show that the above inequality is strict and the corresponding map $\Psi$ is proper. Suppose on the contrary, the above inequality is an equality. Then we have, with probability one,

$$
\sqrt{\phi^{\prime}(Z)}\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right) \equiv \frac{\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right)}{\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)} \sqrt{\phi^{\prime}(Z)}
$$

which is equivalent to, with probability one,

$$
Z-\lambda_{\beta} \equiv \frac{\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left(Z-\lambda_{\beta}\right)}{\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)} \text { or } \sqrt{\phi^{\prime}(Z)} \equiv 0
$$

a contradiction unless $Z$ is degenerate (i.e. $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}=0$ ). Thus we have proved that the forward map $\Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$ is a local diffeomorphism. $\Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$ is also proper under Assumption L.

In fact, for linear and log-linear link functions, it is easy to see that $|\nabla \Psi|$ is strictly positive for strictly bounded $\lambda_{\beta}$ and $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}$. For probit link, we observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}\right| & =\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z)\left\{\mathbb{E}^{2} \phi^{\prime}(Z)+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\left(\mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime}(Z) \mathbb{E} \phi^{\prime \prime \prime}(Z)-\mathbb{E}^{2} \phi^{\prime \prime}(Z)\right)\right\} \\
& =\frac{1}{\left(2 \pi\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}} \exp \left\{-\frac{3 \lambda_{\beta}^{2}}{2\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)}\right\}\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\left\{\frac{\lambda_{\beta}^{2}}{\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)^{2}}-\frac{1}{1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}}-\frac{\lambda_{\beta}^{2}}{\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)^{2}}\right\}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
=\frac{1}{\left(2 \pi\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}} \exp \left\{-\frac{3 \lambda_{\beta}^{2}}{2\left(1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}\right)}\right\} \frac{1}{1+\gamma_{\beta}^{2}}>0
$$

if $\lambda_{\beta}^{2}$ and $\gamma_{\beta}^{2}$ are strictly bounded.
For logit link, there is no analytic expression for $\left|\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}\right|$ but it is easy to numerically show that $\left|\nabla \Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}\right|$ is strictly larger than zero, and hence $\Psi_{\mathrm{GLM}, \beta}$ is a diffeomorphism. The remaining part of Lemma 3 is straightforward to prove and hence omitted.

question: Why is it important for a step size selector to maintain an acceptance probability above a certain threshold in Bayesian inference?
answer: Maintaining a high acceptance probability ensures efficient exploration of the parameter space without getting stuck, which is crucial for accurate Bayesian inference.

We first assess the benefit of using the symmetric step size criterion in Algorithm 2 versus the asymmetric criterion from Biron-Lattes et al. (2024) on three synthetic targets with varying tail behavior: $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, Laplace $(0,1)$, and $\operatorname{Cauchy}(0,1)$. For each $\|x\| \in\left\{10^{-5}, 10^{-4}, \ldots, 10^{2}\right\}$, we simulated $10^{7}$ draws from the target and renormalized them to the specified value. Then, for each draw, we simulated one step of AutoStep RWMH/MALA $\left(\theta_{0}=1\right)$, and recorded the acceptance probability.

The average of these acceptance probabilities is shown in Fig. 1 for AutoStep RWMH, showing that the asymmetric step size selector can get stuck for extended periods near the mode of the target (small $\|x\|$ ) and in the tails (large $\|x\|$ ). This behavior particularly problematic in practice for Bayesian inference, which is often initialized in the tails. In contrast, the proposed symmetric step size selector

Note that the asymmetric criterion yields very low acceptance probabilities for states near the mode (left side of the plot) and in the tails (right side of the plot).
