question: What is the main idea behind the Chapman-Enskog expansion for the Boltzmann equation?
answer: The main idea behind the Chapman-Enskog expansion is based on two important observations about the Boltzmann equation: that stationary states of collision integral are space-varying boosted thermal states, and that collision integral conserves density of particles, momentum, and energy.

evidence.text:
# 3 Chapman-Enskog theory for the Boltzmann equation 

ChE expansion [2-4] was the first theory, which successfully connected microscopic dynamics of Boltzmann equation to the equations of hydrodynamics. It was developed by S. Chapman and D. Enskog more than one hundred years ago. Originally formulated for three-dimensional classical gas, it has uncovered not only the universal NS equations but also provided quantative predicitions for transport coefficients in terms of explicit integral equations. In this section we write a summary of this classic result. It provides context for the generalization of the method to quantum integrable theories developed in the next section.

We start with the Boltzmann equation written as

$$
\partial_{t} \rho+v \partial_{x} \rho=I_{B}[\rho]
$$

where $\rho(x, v)$ is one-particle distribution function on a phase space and $I_{B}[\rho]$ is the Boltzmann collision integral, a nonlinear functional of the $\rho$ distribution. For the sake of this discussion, we do not discuss the of the operator $I_{B}$ and consider one-dimensional system. The main idea behind ChE expansion is based on two important observations about the Boltzmann equation:

- The only stationary states of collision integral $I_{B}[\rho]$ are space-varying boosted thermal states. For classical gas these are given by boosted Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{bth}}(x, v)=\frac{\varrho(x)}{\sqrt{2 \pi T(x)}} \exp \left(-\frac{(v-u(x))^{2}}{2 T(x)}\right)
$$

where $\varrho(x), u(x), T(x)$ are density, velocity and temperature of the gas at the point $x$, respectively. We have set $m=1$ and $k_{B}=1$. The process of relaxation from a generic state towards local boosted thermal states happens on a characteristic relaxation time-scale $\tau_{I_{B}}$, which depends on the interaction potential between particles encoded in collision integral $I_{B}[\rho]$ and on the state itself.
We emphasize here that in general the states (66) are stationary states of collision integral term only and some dynamics is generated by the streaming term $v \partial_{x} \rho$. Global equilibrium states of (65) correspond to boosted thermal states with hydrodynamic fields uniform in space $\varrho(x), u(x), T(x)=$ const, for which the streaming term vanishes as well.

- Collision integral conserves density of particles, momentum and energy. This is equivalent to the existence of three collision invariants $\mathscr{G}_{0}(v)=1, \mathscr{G}_{1}(v)=v, \mathscr{G}_{2}(v)=\frac{1}{2} v^{2}$, such that

$$
\int \mathrm{d} v \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) I_{B}[\rho](v)=0, \quad a=0,1,2
$$

Naturally, collision invariants can be directly related to hydrodynamic fields $\varrho(x), u(x)$, $e(x)$, which are given by

$$
\varrho(x)=\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle, \quad u(x)=\frac{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{1}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle}, \quad e(x)=\frac{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{2}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle}-\frac{1}{2} u(x)^{2}
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes average over velocities with respect to $\rho$. What is more, the temperature field is simply given by $e(x)=\frac{1}{2} T(x)$, assuming that the system is in local thermodynamic equilibrium. We collectively denote the hydrodynamic fields as $\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\}$.

The observations listed above point towards the existence of two characteristic timescales in the system. Starting from an initial distribution, on a timescale given by $\tau_{I_{B}}$ the system will locally thermalize, such that it can be described by hydrodynamic fields $\varrho(x), u(x)$ and $T(x)$. On a longer, hydrodynamic timescale $\tau_{\mathrm{h}}$ the streaming term will be dominant and these fields will evolve according to the standard equations of hydrodynamics. In order to see their structure explicitly, we multiply the Boltzmann equation with collision invariants and integrate over $\mathrm{d} v$, similarly as in Sec. 2.5. We recover three equations which read

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_{t} \varrho+\partial_{x}(\varrho u)=0, \quad \partial_{t}(\varrho u)+\partial_{x}\left(\varrho u^{2}+\mathcal{P}\right)=0 \\
& \partial_{t}(\varrho e)+\partial_{x}(u \varrho e+\mathcal{J})+\mathcal{P} \partial_{x} u=0
\end{aligned}
$$

with dynamical pressure and heat current

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{P} & =\int \mathrm{d} v(v-u) v \rho(v) \\
\mathcal{J} & =\frac{1}{2} \int \mathrm{~d} v(v-u)^{3} \rho(v)
\end{aligned}
$$

The hydrodynamic equations presented above are not closed as the dynamical pressure and heat current depend on the whole distribution $\rho$, not only on its first three moments (or equivalently, on hydrodynamic fields). The closure of equation will be the central point of the ChE expansion procedure, which we now discuss.

The two observations about Boltzmann equation listed before can be turned into perturbative expansion. To formally motivate it, we start with estimating the order of terms in (65). We assume that the state varies at a hydrodynamic length-scale $l_{\mathrm{h}}$ and the particles have some characteristic velocity $\bar{v}$. Then the hydrodynamic timescale associated to the streaming term is $\tau_{\mathrm{h}}=l_{\mathrm{h}} / \bar{v}$. In the dimensionless units $\bar{x}=x / l_{\mathrm{h}}, \bar{t}=t / \tau_{\mathrm{h}}, \bar{v}=v / \bar{v}$ and explicitly extracting the timescale from collision term $\bar{I}_{B}=\frac{1}{\tau_{I_{B}}} I_{B}$ we can write Boltzmann equation as

$$
\partial_{t} \rho+\bar{v} \partial_{x} \rho=\frac{1}{\delta} \bar{I}_{B}[\rho]
$$

where $\delta=\tau_{I_{B}} / \tau_{\mathrm{h}}$ defines the so-called Knudsen number [2]. We wish to address hydrodynamic limit of slow (in comparison to microscopic scales) space and time variation, hence Knudsen number is considered to be small $\delta \ll 1$. The form of Boltzmann equation (72) suggests perturbative solution in $\delta$ and indeed, in the ChE method we essentially assume that

$$
\rho(x, v ; t)=\rho^{(0)}(x, v ; t)\left(1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \rho^{(n)}(x, v ; t)\right)
$$

However, the expansion cannot be considered to be fully systematic as it is supplemented by additional assumptions which we will discuss now. Before that and in what follows we drop tildes from the notation.

Firstly, the crucial aspect of the method is the assumption about the time evolution of distribution $\rho$. We assume that it depends on time through three time-dependent hydrodynamic fields collectively denoted $\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\}$,

$$
\rho(x, v ; t) \rightarrow \rho(x, v \mid\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\})
$$

Moreover, there is an assumption about expansion which can be formulated as the following conditions

$$
\left\langle\mathscr{G}_{a}\right\rangle=\int \mathrm{d} v \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) \rho^{(0)}(x, v), \quad 0=\int \mathrm{d} v \rho^{(0)}(x, v) \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) \rho^{(n)}(x, v)=\left(\mathscr{G}_{a} \mid \rho^{(n)}\right)
$$

for $n \geq 1$, which means that the averages of collision invariants (and in consequence, hydrodynamic fields) are given solely by the zeroth order contribution to the distribution $\rho^{(0)}$. In other words, we essentially assume that the hydrodynamic fields are not expanded in $\delta$ and corrections $\left\{\rho^{(n)}\right\}_{n \geq 1}$ are orthogonal to collision invariants (in the sense of the hydrodynamic inner product $(\cdot \cdot \cdot)$, see (26), note that for classical particles $\mathcal{C}=\rho$ ). However, we crucially assume that dynamical pressure and heat current (70) do admit expansion in $\delta$

$$
\mathcal{P}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \mathcal{P}^{(n)}, \quad \mathcal{J}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \mathcal{J}^{(n)}
$$

Expanding now the problem to different orders in $\delta$ yields hydrodynamic equations at different scales.

question: What is the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism and how does it relate to gauge bosons?
answer: The Brout-Englert-Higgs (BEH) mechanism explains how particles acquire mass through spontaneous symmetry breaking in quantum field theory. It involves the interaction of gauge bosons with a scalar field, leading to massive gauge bosons.

evidence.text:
# V. MASSIVE GAUGE BOSON 

In the BEH model, the mass of gauge boson is derived from the phenomenological coupling $\left|\left(i \partial_{\mu}+g B_{\mu}\right)\left(v_{h}+h_{1}+i h_{2}\right)\right|^{2}$ as $m_{B}^{2} B^{\mu} B_{\mu}=g^{2} v_{h}^{2} B^{\mu} B_{\mu}$. Instead of this, we begin with a simple Lagrangian density $L_{0}(x)$ and the physical vacuum $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$. The physical vacuum $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ is

not a simple system, and therefore the response of $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ to $B_{\mu}$ gives rise to a non-linear effect. The minimal coupling to fermions $L_{0}^{\min }(x)=\bar{\varphi}(x)\left(i \partial_{\mu}+g B_{\mu}\right) \gamma^{\mu} \varphi(x)$ changes its form due to the perturbation of $\mathcal{H}_{I}(x)=g j^{\mu}(x) B_{\mu}(x)$ to $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ [22]. Consider a perturbation expansion of $\int d^{4} x L_{0}^{\min }(x)$ in powers of $g$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} L_{0}^{\min }\left(x_{1}\right) e x p\left(i \int \mathcal{H}_{I}\left(x_{2}\right) d^{4} x_{2}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle \\
& \quad=\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} \bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma^{\mu}\left[i \partial_{\mu}+g B_{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right)\right] \varphi\left(x_{1}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle \\
& \quad+\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} \bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma^{\mu}\left[i \partial_{\mu}+g B_{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right)\right] \varphi\left(x_{1}\right) i g \int d^{4} x_{2} j^{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right) B_{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle+\cdots
\end{aligned}
$$

(1) In the last term of Eq.(19), $B_{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right)$ couples to $B_{\nu}\left(x_{1}\right)$, yielding the following two-point-correlation function between $\bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma^{\mu} \varphi\left(x_{1}\right)$ and $\bar{\varphi}\left(x_{2}\right) \gamma^{\nu} \varphi\left(x_{2}\right)$

$$
\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} \mathcal{H}_{I}\left(x_{1}\right) \int d^{4} x_{2} \mathcal{H}_{I}\left(x_{2}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

Because the gauge field is a transverse one, the excitation induced by this $B_{\mu}(x)$ is a transverse one as well. Since these $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are separated microscopically, an observer at a distant space-time point from it regard it as a local phenomenon at $X=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) / 2$. For such an observer, it is useful to rewrite $d^{4} x_{1} d^{4} x_{2}$ in Eq.(20) as $d^{4} X d^{4} Y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& g^{2} \int\langle\widetilde{0}| \int j_{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right) d^{2} x_{1} \int j^{\mu}\left(x_{2}\right) d^{2} x_{2}|\widetilde{0}\rangle B^{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right) B_{\mu}\left(x_{2}\right) d^{2} x_{1} d^{2} x_{2} \\
= & g^{2} \int\langle\widetilde{0}| \int j_{\mu}(Y) j^{\mu}(0) d^{4} Y|\widetilde{0}\rangle \times B^{\mu}(X) B_{\mu}(X) d^{4} X \\
\equiv & M^{2} \int B^{\mu}(X) B_{\mu}(X) d^{4} X
\end{aligned}
$$

The relative motion along $Y=x_{2}-x_{1}$ is indirectly observed as a following constant $M$ for $\mu=\nu$,

$$
M^{2}=g^{2}\langle\widetilde{0}| \int j_{\mu}(Y) j^{\mu}(0) d^{4} Y|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

(2) The correlation of currents in Eq.(22) is strongly influenced by permutation symmetry of Bose statistics. Within the coherent region $Z_{c}$, the physical vacuum is rigid and remains in the ground state, and $\langle\widetilde{0}| \partial_{\mu}[\bar{\varphi}(Y) \gamma^{\mu} \varphi(Y)]|\widetilde{0}\rangle=0$ holds for the transverse component of $Y$, and the correlation of currents in Eq.(22) is reduced to

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\widetilde{0}| j_{\mu}(Y) j^{\mu}(0)|\widetilde{0}\rangle & =\langle\widetilde{0}|\left(j_{\mu}(0)+\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y_{\mu}}\left[\bar{\varphi}(Y) \gamma_{\mu} \varphi(Y)\right]\right]_{Y_{\mu}=0} Y^{\mu}+\cdots\right) j^{\mu}(0)|\widetilde{0}\rangle \\
& \Rightarrow\langle\widetilde{0}| j_{\mu}(0) j^{\mu}(0)|\widetilde{0}\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

![img-3.jpeg](img-3.jpeg)

FIG. 4. The coherent space-time region is a small cone specified by $l_{c}$ at the bottom of the light cone (a shaded area). (a) The gauge boson $B_{\mu}$ (a wavy line) induces vacuum polarization only outside the coherent space-time region. (b) The Higgs field $H(x)$ (black circles) induces vacuum polarization both inside and outside the coherent space-time region.

With Eq.(23), $M^{2}$ in Eq.(22) is identified as the gauge boson's mass $m_{B}^{2}$. Using $j^{\mu}(0)=$ $\left(\varphi^{\dagger} \varphi, i \varphi^{\dagger} \gamma^{0} \gamma \varphi\right)$, we obtain $\langle\widetilde{0}| j_{\mu}(0) j^{\mu}(0)|\widetilde{0}\rangle=2\langle\widetilde{0}|\left[\varphi^{\dagger}(0) \varphi(0)\right]^{2}|\widetilde{0}\rangle$. The $m_{B}^{2}$ in Eq.(22) is given by

$$
m_{B}^{2}=2 g^{2}\langle\widetilde{0}| \int_{Y \in 2 Z_{c}}\left[\varphi^{\dagger}(0) \varphi(0)\right]^{2} d^{4} Y|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

The coherent space-time region $Z_{c}$ is a small cone at the bottom of the light cone as illustrated in Figure 4 for one spatial direction. Its space length is less than $l_{c}$, and time width is smaller than $l_{c} / c$, so that the causal relation is possible between two spatial ends separated by $l_{c}$. (The life time of virtual massless pair of fermion and antifermion in $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ is related to $l_{c} / c$.) The volume of coherent space-time region $\int_{Y \in Z_{c}} d^{4} Y=l_{c}^{2} \times \frac{1}{2}\left[l_{c} \times c\left(l_{c} / c\right)\right] \times 2=l_{c}^{4}$ in Figure 4 is Lorentz invariant. Since the vacuum is rigid in $Z_{c}$, the vacuum polarization induced by $B_{\mu}$ occurs only outside of this region as shown in Figure 4(a).

In Eq.(24), the normalization volume $V$ of $\varphi(x)$ in Eq.(3) is $V_{c}=d_{m}^{3}$. Every fermion and antifermion in $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ make the same contribution to $\langle\widetilde{0}|\left[\varphi^{\dagger}(0) \varphi(0)\right]^{2}|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\widetilde{0}|\left[\varphi^{\dagger}(0) \varphi(0)\right]^{2}|\widetilde{0}\rangle & =\langle\widetilde{0}| \frac{1}{d_{m}^{6}} \sum_{p, s}\left(\left[a^{s \dagger}(\boldsymbol{p}) u^{s \dagger}(p)+b^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p}) v^{s \dagger}(-p)\right]\left[a^{s}(\boldsymbol{p}) u^{s}(p)+b^{s \dagger}(-\boldsymbol{p}) v^{s}(-p)\right]\right)^{2}|\widetilde{0}\rangle\right. \\
& =\frac{1}{d_{m}^{6}} \prod_{p, s}\left(\sin ^{2} \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}}+\cos ^{2} \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{d_{m}^{6}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, for the 4-dimensional volume $l_{c}^{4}$ of the region $Z_{c}$, we obtain

$$
m_{B}^{2}=2 g^{2} \frac{1}{d_{m}^{6}} \int_{Y \in 2 Z_{c}} d^{4} Y=g^{2}\left(\frac{2 l_{c}^{2}}{d_{m}^{3}}\right)^{2}
$$

This $2 l_{c}^{2} / d_{m}^{3}$ is the content of vacuum condensate $v_{h}$, which is phenomenologically assumed as $m_{B}^{2}=g^{2} v_{h}^{2}$ in the BEH model.
(3) The Goldstone mode exists in the last term of Eq.(19). For the first-order term of $B_{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right)$, integrate $\bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) i \partial^{\mu} \gamma_{\mu} \varphi\left(x_{1}\right)$ over $x_{1}$ by parts, and use the fact that $\varphi\left(x_{1}\right)$ vanishes at $x_{1} \rightarrow \infty$. As a result, we obtain two types of terms, one including $i \partial^{\mu} \bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma_{\mu} \varphi\left(x_{1}\right)$, and the other including $\partial^{\mu}|\widetilde{0}\rangle$. The latter is given by

$$
g\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} j_{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right) \int d^{4} x_{2} j^{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right) B_{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right) \partial^{\mu}|\widetilde{0}\rangle+g \partial^{\mu}\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} j_{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right) \int d^{4} x_{2} j^{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right) B_{\nu}\left(x_{2}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

Because the physical vacuum $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ in Eq.(7) has an explicit $x$-dependence in the phase $\alpha(x)$, $\partial^{\mu}|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ contains $\partial^{\mu} \alpha(x)$. The distant observer regards Eq.(27) as a local phenomenon at $X$, and rewrites it using $d^{4} x_{1} d^{4} x_{2}=d^{4} X d^{4} Y$ as

$$
\frac{2 i}{g} m_{B}^{2} \int B_{\mu}(X) \partial^{\mu} \alpha(X) d^{4} X \equiv m_{B} \int B_{\mu}(X) \partial^{\mu} G(X) d^{4} X
$$

Here the Goldstone mode is defined as $G(X)=2 i g^{-1} m_{B} \alpha(X)$. (In the BEH model, the coupling of the Goldstone mode $h_{2}$ to the gauge boson is derived from the phenomenological term $\left|\left(i \partial_{\mu}+g B_{\mu}\right)\left(v_{h}+h_{1}+i h_{2}\right)\right|^{2}$. Equation.(28) shows that this coupling has an origin in the response of the physical vacuum $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ to $B_{\mu}$.)
(4) In the system without the long-range force, the global phase-rotation of fermion's field requires no energy, and therefore the propagator of the Goldstone mode is given by

$$
\int \frac{d X^{4}}{(2 \pi)^{4}}\langle\widetilde{0}| T[G(X) G(0)]|\widetilde{0}\rangle e^{i q X}=\frac{i}{q^{2}}
$$

However, the long-range force mediated by the gauge boson prohibits a free rotation of the global phase $\alpha(x)$, then preventing the Goldstone mode. This discrepancy is solved by the generation of the gauge-boson's mass that converts the long-range force into a shortrange one. The Fourier transform of Eqs.(21) and (28) are given by $m_{B}^{2} B^{\mu}(q) B_{\mu}(q)$ and $m_{B} q^{\mu} G(q) B_{\mu}(q)$, respectively. Following the usual way, regard the latter as a perturbation to the former, and the second-order perturbation is obtained as

$$
B^{\mu}(q)\left[i m_{B}^{2} g^{\mu \nu}-m_{B} q^{\mu} \frac{i}{q^{2}} m_{B} q^{\nu}\right] B_{\nu}(q)=i m_{B}^{2}\left(g^{\mu \nu}-\frac{q^{\mu} q^{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right) B^{\mu}(q) B^{\nu}(q)
$$

Adding Eq.(30) to the Fourier transform of $-\frac{1}{4} F^{\mu \nu} F_{\mu \nu}$, and performing an inverse transformation on the resulting matrix, we obtain

$$
D^{\mu \nu}(q)=\frac{-i}{q^{2}-m_{B}^{2}}\left(g^{\mu \nu}-\frac{q^{\mu} q^{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right) \equiv i D\left(q^{2}\right)\left(g^{\mu \nu}-\frac{q^{\mu} q^{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)
$$

which is the propagator of the massive gauge boson in the Landau gauge. Spontaneous gauge-symmetry breaking comes from the rigidity of the physical vacuum in the transverse perturbation. Additional terms to $L_{0}(x)$ necessary for this phenomenon are $m_{B}^{2} B^{\mu}(q) B_{\mu}(q)$, $m_{B} B_{\mu}(x) \partial^{\mu} G(x)$ and $\left(\partial_{\mu} G(x)\right)^{2}$.
(5) In the BEH model, the coupling of the Goldstone mode to fermions comes explicitly from the Yukawa interaction. In the present model, such a coupling is included implicitly in the first term in the right-hand side of Eq.(19). For the zeroth-order term of $B_{\mu}$, the integration over $x_{1}$ by parts yields two types of terms, one including $i \partial^{\mu} \bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma_{\mu} \varphi\left(x_{1}\right)$, and the other including $\partial^{\mu} \mid \widetilde{0}\rangle$. The latter term is given by

$$
i\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} j^{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right) \partial_{\mu}|\widetilde{0}\rangle+i \partial_{\mu}\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} j^{\mu}\left(x_{1}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

Since $\partial_{\mu}|\widetilde{0}\rangle=\partial_{\mu} \alpha(x)|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ contains the Goldstone mode $G(x)=2 i g^{-1} m_{B} \alpha(x)$, Eq.(32) gives the coupling of the Goldstone mode $G$ to fermion

$$
\frac{g}{m_{B}}\langle\widetilde{0}| \int d^{4} x_{1} \bar{\varphi}\left(x_{1}\right) \gamma^{\mu} \varphi\left(x_{1}\right) \partial_{\mu} G\left(x_{1}\right)|\widetilde{0}\rangle
$$

As a result, $\left(g / m_{B}\right) \bar{\varphi}(x) \gamma^{\mu} \varphi(x) \partial_{\mu} G(x)$ appear in the Lagrangian density, which is different from $g\left(m_{f} / m_{B}\right) \bar{\varphi}(x) \varphi(x) h_{2}(x)$ in the BEH model.

question: Can the posterior distribution over future observations be computed using a sum?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# Future observation inference 

In order to compute $G$ in (2), we need a posterior distribution $q\left(o_{\tau} \mid o_{1: t}, a_{1: \tau-1}\right)$ over future observations $o_{\tau}$. This can be computed as follows:

$$
q\left(o_{\tau} \mid o_{1: t}, a_{1: \tau-1}\right)=\sum_{s_{\tau}} p\left(o_{\tau} \mid s_{\tau}\right) q\left(s_{\tau} \mid o_{1: t}, a_{1: \tau-1}\right)
$$

question: What is the purpose of using the Hellinger distance in numerical experiments?
answer: The Hellinger distance is used to quantify how close two probability density functions are, helping to validate the accuracy of an approximate analytical solution compared to a numerical solution.

evidence.text:
# 2.2 Numerical experiment 

In (13) we obtain an approximate analytical solution of the von Mises process. To validate the accuracy of the approximate analytical solution we compare it with a numerical solution of the transition probability density.

One possible approach is to solve the forward equation (12) numerically. Towards this a standard approach is the Crank-Nicholson scheme which was also considered in Section 3.4.1, García-Portugués et al. 2019. In this approach a uniform discretization of the space, i.e., $(-\pi, \pi]$ is considered into $k$ points and similarly time $(0, T]$ is discretized uniformly into $m$ points. The PDE is also further discretized and the resulting numerical estimate of the density is obtained at these $k$ points for each $m$ time points. The reader may refer

to Section 3.4.1, García-Portugués et al. 2019 for an exposition of the Crank-Nicholson scheme.

Let $p$ and $q$ denote two probability density functions, then the Hellinger distance (see Le Cam and Yang 2000) is defined as,

$$
h(p, q)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\sqrt{d p}-\sqrt{d q})^{2}}
$$

Hellinger distance is used to quantify the similarity between two probability densities. It is known that $0 \leq h(p, q) \leq 1$, where if $h(p, q)$ is close to 0 , then $p$ and $q$ are interpreted to be similar.

Let $p$ denote the density of the approximate analytical solution and let $q$ denote the density of the numerical solution. Since the numerical solution $q$ via the Crank-Nicholson scheme is discrete, we consider the discrete version of the Hellinger distance by discretizing $p$ at the same $k$ points. This is given by,

$$
h(p, q)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(\sqrt{p_{i}}-\sqrt{q_{i}}\right)^{2}}
$$

We use the function dTpdPde1D in the R package sdetorus (García-Portugués 2023) to utilize the implementation of Crank-Nicholson scheme to numerically solve the forward equation of the von Mises process. We compare analytical approximate solution $p\left(\theta ; \theta_{0}, t\right)$ (13) with the numerical solution via the Hellinger distance between them. We set $k=$ $3000, m=20000$ for the Crank-Nicholson scheme. We set $\theta_{0}=0$ and we compare the densities after time $t$ has elapsed, where $t \in\{0.0001,0.001,0.01,0.1\}$ for varying $\mu \in$ $\left\{-\frac{\pi}{2},-\frac{\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right\}$. For each $t$ and $\mu$ we also evaluate the Hellinger distance for different values of $\kappa$, i.e., $\kappa=0.5(\lambda=1, \sigma=2), \kappa=1(\lambda=2, \sigma=1), \kappa=2(\lambda=1, \sigma=2)$ and $\kappa=4(\lambda=2, \sigma=2)$. We report the results in Figure 1. We find that for all cases considered the Hellinger distance is very low $(\lesssim 0.01)$, which indicates the accuracy of the

approximate analytical solution.

![img-0.jpeg](img-0.jpeg)

Figure 1: Hellinger distance between the analytical $\left(p\left(\theta ; \theta_{0}, t\right)\right)$ and numerical approximation of the forward equation of the von Mises process. The parameters are $\theta_{0}=0$ and $\kappa=0.5(\lambda=1, \sigma=2), \kappa=1$ $(\lambda=2, \sigma=1), \kappa=2(\lambda=1, \sigma=2)$ and $\kappa=4(\lambda=2, \sigma=2)$. We compare the Hellinger distance at $\mu=-\frac{\pi}{2},-\frac{\pi}{2},-\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}$. For a given $\mu$ we plot the Hellinger distance between the numerical and the analytical density for different values of $t$, where $t$ is the time elapsed. For the Crank-Nicholson scheme for the numerical solution we set $k=3000, m=20000$.

question: What is the purpose of using a 19-feed array in radio astronomy?
answer: The 19-feed array is used to enhance the sensitivity and resolution of radio observations, allowing for detailed mapping of hydrogen intensity across different regions in space.

evidence.text:
## 4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The positions of the 19 feeds within the FAST L-band 19feed array (19FA) frame are shown in Figure 2. Here, the $H$-axis and $V$-axis correspond to the horizontal and vertical feed axes. We group the 19 feeds into four subsets according to their separation distance to the feed array center, i.e. as shown in Figure 2, the center beam (red), inner-circle beams (blue), middle-circle beams (green), and the outercircle beams (black). During the drift scan observation, the rotation angle of the feed array was fixed at $23.4^{\circ}$. The cyan dashed line with an arrow indicates the drift scanning direction, which is aligned with the R.A. direction in the observational frame.
![img-2.jpeg](img-2.jpeg)

question: In what ways are auditory LLMs used for evaluating text-to-speech models?
answer: Auditory LLMs are used in evaluating text-to-speech models by predicting quantitative metrics like MOS and SIM, conducting A/B testing between samples, and providing natural-language-based evaluations on aspects such as noisiness and distortion.

evidence.text:
## I. InTRODUCTION

With the rapid development of generative models, the task of automatic speech quality assessment has become increasingly more important, for purposes from training data filtering to evaluating text-to-speech (TTS) models [1]-[5]. However, considering the variety of aspects humans take into account in listening tests, it is challenging for small models trained for the end-to-end prediction of mean opinion score (MOS) [2], [3] and speaker similarity score (SIM) [6] to achieve as comprehensive and interpretable speech quality assessment as humans. Recently, auditory large language models (LLMs) [7][12] have been developed and demonstrated remarkable performance across a variety of speech perception and understanding tasks [13][16], which are thus possible to achieve evidence-based and multiperspective speech quality assessment using natural language.

In this paper, we propose to enhance existing auditory LLMs with the ability to evaluate speech quality from two key perspectives: MOS and SIM. Under an LLM multitask setting empowered by task-specific prompts, the auditory LLMs are evaluated using four speech quality evaluation tasks. These tasks include the predictions of real-valued quantitative metrics like MOS and SIM and an A/B testing to choose the better one from two speech samples, which are commonly used in TTS performance evaluation. Furthermore, we explore natural-language-based speech quality evaluation tasks, such as speech descriptions from the perspectives of noisiness, distortion, discontinuity, and overall quality. These tasks leverage the key strengths of the LLM backbone and are unique abilities of auditory LLMs. Experimental results on the widely used NISQA, BVCC,

SOMOS and VoxSim show that finetuned auditory LLMs can serve as a versatile evaluation model for speech quality, outperforming a strong self-supervised learning (SSL) baseline and being competitive to state-of-the-art results achieved using separate small models.

question: Is the coalescent term a polynomial function?
answer: Yes, the coalescent term \( h_{\text {coa }}(\chi \mid \sigma) \) is a polynomial in the transformed branch lengths.

evidence.text:
# 3.2 Decomposition into species and coalescent terms 

In performing analysis with the expected branch lengths, it can be helpful to first decompose the expected heights $h(\chi \mid \sigma)$ as the height $h_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)$ of the species MRCA of the taxa in $\chi$ in the species tree $\sigma$, plus the expected height $h_{\text {coa }}(\chi \mid \sigma)$ of the MRCA of the lineages in $\chi$ above the species MRCA of the taxa in $\chi$. We will call these terms the 'species' and 'coalescence' terms respectively; Efromovich and Salter Kubatko (2008) refers to the coalescence term as the 'species-gene coalescent time'.

$$
h(\chi \mid \sigma)=h_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)+h_{\mathrm{coa}}(\chi \mid \sigma)
$$

The species term $h_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)$ is the sum of a collection of branch lengths of $\sigma$. Meanwhile the coalescent term $h_{\text {coa }}(\chi \mid \sigma)$ is a polynomial in the transformed branch lengths $X_{i}:=\exp \left(-x_{i}\right)$, since the coalescent transition probabilities are a polynomial function of $\exp (-t)$ (Tavaré, 1984).

By grouping any species and coalescence terms that appear together in an expression, we can similarly define a decomposition for terms such as the expected subtending length $\ell^{+}(\chi \mid \sigma)$, the expected length $\ell(\chi \mid \sigma)$, and the expected cost per locus $C(\psi \mid \sigma)$. For instance, in the decomposition

$$
\ell(\chi \mid \sigma)=\ell_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)+\ell_{\mathrm{coa}}(\chi \mid \sigma)
$$

the species term $\ell_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)$ is nothing but the length of the branch in $\sigma$ that subtends exactly the tips in $\chi$, if such a branch in $\sigma$ exists; otherwise it is 0 . It is also useful to write the decomposition for the expected cost per locus:

$$
C(\psi \mid \sigma)=\underbrace{\sum_{\chi} c(\psi \mid \chi) \ell_{\mathrm{sp}}(\chi \mid \sigma)}_{C_{\mathrm{sp}}(\psi \mid \sigma)}+\underbrace{\sum_{\chi} c(\psi \mid \chi) \ell_{\mathrm{coa}}(\chi \mid \sigma)}_{C_{\mathrm{coa}}(\psi \mid \sigma)}
$$

We think of $C_{\mathrm{sp}}(\psi \mid \sigma)$ as the expected cost per locus in the absence of gene tree heterogeneity. On the other hand, $C_{\text {coa }}(\psi \mid \sigma)$ represents an additional cost that arises due to ILS and gene tree discordance.
$C_{\text {coa }}(\psi \mid \sigma)$ is easy to compute in the limit where $\sigma$ is a star tree (i.e. all internal branch lengths of $\sigma$ are 0 ). We denote a star tree by $\star$. Note once again that the external branch lengths of the star tree are irrelevant, since no coalescent events occur along these branches. For a star tree, the coalescence term in fact comprises the entirety of the expected cost. Under our modeling assumptions, the coalescent

process in the singular ancestral population (where all internal branches of the gene trees arise) is that of the Kingman coalescent, and so the expected length of internal branches of the gene tree subtending exactly $2 \leq i \leq n-1$ tips is $2 / i$ ( $\mathrm{Fu}, 1995$ ). We then have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\text {coa }}(\chi \mid \star) & =\frac{2}{|\chi|}\binom{n}{|\chi|}^{-1} \\
C_{\text {coa }}(\psi \mid \star) & =\sum_{\chi} c(\psi \mid \chi) \frac{2}{|\chi|}\binom{n}{|\chi|}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the expression for $\ell_{\text {coa }}(\chi \mid \star)$ follows by symmetry, as there are $\binom{n}{|\chi|}$ possible branches subtending exactly $|\chi|$ tips. This provides a simple criterion to show inconsistency: if there exist two topologies $\psi, \psi^{\prime} \in \mathbb{T}_{n}$ such that

$$
C(\psi \mid \star)<C\left(\psi^{\prime} \mid \star\right)
$$

then, owing to the continuity of $C(\psi \mid \sigma)$ as a function of $\boldsymbol{x}$, the concatenated counting estimator will always prefer $\psi$ over $\psi^{\prime}$ for sufficiently short branch lengths $\boldsymbol{x}$, even if the true species topology is $\psi_{*}=\psi^{\prime}$.

question: How large is the surface footprint scanned by the GEDI instrument?
answer: The surface footprint scanned by the GEDI instrument is 25 meters.

evidence.text:
### 8.5 GEDI AGB Estimates

The GEDI instrument uses a LiDAR laser to repeatedly scan a 25 m surface footprint, where each measurement consists of a waveform from the laser's returned signal. From the cumulative return energy, the GEDI team identifies the ground return, which is used as the reference for the relative height (RH) metrics. The RH[X] metrics correspond to the relative height at which [X] percent of the total accumulated energy is returned. From the RH metrics, the GEDI team estimates biomass. To do so, they developed their own allometric equations, based on the Plant Functional Type (PFT), the region of the world, and the RH metrics. In order to calibrate them, they leveraged world-wide crowd-sourced data. Coincident airborne LiDAR and ground plot field inventory were put together. The airborne LiDAR data was used to simulate GEDI-like waveforms and derived RH metrics. These simulated RH metrics were then used to calibrate the biomass equations with the field biomass values as reference data. Further information can be found in the Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document[33].

question: How do behavioral expectations compare to rational expectations in modeling India's output gap during the COVID-19 recovery?
answer: Behavioral expectations align more closely with the actual Indian output gap data, which is characterized by negative skewness and high kurtosis. In contrast, rational expectations produce unrealistic positive skewness and lower kurtosis values, failing to capture the non-normality observed in real data.

evidence.text:
## 4 Results
### 4.1 Behavioral Expectations vs Rational Expectations: Analysis of Output Gap Moments in India

Table 2 compares the statistical moments of the simulated output gap data under rational and behavioral expectations with the actual Indian output gap data ${ }^{7}$. We find

Table 2: Comparison of Moments for Expectation Formation Models and Real Data

![table_1](table_1)

that the actual output gap data, derived using both the Kalman filter and the HP filter, reveal significant non-normality characterized by negative skewness and high kurtosis. Specifically, the Kalman output gap exhibits a skewness of -1.48 and kurtosis of 9.12 ,

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{6}$ See, Goyel and Arora (2016) for a similar analysis using the HP and Kalman filter to estimate the potential GDP of India.
    ${ }^{7}$ we apply identical shocks to both models.

while the HP output gap closely mirrors these values with a skewness of -1.45 and kurtosis of 9.32. In contrast, the simulated behavioral expectations, with a skewness of -0.23 and kurtosis of 1.58 , align more closely with the actual output gap data than the rational expectations model. The latter generates highly unrealistic moments, including a positive skewness of 0.56 and a kurtosis of 2.90 , suggesting that rational expectations fail to replicate the complex patterns observed in actual output gap data.

To further assess the statistical moments of these models, we perform normality tests such as the Jarque-Bera (JB) test. The results show that the actual Kalman and HP output gaps are definitively non-normal, as evidenced by p-values less than 0.001 . The behavioral expectations model exhibits non-normality, with a p-value less than 0.05 . On the other hand, the rational expectations model produces normal output gap data with a p-value greater than 0.05 , underscoring its limitations in capturing the non-normality of the output gap data for India.

From the above analysis, it is evident that behavioral expectations outperform rational expectations in representing India's output gap. This replicates the seminal work of De Grauwe (2012) for the US economy.

question: What is the role of symmetric matrices in algebraic K-theory with involution?
answer: Symmetric matrices in algebraic K-theory with involution are used to form fixed points under a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$ action, which are crucial for constructing classifying spaces and group-completions relevant to KR-theory.

evidence.text:
# A The trace map for rings with involution 

Let us finish the paper with a construction of a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant lift of the trace map tr: $\mathrm{K} \rightarrow$ $\mathrm{TC}(-; p)$, for every prime $p$. The trace was first constructed by Bökstedt-Hsiang-Madsen in [BHM93] as a natural transformation $\mathrm{K} \rightarrow \mathrm{TC}$ on the category of ring spectra. This construction has been extended to various settings, most notably as a natural transformation of functors from stable infinity categories, see e.g. [BGT14].

A $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant extension of this map as a natural transformation $\mathrm{KR} \rightarrow \mathrm{TCR}$ of functors from Poincaré categories will appear in forthcoming work of Harpaz-Nikolaus-Shah [HNS21]. For the purpose of this article, it will be more than sufficient to define the $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant trace map on the category of discrete rings with involution. We will give a construction in line with the construction of the Dennis trace as carried out in [Mad94, §2.6]. After restricting down to THR this construction agrees with the one from [DO19], which was defined for ring spectra with involution.

Let $A$ be a ring with involution $w: A^{v p} \rightarrow A$, and $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ the group of invertible $n \times n$ matrices with the involution that sends $M$ to $M^{*}:=w(M)^{T}$, where $(-)^{T}$ denotes the matrix transposition and $w$ is applied to $M$ entrywise. The set of fixed points of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ is the set of symmetric matrices

$$
\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}=\left\{M \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(k) \mid M^{*}=M\right\}
$$

and $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ acts on it by $g \cdot M=g M g^{*}$. We let $B^{\sigma} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ be the classifying space $B \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ with the involution of [BF84, Proposition 1.1.3]. Its $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-fixed-points space is the bar construction of the action of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ on $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$ above (see also [DO19, §2.1] for the details). For the purpose of this paper, we define $\operatorname{KR}(A)$ to be the $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant group-completion of the $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant $E_{\infty}$-monoid with involution

$$
\coprod_{n \geq 0} B^{\sigma} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)
$$

where the monoid operation is induced by the direct sum of matrices. This is in fact the classifying space of the symmetric monoidal category with duality of finite dimensional free $A$ modules, and therefore indeed a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant $E_{\infty}$-monoid. By construction, $\pi_{0}\left(\operatorname{KR}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right)$ is the group-completion of the commutative monoid

$$
\coprod_{n \geq 0} \pi_{0}\left(\left(B^{\sigma} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)\right)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \cong \coprod_{n \geq 0} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} / \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)
$$

which is the Grothendieck-Witt group $\mathrm{GW}^{*}(A)$ of symmetric forms of free $A$-modules. The transfer map is induced by the functor that sends a free module of rank $n$ to the hyperbolic matrix of size $2 n$, and therefore $\pi_{0}\left(\operatorname{KR}(A)^{\# \mathbb{Z} / 2}\right)$ is the symmetric Witt group $W^{s}(A)$ (again of free $A$-modules).

Let us also recall from [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1] that there is an isomorphism of abelian groups

$$
\pi_{0}\left(\operatorname{THR}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \cong\left(A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T
$$

where $A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$ is the subgroup of fixed points of the involution $w$, and the quotient is by the subgroup $T$ generated by the elements of the form (i) and (ii) from [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1]. In particular, for $A=k$ a ring of characteristic 2 with trivial involution, this is $k \otimes_{S} k$, and since the transfer map $(a+w(a)) \otimes 1$ of [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1] is in this case zero, we have as well that $\pi_{0}(\operatorname{THR}(k)^{\phi \mathbb{Z} / 2}) \cong k \otimes_{S} k$.
Proposition A.1. Let $A$ be a ring with involution. For every prime $p$, there is a map of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$ spectra $\operatorname{tr}: \mathrm{KR}(A) \rightarrow \operatorname{TCR}(A ; p)$ which forgets to the $K$-theoretic trace map of [BHM93]. The composite

$$
\mathrm{GW}^{s}(A)=\pi_{0}\left(\mathrm{KR}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{tr}} \pi_{0}\left(\operatorname{TCR}(A ; 2)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \xrightarrow{R} \pi_{0}\left(\operatorname{THR}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \cong\left(A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T
$$

sends the element of $\mathrm{GW}^{s}(A)$ represented by a symmetric form $x$ on $A^{\otimes n}$ to

$$
\operatorname{tr}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\left(x^{-1}\right)_{i i} \otimes x_{i i}-\left(x^{-1}\right)_{i i} x_{i i} \otimes 1\right)+n \otimes 1
$$

where $x_{i i}$ are the entries of the matrix of $x$ for the standard basis of $A^{\otimes n}$, and $x^{-1}$ denotes the inverse matrix.

Proof. We construct the trace by employing a construction completely analogous to the one from Dennis and Bökstedt-Hsiang-Madsen, as explained in [Mad94, §2.6]. Let $B^{d i} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ be the dihedral bar construction of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$, defined as the geometric realisation of the dihedral nerve $N^{d i} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$, which is the cyclic nerve of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ with the involution analogous to the one of $\operatorname{THR}(k)$ from $\S 1$. Its $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-fixed-points space is the two-sided bar construction of the action of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ on $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$, and we refer to [DO19, §2.1] for the details.

We define the trace map from maps of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spaces

$$
B^{\sigma} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A) \xrightarrow{\star} B^{d i} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A) \rightarrow B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A) \rightarrow \Omega^{\infty}\left(\operatorname{THR}\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}}\right) \stackrel{m}{=} \Omega^{\infty}\left(\operatorname{THR}(A)^{C_{r}}\right)
$$

for every $r \geq 1$, by taking the disjoint union over $n \geq 0$ and group-completing the source with respect to direct sums. The maps in this composite are defined as follows. The map $s$ is the canonical section, which is defined on an $n$-simplex $\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}\right)$ by

$$
s\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}\right)=\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{n}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}\right)
$$

The second map of (9) is the inclusion of invertible matrices into the monoid of all $(n \times n)$-matrices $\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$, again with the transposition of matrices and entrywise $w$ as involution. For the third map, we use that $B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$ is the geometric realisation of the dihedral nerve $N^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$, and therefore has an action of the dihedral group $D_{r}$ of order $2 r$, for every integer $r \geq 1$. The realisation of the $r$-subdivision $\mathrm{sd}_{r}$ of [BHM93, §1] applied to the dihedral nerve $N^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$ has a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-action, and its geometric realisation is $D_{r}$-equivariantly isomorphic to $B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$ (see [DMP24, §1.2] for a detailed discussion about subdivisions of dihedral objects). Thus, we obtain $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant isomorphisms

$$
B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A) \xrightarrow{\Delta_{r}} \mid\left(\operatorname{sd}_{r} N^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}} \mid \xrightarrow{E_{r}} \left(B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}}
$$

where the first map is induced by the diagonal map degreewise, and the second map is the canonical isomorphism $E_{r} \cdot\left|\operatorname{sd}_{r} X\right| \rightarrow|X|$ for a dihedral set $X$, from [BHM93, Lemma 1.1] (which is denoted by $D_{r}$ there). By denoting $\Delta^{k}$ the standard $k$-simplex space

$$
\Delta^{k}:=\left\{\left(t_{0}, \ldots, t_{k}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1} \mid t_{0}+t_{1}+\cdots+t_{k}=1, t_{i} \geq 0 \text { for all } 0 \leq i \leq k\right\}
$$

the map $E_{r}$ sends the equivalence class of $(x ; t)$, with $x \in\left(\operatorname{sd}_{r} X\right)_{k}=X_{r(k+1)-1}$ and $t \in \Delta^{k}$, to the class of $\left(x ; \delta_{r}(t)\right)$, where $\delta_{r}: \Delta^{k} \rightarrow \Delta^{r(k+1)-1}$ sends $t$ to $(t, \ldots, t) / r$ (with $r$-many components). The third map of (9) is then defined to be the adjoint of the composite of the maps of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spectra

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma_{r}^{\mathrm{ac}} B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A) \xrightarrow{\Sigma_{r}^{\mathrm{ac}}\left(E_{r} \Delta_{r}\right)} \Sigma_{s}^{\mathrm{ac}}\left(B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}} \longrightarrow\left(\Sigma_{r}^{\mathrm{ac}} B^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{~S}}\left(B^{d i} \Sigma_{s}^{\mathrm{ac}} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}} \\
& \mathrm{THR}\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}} \stackrel{\times}{\longleftrightarrow}\left(B^{d i} \mathrm{H} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)^{C_{r}}
\end{aligned}
$$

which are respectively $\Sigma_{r}^{\mathrm{ac}}\left(E_{r} \Delta_{r}\right)$, the tom Dieck splitting, the monoidality of the equivariant suspension spectrum functor, and the Hurewicz map. Finally, the last map of (9) is induced by the inclusion of $A$ into $\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$ as $(1,1)$-entry, and it is a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivalence by [DMPR21, Theorem 4.9] (which visibly restricts to $C_{r}$-fixed points).

A direct verification shows that the map of (9) is compatible with the direct sum of matrices and with its symmetry isomorphism, and therefore by setting $r=p^{m-1}$ we obtain a map of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spectra

$$
\operatorname{tr}^{m}: \operatorname{KR}(A) \longrightarrow \operatorname{THR}(A)^{C_{p^{m-1}}}=\operatorname{TRR}^{m}(A ; p)
$$

for every integer $m \geq 1$ and prime $p$. To obtain a map to $\operatorname{TCR}(A ; p)$ we need to show that the maps $\operatorname{tr}^{m}$ are compatible with the restriction and Frobenius $R, F: \operatorname{TRR}^{m+1}(A ; p) \rightarrow \operatorname{TRR}^{m}(A ; p)$. Unravelling the definitions, it is sufficient to provide $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant homotopies between the composites from the bottom left to the bottom right $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spaces of the diagram
![img-15.jpeg](img-15.jpeg)

The vertical map $R$ is defined by identifying the $C_{p}$-fixed points of the $p^{m}$-fold subdivision with the $p^{m-1}$-fold subdivision, and then taking $C_{p^{m-1}}$-fixed points. It follows from [BHM93, (1.12)] that the inner most triangle commutes strictly. The vertical map $F$ is the inclusion of fixed points. To see how the outer triangle commutes when restricted along $s$, we decompose the diagram as
![img-16.jpeg](img-16.jpeg)
where the unlabelled map is the inclusion of fixed points. The lower right triangle commutes by [BHM93, (1.12)], and the square above it by naturality of the inclusion of fixed points. We then need to define a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant homotopy that makes the the triangle on the left commute when restricted along $s$. By factoring $\Delta_{p^{m}}=\Delta_{p^{m-1}}+\Delta_{p}$, it is sufficient to treat the case where $m=1$. The homotopy provided in [BHM93, Proposition 2.5] is not quite $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant, but we can use a small variation of it. Let us define $h_{k}: \Delta^{k} \times[0,1] \rightarrow \Delta^{p(k+1)-1}$ for every $k \geq 0$, by

$$
h(t, s)=(s t / p+(1-s) t, \ldots, s t / p, s t / p)
$$

where the right-hand side has $p$ components. If we apply the subdivision $\mathrm{sd}_{r}$ as in [DMP24, $\S 1.2]$ to make the $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-actions on the spaces of the diagram simplicial, the upper composite sends

the equivalence class of $\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1} ; t\right)$, with $\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right)$ a $k$-simplex of $\operatorname{sd}_{e} N^{\sigma} \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ and $t \in \Delta^{k}$, to the equivalence class of

$$
\left(\Delta_{p}\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right) ; \delta_{p}(t)\right)
$$

The lower composite is simply the functor $\mathrm{sd}_{e}$ applied to the section $s$. Thus by sending the same equivalence class to the class of $\left(\Delta_{p}\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right) ; h_{k}(s, t)\right)$, we obtain a $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-equivariant homotopy from the upper composite to

$$
\left[\Delta_{p}\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right) ; t, 0, \ldots, 0\right]=\left[d_{l}^{(k+1)(p-1)} \Delta_{p}\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right) ; t\right]
$$

where each 0 on the left is the zero vertex of $\Delta^{k}$, and $d_{l}$ is the last face map of $\operatorname{sd}_{e} N^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$. Since this last face map multiplies the central three components $a_{q}, a_{q+1}$ and $a_{q+2}$ of a $q$-simplex $\left(a_{0}, \ldots, a_{2 q+1}\right)$ of $\operatorname{sd}_{e} N^{d i} \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$, we find that, by denoting $g_{0}:=\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}$,
$d_{l}^{(k+1)(p-1)} \Delta_{p}\left(g_{0}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right)=\left(g_{0}, \ldots, g_{k},\left(g_{k+1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\left(g_{0} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{p-2} g_{0} \ldots g_{k+1}\right), g_{k+2}, \ldots, g_{2 k+1}\right)$.
The middle entry is equal to $g_{k+1}$ since $g_{0}=\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{2 k+1}\right)^{-1}$, and it follows that the end of the homotopy is indeed the subdivision of $s$. We can therefore lift $\operatorname{tr}^{m}$ along $R$ and $F$ to obtain a map of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spectra $\operatorname{tr} \operatorname{KR}(A) \rightarrow \operatorname{TCR}(A ; p)$, for every prime $p$.

Let us now identify the effect of the trace in $\pi_{0}$ of the fixed points. By construction, if we compose $\operatorname{tr}$ with the map $R$ all the way to $\operatorname{THR}(A)$ we recover the map $\operatorname{tr}^{0}: \operatorname{KR}(A) \rightarrow \operatorname{THR}(A)$. Thus for this calculation, we need to describe the map (9) for $r=1$. On fixed points, the map $s$ is the map of bar constructions

$$
B\left(\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A) ; \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) \xrightarrow{s} B\left(\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} ; \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A) ; \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right)
$$

which sends a $k$-simplex $\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{k}, x\right)$, with $g_{i} \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$ and $x \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$, to

$$
s\left(g_{1}, \ldots, g_{k}, x\right)=\left(\left(g_{1} \ldots g_{k} x g_{k}^{*} \ldots g_{1}^{*}\right)^{-1}, g_{1}, \ldots, g_{k}, x\right)
$$

where $(-)^{*}$ denotes the involution on $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$. Thus, after applying $\pi_{0}$ and identifying the components of THR using [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1], the map of (9) becomes a map
$\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} f_{-} \xrightarrow{s}\left(\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \rtimes \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) f_{-} \rightarrow\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T \stackrel{m}{\cong}\left(A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T$,
where the quotients on the two sets on the left are for the respective actions of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)$. By the calculation of $s$ above, this map sends the isomorphism class of a form of rank $n$, represented by a matrix $x \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$, to $m\left(x^{-1} \otimes x\right)$. For the proof of Theorem 3.9 we were only interested in rank 1 forms (since these generate the Witt group of a field), and since for $n=1$ the map $m$ is the identity, we immediately find that the class of a symmetric form determined by a unit $a$ of $A$ fixed by the involution is sent to $a^{-1} \otimes a$.

For larger values of $n$ we need to determine the isomorphism

$$
m:\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T \xrightarrow{\circ}\left(A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T
$$

Let us decompose a symmetric matrix $M \in \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$ as $M=\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n}\left(M_{i j} e_{i j}+\right.$ $\left.w\left(M_{i j}\right) e_{j i}\right)$ where $e_{i j}$ is the canonical basis element with 1 in the entry $(i, j)$ and with all the other entries equal to zero. By regarding the abelian group with involution $\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)$ as a Mackey functor, we can then write the fixed point $M$ as

$$
M=\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{i j} e_{i j}\right)
$$

where tran denotes the transfer map of the Mackey functor, which sends a matrix $N$ to $N+N^{*}$. By applying the same decomposition to a second fixed point $M^{\prime} \in \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
M^{\prime} \otimes M & =\sum_{l, i=1}^{n} M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} \otimes M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{l=1}^{n} \sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} \otimes \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{i j} e_{i j}\right) \\
& +\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} e_{l k}\right) \otimes M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n}^{n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} e_{l k}\right) \otimes \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{i j} e_{i j}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

By the relation (ii) of [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1] defining the subgroup $T$, this is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}
M^{\prime} \otimes M & =\sum_{l, i=1}^{n} M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} \otimes M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{l=1}^{n} \sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} M_{i j} e_{i j}\right) \otimes 1 \\
& +\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 \otimes \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} e_{l k} M_{i i} e_{i i}\right)+\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} e_{l k}\left(M_{i j} e_{i j}+w\left(M_{i j}\right) e_{j i}\right)\right) \otimes 1 \\
& =\sum_{l, i=1}^{n} M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} \otimes M_{i i} e_{i i}+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{i i}^{\prime} M_{i j} e_{i j}\right) \otimes 1+\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} 1 \otimes \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} M_{k k} e_{l k}\right) \\
& +\sum_{1 \leq l<k<j \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} M_{k j} e_{l j}\right) \otimes 1+\sum_{1 \leq l, i<k \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} w\left(M_{i k}\right) e_{l i}\right) \otimes 1
\end{aligned}
$$

where the last equality follows from carrying out the matrix multiplication on the canonical basis. Again by [DMPR21, Theorem 5.1], the transfer map of the Mackey functor $\underline{Z}_{0} \operatorname{THR}\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right)$ sends the equivalence class of a matrix $M$ in $\pi_{0} \operatorname{THH}\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right) \cong \mathrm{M}_{n}(A) /\left[\mathrm{M}_{n}(A), \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)\right]$, to $1 \otimes \operatorname{tran}(M)=\operatorname{tran}(M) \otimes 1$ in $\left(\mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes \mathrm{M}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T$. The map $m$ from [DMPR21, Theorem 4.9] is a map of $\mathbb{Z} / 2$-spectra, and therefore it commutes with the transfer. Moreover, since the underlying map of spectra is the trace map of [BHM93], in $\pi_{0}$ it sends a matrix to its trace, and therefore the terms involving $e_{i j}$ vanish for $i \neq j$. We then find that

$$
m\left(M^{\prime} \otimes M\right)=\sum_{l, i=1}^{n} m\left(M_{l l}^{\prime} e_{l l} \otimes M_{i i} e_{i i}\right)+\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} w\left(M_{l k}\right)\right) \otimes 1
$$

in $\left(A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2} \otimes A^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}\right) / T$. By the definition of $m$ of [DMPR21, Proof of Theorem 4.9], it sends $e_{i j} \otimes e_{l k}$ to 1 if $j=l$ and $k=i$, and to zero otherwise. Thus

$$
m\left(M^{\prime} \otimes M\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i i}^{\prime} \otimes M_{i i}+\sum_{1 \leq l<k \leq n} \operatorname{tran}\left(M_{l k}^{\prime} w\left(M_{l k}\right)\right) \otimes 1
$$

Since $M$ is symmetric, i.e. $w\left(M_{l k}\right)=M_{k l}$, we may write this expression as

$$
m\left(M^{\prime} \otimes M\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i i}^{\prime} \otimes M_{i i}+\operatorname{tr}\left(M^{\prime} M\right) \otimes 1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i i}^{\prime} M_{i i} \otimes 1
$$

where $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the usual trace of a matrix. When $M^{\prime} \otimes M=x^{-1} \otimes x$ for some $x \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(A)^{\mathbb{Z} / 2}$, this gives the formula we wanted.

question: Is antifermion necessary when $\boldsymbol{p}^{2} \rightarrow \infty$?
answer: No, antifermion is not needed when $\boldsymbol{p}^{2} \rightarrow \infty$.

evidence.text:
# II. TIME DIRECTION IN RELATIVISTIC VIRTUAL MASSLESS FERMIONS 

Consider the second-order perturbation process of a moving massless Dirac fermion under disturbances in Figure.2(a). There are two disturbances, $U_{1}$ in $A$ at a time $t_{1}$, and $U_{2}$ in $B$ at a later time $t_{2}$, in which the second disturbance $U_{2}$ restore the fermion to its original state with a momentum $\boldsymbol{p}$. Such an amplitude is calculated by summing all possible, timelike or spacelike, intermediate states between $A$ and $B$ over their momenta $\boldsymbol{p}^{\prime}$. Suppose that in the inertial system of a coordinate $(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$, a fermion with a negative electric charge and momentum $\boldsymbol{p}$ leave $A$ at $x_{1}$ and $t_{1}$, and reach $B$ at $x_{2}$ and $t_{2}\left(>t_{1}\right)$. When this motion is viewed from another inertial system moving in the $x$-direction at a relative velocity $v$ to the original one, it follows a Lorentz transformation to a new coordinates $\left(\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}, t^{\prime}\right)$. The time

difference $t_{2}-t_{1}$ between $A$ and $B$ is Lorentz transformed to

$$
t_{2}^{\prime}-t_{1}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v / c)^{2}}}\left[t_{2}-t_{1}-\frac{v}{c^{2}}\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)\right]
$$

For events on the spacelike path, the Lorentz transformation does not leave the temporal order invariant. When the fermion has a small velocity, the observer has more options of a large or small relative velocity $v$ to the fermion. A sufficiently large spacelike interval between two events, such as $c\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)<(v / c)\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)$ in Eq.(4), reverses the temporal order of two events, $t_{2}^{\prime}<t_{1}^{\prime}$ as shown in Figure.2(b). The natural interpretation of such situations is that a positively-charged antifermion runs in the opposite spatial direction without the reversal of temporal order. Hence, either an annihilation of massless fermion in Figure.2(a), or a creation of massless antifermion in Figure.2(b) is observed at $A$, according to the choice of inertial frame that the observer sits on.

When the virtual many-body state is formulated, antifermion should be used so that the time direction in every particle is not reversed even if it is viewed by any observer [14]. Momentum, electric charge and spin, which prescribe all properties of massless fermion, are not positive definite, and therefore the effect of annihilation operator $a^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})$ on the state in Figure.2(a) is equivalent to that of creation operator $b^{s \dagger}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ on the state in Figure.2(b). To derive the state ensuring this equivalence, a new operator $\widetilde{a}^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})$ is defined so as to derive such a state as its eigenstate,

$$
\widetilde{a}^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})=\cos \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}} a^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})+\sin \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}} b^{s \dagger}(-\boldsymbol{p})
$$

If the fermion is massive, the creation and annihilation cause different effects on the state because mass is positive definite, and their superposition is impossible. Hence, this superposition is possible only for the massless fermion in the primitive world. The necessity of antifermion changes according to the relative velocity between the incident particle and the observer, which is reflected in $\sin \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}}$. When $\boldsymbol{p}=0$, the difference between $a^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})$ and $b^{s \dagger}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ in momentum vanishes. Therefore, the number of observers for whom the process of Figure.2(a) and (b) have the same probability increases as $\boldsymbol{p} \rightarrow 0$, resulting in $\cos \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}}=\sin \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}}$ at $\boldsymbol{p}=0$. On the contrary, when $\boldsymbol{p}^{2} \rightarrow \infty$, such observers cannot be found, and antifermion is not needed. Hence, $\sin \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}} \rightarrow 0$ is expected.

The same interpretation is possible also for the event at $B$ in Figure.2. Another new operator $\widetilde{b}^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ is defined as a superposition of the annihilation $b^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ of massless antifermion

in Figure.2(b), and the creation $a^{s \dagger}(\boldsymbol{p})$ of massless fermion in 2(a)

$$
\widetilde{b}^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})=\cos \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}} b^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})-\sin \theta_{\boldsymbol{p}} a^{s \dagger}(\boldsymbol{p})
$$

This $\widetilde{b}^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ is orthogonal to $\widetilde{a}^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})$ [15]. These $\widetilde{a}^{s}\left(\boldsymbol{p}^{\prime}\right)$ and $\widetilde{b}^{s}\left(-\boldsymbol{p}^{\prime}\right)$ are useful not only for the two-body state, but also for general many-body states. Among various virtual many-body states, these superposed operators define the lowest-energy one $|\widetilde{0}\rangle$ by imposing $\widetilde{a}^{s}(\boldsymbol{p})|\widetilde{0}\rangle=\widetilde{b}^{s}(-\boldsymbol{p})|\widetilde{0}\rangle=0$ on it. This lowest-energy state implies physical vacuum.

question: How do different amplifier structures compare in terms of precision and application suitability?
answer: Different amplifier structures have varying strengths; TIA offers high precision due to its low input burden voltage but requires precise resistors. Shunt amplifiers are simpler and cost-effective but less precise. Integrating-differentiating structures achieve low noise but may introduce nonlinearity errors affecting DC measurements' stability.

evidence.text:
## 1 Introduction

Accurate measurement of small currents ranging from femtoamperes to nanoamperes is essential in radionuclide metrology. In the process of activity determinations, a factor that often restricts the uncertainty lies in the measurement of the ionization current[1]. In recent years, picoamperemeters (picoammeters) have attained higher levels of precision and have been widely applied in various fields, including fundamental metrology [2], physical experiments [3], and biosensors[4]. In the National Institute of Metrology (NIM), China, researchers are dedicated to improving the $4 \pi \gamma$ ionization chamber (IC) radioactivity standard, thereby raising the demand for high-precision picoammeters.

The ultra-stable low-noise current amplifier (ULCA), based on the feedback trans-impedance amplifier (TIA) structure, was introduced by the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB). Its key element, the resistor array, provides very stable amplification gain, enabling achievement of the state-of-the-art uncertainty of 0.1 ppm in 100 pA [5]. The well-known commercial electrometers Keithley model 6430 and Keysight model B2980 both employed TIA to amplify small currents, and they have multiple ranges and functionalities to support different scenarios [6, 7]. The TIA structure is relatively mature and precise, and it's widely applied in recent researches [8-10]. However, limited by the precision resistor techniques, large resistors providing high gain are basically less precise and less stable. In comparison with another structure known as the shunt amplifier, the TIA structure can be more precise for its low input burden voltage, but the shunt type is more commonly seen in portable multi-meters because its simpler circuit and lower cost [3, 11]. Certain studies adopted the integrating-differentiating (int-diff) structure to achieve the least noise level by replacing the TIA's noisy feedback resistor with a capacitor in the integrating stage (integrator) [4, 12]. Other than ultra-low noise performance, this structure can also accomplish high bandwidth that more than 100 kHz [13]. However, its drawbacks are as follows: the capacitor significantly influences

the precision and stability of the gain as well as the analog differentiating stage can introduce nonlinearity errors. Thus previous researches on this kind of amplifiers seldom took into account the stability and precision for DC measurements [4].

In our previous work [14], we proposed a precise small currents measurement system (SCMS). This system is based on the int-diff method to achieve low noise. It integrates the direct current (dc) in the analog amplification circuit and differentiates it in a field programmable gate array (FPGA) to restore a dc output. The analog circuit combines careful circuit design and techniques. For instance, by means of the averaging effect of the integrating capacitor array, we took stability into considerations.

In this paper, we further optimized the design of the SCMS through analysis and simulation, and conducted more comprehensive tests. The capacitor array structure was optimized through simulations to suppress gain errors due to parasitic capacitance. The leakage current performance of the SCMS was analyzed and optimized. We replaced the CMOS-based switches with a reed relay, and observed improved noise and leakage performance. Additionally, the host software of the SCMS is upgraded to enhance its functionality. We also developed different test platforms utilizing the standard small current source equipment at NIM China and a $4 \pi \gamma$ IC to evaluate various performance indicators of the SCMS. The test results exhibit an ultra-low noise floor ( $<1 \mathrm{fA} / \sqrt{ } \mathrm{Hz}$ ), a fA-level current bias, a low temperature coefficient ( $2.1 \mathrm{ppm} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), short-term stability and linearity comparable to those of the Keithley 6430, as well as reasonable long-term reproducibility for an IC application.

The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, the architecture of the SCMS is introduced, with a primary focus on the optimizations made to its design. Section 3 presents the test setups devised for evaluating noise and stability performances and provides an analysis of the test results. Section 4 concludes the paper.

question: Why is there a need for an On-Chain Credit Risk Score in DeFi?
answer: An On-Chain Credit Risk Score (OCCR Score) is needed in DeFi to provide an objective measure of a wallet's creditworthiness by integrating historical performance with current status and future predictions. This score helps quantify the probability of default when opening borrow positions within the ecosystem, enabling more informed lending decisions based on data-driven risk assessments.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

The ongoing digital revolution is driving a profound transformation in the financial sector. A key development in this evolution is decentralized finance ( DeFi ), which uses blockchain technology to facilitate open and permissionless financial services (Sahu and Kumar, 2024). DeFi signifies a paradigm shift in financial systems that reshapes the future of global finance. DeFi provides financial services without the intervention of any centralized intermediaries. They operate mainly as automated protocols on a blockchain (Doerr et al., 2021). Although much more new in concept, DeFi is a fast-growing market for quick and safe interaction between lenders and borrowers. It is one of the best ways to seamlessly perform verifiable cross-border transactions in a much faster way compared to Traditional Finance. Numerous avenues can be explored to make DeFi more robust and capital-efficient. However, for such explorations, we need to understand the creditworthiness of each user. It should be noted that 'user' means the specific wallet interacting with the DeFi ecosystem, and in this article, user and wallet are used interchangeably.

Unlike conventional credit scoring, which depends on centralized credit bureaus and financial history of an user, DeFi credit scoring leverages on-chain data and smart contract interactions to evaluate an user's borrowing and repayment behavior. Credit risk scoring is a systematic process used to assess the risk involved in a user's creditworthiness by analyzing their on-chain transaction history, repayment behavior, outstanding liabilities, and other relevant economic indicators. This analytical approach enables financial institutions to quantify the probability of default, facilitating data-driven risk assessment and informed lending decisions (Moghe and Johri, n.d.). An 'On-Chain Credit Risk Score (OCCR Score)' for a wallet might be an answer to quantifying the credit risk of the particular wallet in DeFi ecosystem. Through the OCCR Score of a wallet, we have estimated the probability that the particular wallet may face liquidation when any borrow position is opened. Throughout the paper, we have used borrow positions and loans interchangeably.

There are different ways to give credit scores to users in the current TradFi landscape, but this is not very prevalent in DeFi. However, there have been previous attempts to measure the creditworthiness of a wallet, including those by Cred (CRED Protocol, n.d.), Credit Data Alliance (CreDA) (CreDA, 2022), Credit scoring of Aave accounts (Wolf et al., 2022) and Levon (Block Analitica, n.d.). The main limitation of these existing credit scoring models is the absence of a comprehensive framework that integrates historical, current, and future predictive scenarios. The Cred Protocol scoring model combines financial metrics such as loan history, account composition, account health, and new credit with qualitative factors such as ecosystem participation and attributes related to trust and transparency, which are described in a very vague way (Packin and Lev-Aretz, 2024). The CreDA credit scoring model relies heavily on social activity data, which could obscure more concrete financial indicators such as asset holdings, lending and borrowing behavior, and off-chain data (CreDA, 2022). This emphasis on decentralized social engagement raises concerns about the model's ability to provide a reliable and objective assessment of creditworthiness (Packin and Lev-Aretz, 2024). In addition, most of the existing scores take natural numbers on a variable scale. This scaling cannot be directly associated with a probability, which might make them subjective in nature. So, we have tried to develop a score that can bridge the three scenarios of historical, current, and predictive future and is equivalent to the probability of default for that particular wallet.

## C. Neural beamforming

The neural beamforming is the final stage of our proposed method, unlike the target sound extraction and precise tracking module, it is trained after the initial tracking and mutual facilitation.

The neural beamformer is trained on the refined multichannel signal $\mathbf{X}_{\text {sep2, } c}$ and intensity trajectory $\mathbf{I}_{-} \mathbf{t r a} \mathbf{j}_{\text {prec2, } c}$, as well as the signal mixture to utilize the multi-channel information and generate a cleaner single-channel signal. In this paper, the zeroth-order signal of the FOA signal is selected as the signal of the reference channel. The network of the neural beamformer is also based on SpatialNet with Mamba.
